    POST /dnd/play/session/{id}/mark — Annotate A Timeline Block

    Names one block of the timeline and says what happened there. The annotation is the one part of the timeline that is stored: everything else about a block is worked out from the logs each time it is drawn, and would go stale the moment a roll was corrected.

    Method: POST

    Body:

    Field Type Description
    time string The clock the block starts at (HH:MM). Required.
    kind string What sort of block - fight, note, rolls, roll.
    title string What to call it. "Ambush at the ford".
    note string Anything worth saying about it, org markup, as typed.

    The time and the kind together are the anchor, so annotating the same block twice rewrites the annotation rather than leaving two of them. One of title or note is required - an annotation with neither is a deletion, which is the DELETE.

    An annotation is written as an entry under a * Timeline heading in the session file, tagged with its kind, so it reads as ordinary org and can be edited there.

    An anchor that matches no block is not an error. The annotation is drawn as a beat of its own at the time it carries, which is what lets a moment nobody rolled for - the room, the door, who was waiting behind it - be written on the timeline at all.

    Response: The session, read back in full.

    POST /dnd/play/session/{id}/undo — Take The Last Change To This Session Back

    Puts one session file back as it stood before the last change this server made to it. A whole timeline block thrown away comes back in one press, because throwing it away was one write.

    Method: POST

    Response: The session read back in full, with undone saying what was taken back and undo saying what pressing it again would do.

    Only the newest change to that file is ever offered, and only while the file is still exactly as that change left it. Anything else - another window, the command line, a text editor - and putting the old text back would throw that away, so the call is refused with a 400 rather than guessing.

    POST /dnd/random — Roll a Complete Character

    Generates a finished character without any interaction. Handy for NPCs, for filling a table with pregenerated characters, or for seeing what the module can do.

    Method: POST

    Body: NewSessionRequest, all fields optional:

    {"ruleset": "srd", "level": 5, "name": "Bandit Captain"}

    Response: SaveResponse shaped object containing the rendered org text, with the computed sheet under sheet.

    POST /dnd/refresh — Regenerate the Derived Sections of a Sheet

    Reads a character sheet, recomputes everything and writes it back. Use this after editing the property drawer by hand: change DND_CLASSES to wizard:evocation:4 and refresh, and the skills, attacks, hit points, spell slots and feature list all catch up.

    Method: POST

    Body:

    {"filename": "lyra.org"}

    Response: SaveResponse containing the rewritten org text.

    POST /dnd/reload — Reload D&D Ruleset Modules

    Rereads every yaml module on the dnd search path. Use this after editing homebrew content instead of restarting the server.

    Method: POST

    Response: The refreshed ruleset list, exactly like GET /dnd/rulesets.

    POST /dnd/save — Write a Character Sheet to an Org File

    Writes a finished character out as an org file and loads it into the org database. Either pass a session id (the character being built) or a complete character.

    Method: POST

    Body: SaveRequest

    {"session": "6f1c...", "filename": "characters/lyra.org", "overwrite": false}

    A relative filename is resolved against the first configured orgDirs entry. Existing files are never clobbered unless overwrite is true.

    Response: SaveResponse with the absolute filename that was written.

    POST /dnd/session — Start Interactive Character Creation

    Opens a character build session and returns the first prompt. Every prompt carries the full list of valid choices, a short summary and a detail blurb for each one, plus advice based on what has been picked so far, so a client needs no rules knowledge of its own.

    Method: POST

    Body: NewSessionRequest

    {"ruleset": "srd", "name": "Lyra", "player": "Ian", "level": 3, "filename": "lyra.org"}

    Response: A Prompt:

    {
  "session": "6f1c...", "step": "class", "kind": "select",
  "title": "Class", "question": "Choose your class.",
  "options": [{"id": "wizard", "name": "Wizard", "summary": "...", "recommended": false}],
  "progress": {"step": 2, "total": 24}
}

    The kind field tells the client what widget to use: select, multiselect, text, longtext, number, abilities, fields or done.

    A fields prompt carries one Field per line of the answer, and the answer posts one entry in values per field, in the same order. Each field names the kind of value it holds, may carry options to suggest and min / max to bound it, and allowCustom says whether anything outside the suggestions is accepted. The bounds are checked again on the way in, so a client that skips the check gets a 400 with the reason rather than a character with 44 for an eye colour.

    POST /dnd/sounds/cache — Keep a Sound from the Web

    Downloads a web sound into the sound folder's cache/<service>/, and notes where it came from, its licence and its author in cache/sounds.json. A sound kept already is not fetched again.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {source, name, url, page, license, author, duration}, a sound as GET /dnd/sounds/search gives it.

    Response: {Ok, Msg, Path}, the sound's path in the sound folder; or, for a sound still downloading after fifteen seconds (a long recording), {Ok, Pending: true}: it goes on in the background, and asking again answers its path once it is kept.

    POST /dnd/undo — Take The Last Thing Back

    Reverses the last operation on a character sheet and writes the sheet back with the lines it wrote taken out of the history. An accident leaves no trace rather than leaving a correction.

    Method: POST

    Body:

    Field Type Required Description
    filename string no The org character sheet. One of filename or id is required.
    id string no The character's DND_ID. 
    {"id": "lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a"}

    Response: The InventoryState after the undo, with undone saying what was taken back, undo saying what pressing it again would do, and healthHistory carrying the Health History, since a line may have come off that too.

    There are two ways it can take something back. The first is a copy of the file as it stood before the change, kept in memory for the last thirty changes this server made (see dndjournal.go); that is what reaches the changes which deliberately write nothing down - an inventory line taken off the sheet as a correction, a note rewritten, a roll thrown away - and it reaches session files as well as character ones. The second, used when the journal has nothing to say, works the last operation out of the character's own history tables; that one survives a restart and works on a file something else changed.

    One operation, and only ever the last one. A potion drunk puts the potion back and the hit points with it; a purchase puts the coin back and takes the item away again. Where anything has happened since - a blow taken, a rest, an edit by hand - there is nothing safe to reverse and the call is refused with a 400 saying so, rather than guessing.

    POST /drill/review — Rate a Flashcard

    Records how well a card was remembered and schedules its next review, the way org-drill does: the DRILL_* properties are rewritten, SCHEDULED is set to the next review (or taken off, after a failure, so the card is asked again next session), and a card failed more often than the deck's leech threshold is tagged leech. Only the card's own lines change.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    {"hash": "hOpOB7vIg6oiYz5sMVSlzGiJXic=", "quality": 4, "deck": "Spanish"}

    quality is 0-5; at or below the deck's failure quality (2) is a failure.

    Response: {ok, msg, days, scheduled, data, leech, failed}.

    POST /ext/capture/template — Create or Update a User Capture Template

    Creates a new per-user capture template or updates an existing one (matched by name). The template is persisted to the extensions YAML file.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): A CaptureTemplate object.

    Field Type Required Description
    name string yes The template name (used for matching and display).
    type string no Entry type (e.g. entry).
    target Target no Where captured content should be filed.
    template string no Template text suggestion for the calling program.

    Response: A ResultMsg JSON object confirming the save.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if name is empty.

    POST /ext/drill/decks — Replace Every Flashcard Deck

    Writes the user's whole deck list at once, which is what adding, renaming, reordering and deleting all go through.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): An array of DrillDeck objects.

    Response: A ResultMsg. Refused when a deck has no name, two share one, or a deck has neither a query nor a saved search.

    POST /ext/gantt/views — Replace Every Saved Gantt View

    Writes the user's whole list of gantt views at once, which is what saving, renaming and deleting a view all go through.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): An array of GanttView objects.

    Response: A ResultMsg. Refused when a view has no name, two share one, or a view has neither a saved query nor a query of its own.

    POST /ext/kanban/board — Create or Update One Kanban Board

    Creates a board or replaces the one that already has its name, leaving the rest of the user's boards alone. Use POST /ext/kanban/boards to rename a board or change the order of the tabs.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): A KanbanBoard object. Only name is required; a board with no query shows no cards, and one with no columns offers to fill them in from whatever the query finds.

    Response: A ResultMsg JSON object confirming the save.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if the body is not a board, or name is empty.

    POST /ext/kanban/boards — Replace Every Kanban Board

    Writes the user's whole board list at once. This is what renaming a board and reordering the tabs go through: both change the list rather than one entry, and doing them as a delete followed by an add would leave the boards half written if the second call never arrived.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): An array of KanbanBoard objects, in tab order. An empty array removes every board.

    Response: A ResultMsg JSON object confirming the save.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if the body is not an array of boards, or a board has no name.

    POST /ext/query — Create or Update a Stored Query

    Creates a new stored query or updates an existing one (matched by name) for the authenticated user. The query is persisted to the extensions YAML file.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    Field Type Required Description
    name string yes The name for the stored query.
    query string yes The search expression to save.

    Response: A ResultMsg JSON object confirming the save.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if name or query is empty.

    POST /focus/extend — More Time

    Gives the phase under way more minutes. Answers the FocusState.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"Minutes": 5}; 5 when left out.

    POST /focus/skip — Skip Ahead

    Ends the phase under way as though its time were up. A work phase is finished early and counts as a pomodoro (clocked out, noted, break begins); a break is skipped and the next pomodoro starts on the same heading. Answers the FocusState.

    Method: POST

    POST /focus/start — Start a Pomodoro

    Clocks in on a heading and starts a work phase. When it runs out the server clocks out (writing the CLOCK: line), adds - Pomodoro: 25 min focus, 5 min break [stamp] to the heading's logbook, and starts a break; when the break runs out the session goes idle, or with AutoNext starts the next pomodoro. Every fourth break (LongEvery) is a long one. A session already running is ended first.

    The timer runs on the server and survives a restart. Stopping the clock or clocking into another heading from anywhere else stops the session.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    Field Type Required Description
    Hash string no The heading. With neither this nor Target, the last task.
    Target Target no The heading as a target (file+olp, id, …).
    Work number no Minutes of work. Fractions allowed.
    Short number no Minutes of a short break.
    Long number no Minutes of a long break.
    LongEvery int no Every how many pomodoros the break is long.
    AutoNext bool no Start the next pomodoro when a break ends.

    A field left out or zero keeps what was used last (25, 5, 15, 4, false at first), so every client starts with the same lengths.

    Response: The FocusState after the change. A refusal is the state with Ok: false and the reason in Msg, status 409.

    Events: focusstart, and later focusend, breakstart, breakend; focusstop when stopped early; focusextend when given more time. Each carries the heading's hash, headline and file.

    POST /focus/stop — Stop the Focus Session

    Ends the session now. A work phase is clocked out and remembered as not finished (no logbook note); a break simply ends. Answers the FocusState, or Ok: false when nothing is running.

    Method: POST

    POST /forge/sync — Poll GitHub and GitLab Now

    Runs every github and gitlab poller in server.plugins once, now, instead of waiting for its next tick: new items written, changed ones updated, headings marked DONE closed upstream. orgs forge sync calls it.

    Method: POST, no body.

    Response: A ForgeReply {Ok, Msg, Results}, a ForgeSync per poller:

    Field Meaning
    Name github or gitlab
    File, Url The org file it writes and the api it reads
    Ok, Msg Whether the poll worked, and why not (a rate limit, a bad token)
    Added, Updated Headings written for new items; headings changed
    Closed, Reopened, Gone Keyword changes that came from upstream
    Pushed Closes and reopens sent upstream
    Notes A line per thing worth telling a person

    POST /gantt/link — Make One Task Wait on Another

    Writes the dependency a gantt arrow stands for: AFTER on Task, naming After by its ID (or CUSTOM_ID). A heading with neither is given an ID first, made from its title and hash the way worg makes one. An ORDERED parent's chain is overridden (that is what AFTER on a step does), and the answer says so.

    Refused: a heading waiting on itself, on a heading it is part of, or on one that already waits (through any chain) on it; and a task whose AFTER already names another heading, because AFTER holds one: remove that first.

    With Remove, Task stops waiting on After: an AFTER naming it is cleared, and when the wait comes from an ORDERED parent (or clearing the AFTER would hand it straight back to such a chain) NOBLOCKING: t takes it out of the chain. Nothing is written when it did not wait on After.

    Both are line edits of the property drawers; no hash changes.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: A GanttLinkReq.

    Field Type Description
    Task string Hash of the heading that waits.
    After string Hash of the heading it waits on.
    Remove bool Take the dependency away instead of adding.

    Response: A ResultMsg: Ok, and Msg saying what was written.

    POST /gantt/marker — Add, Change or Delete a Marker

    A marker is a heading whose date a gantt view draws as a line down the chart (one day) or a band (a range of days). This writes one: a new heading, or the title, tags and date of an existing one, or deletes it. Only the heading's own lines are touched.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: A GanttMarkerEdit object.

    Field Type Description
    Hash string The marker to change or delete. Empty adds a new one.
    ParentHash string Add under this heading, as its last child.
    Filename string Or: add at the end of this file.
    Delete bool Delete the marker named by Hash.
    Headline string The title.
    Tags list Its tags, written when SetTags is true.
    Kind string "date" (its own timestamp) or "deadline".
    Start object {Date, Time, Until}: a day, an optional time and the end
    of a span within that day.
    End object The same for the last day of a range; absent for one day.
    Repeat string A repeater for the date, +1w, .+2d; empty for none.

    A range is written as <a>--<b>, and each end may be a span of its day, <2004-08-23 Mon 10:00-11:00>--<2004-08-26 Thu 10:00-11:00>. A repeater goes at the end of each stamp, <2026-10-05 Mon +1w>.

    Response: A ResultMsg.

    POST /gantt/suggest — Suggestions for Setting Up a Chart

    What a chart built from a query could be told that it is not yet, read from the tasks themselves and from finished work. Nothing is written: a client shows the suggestions, a person picks, and the picks are written with /gantt/link (dependencies) and /property (EFFORT, a lane property). The tasks are exactly what /gantt/tasks finds for the query.

    • Dependencies come from each task's own body (not its children's): "blocked by", "depends on", "dependent on", "waiting on/for", "after", "requires", "needs", "follows", "prerequisite:" name what it waits on; "blocks", "before", "prerequisite for", "required by" what waits on it. What the phrase names is found by org link ([[id:..]], [[#custom]], [[*Heading]], [[file:x.org::*Heading]]; Source "link"), by ticket key such as ABC-123 against another task's CUSTOM_ID, LINK or headline ("jira" when that task came from the jira import, else "key"), and otherwise by matching the words against task headlines ("text", confidence by how well they match). Issue links kept as BLOCKED_BY, DEPENDS_ON, BLOCKS or ISSUELINKS properties count as "jira", and numbered siblings (1., 2), Step 3, Phase II) as "sequence". AFTER holds one id, so a task that already waits on something (AFTER, or an ORDERED parent) is given none, each task is given at most one, and none closes a circle with the existing links and the more certain suggestions before it. Most certain first.
    • Redundant lists AFTER links the chart would keep without: the ORDERED chain the task would fall back to already comes after the same heading. Cycles lists tasks already waiting on each other in a circle.
    • Estimates are for open tasks with no EFFORT: the median clocked time of finished tasks in the window most like it (same person and tag, same tag, same person, same file, similar title; three or more needed), else the median EFFORT already in the chart. Rounded to quarter hours under two hours, half hours under a day, half days above.
    • Lanes are the five best ways to split the tasks into swim lanes: by tag, parent heading, file, dependency chain, or any property with two to ten values on 60% of the tasks. Scored on coverage, balance, two to eight groups and few dependencies crossing between lanes.
    • Ratios are actual over estimated for every finished task in the window with both an EFFORT and clocked time, for a forecast.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: A GanttSuggestReq.

    Field Type Description
    Query string The chart's query.
    Kinds list Any of deps, estimates, lanes, ratios. Empty means all.
    DayHours number Hours in a day of effort. Default 8.
    From string Start of the history window, as typed anywhere. Default -180d.

    Response: A GanttSuggest: Ok, Msg, Query, Deps (Task, After, AfterTitle, Evidence, Source, Confidence), Redundant (Task, After, Via, Removable), Cycles (lists of hashes, each waiting on the next), Estimates (Task, Effort, Mins, Basis, Samples, Confidence), Lanes (By, Prop, Label, Score, Groups of Name and Tasks, CrossLinks) and Ratios.

    POST /habits/untick — Take Today's Tick Off A Habit

    Removes the completion recorded for today on one :STYLE: habit heading, and puts back what the tick moved: the repeating date goes back one interval, :LAST_REPEAT: comes off, and a habit left sitting on a done keyword goes back to the one the log line says it had.

    Method: POST

    Request: A HabitUntick — Hash, the heading. Required.

    Response: A HabitUntickResult. Ok is false with a Msg when there is nothing recorded for today, which is not an error: it is the answer, and it is what makes pressing the key twice harmless.

    This is deliberately not an undo. It is worked out from the file rather than from anything the server remembers, so it works on a habit ticked off in Emacs this morning, on one ticked off twice, after a restart, and under -local.

    Three things it decides:

    • A day is the unit. Every completion recorded today comes off, not just the last one. A habit ticked twice in an afternoon is one filled square in the tracker and is cleared as one.
    • What comes off is exactly what fills the square — the lines parseHabitCompletions counts. A tracker and its eraser disagreeing about which lines count would leave a square that cannot be cleared.
    • The date only goes back if it went forward today, which :LAST_REPEAT: is the evidence for. One interval back is exact for +2d, lands on the day of the tick for .+2d, and is the latest possible date for ++2d — which may have taken several steps with nothing in the file to say how many. Doing that sum against a stamp written today has evidence behind it; doing it to a date nothing says moved would be a guess.

    POST /harper/lint — Check Prose with Harper on the Server

    Body {Texts, Dialect, Off}: paragraphs of plain prose, the English (american, british, australian, canadian, indian) and Harper rule names switched off. Needs harper: enabled: true; harper-ls is started on the first call.

    Response: {Ok, Msg, Lints}, Lints a list per text of {rule, kind, start, end, msg, fixes}, offsets in UTF-16 units.

    POST /heading/parts — Set a Heading's Tags or Priority

    Rewrites the heading's headline line with new tags, a new priority, or both, keeping the stars, keyword and title as written and right-aligned tags at the column they ended at. Only that one line changes.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Hash, Tags, Priority}. Tags is the whole list (empty takes them all off); Priority is one letter, or empty to take it off. A field left out is left as it is.

    Response: A ResultMsg.

    POST /import/ipynb — Import A Jupyter Notebook

    { "Notebook": "<the .ipynb text>", "Name": "analysis.ipynb",
  "Filename": "science/analysis.org", "Overwrite": false, "DryRun": false }

    Writes the notebook as an org file - markdown as org, code cells as source blocks sharing one python session, outputs as their #+RESULTS: - and its pictures into <name>_files/ beside it, then loads the file.

    Filename is relative to the first org directory or absolute inside one; empty means the notebook's name in the first org directory. A file or picture already there is refused unless Overwrite. DryRun writes nothing and answers the org text in Org.

    The answer says where everything went (Filename, Files), what the notebook was (Title, Language, Session, Nbformat) and what it held (Cells, Markdown, Code, Raw, Blocks, Outputs, Images, Errors). A refusal is Ok: false with the reason in Msg.

    POST /import/org — Write Org Text Converted Elsewhere

    { "Files": [ { "Filename": "inbox/todo.org", "Org": "* TODO ..." } ],
  "Assets": [ { "Filename": "vault/pics/a.png", "Data": "<base64>" } ],
  "Overwrite": false, "Append": false, "SkipKnown": false,
  "KeyProp": "ID", "DryRun": false }

    What orgs import sends for markdown and Obsidian vaults, todo.txt and iCalendar files: those are converted on the client, where the file is, and written here. Each Filename is relative to the first org directory or absolute inside one.

    A file already there is refused unless Overwrite replaces it or Append adds the new entries to its end (leaving off the new text's #+KEYWORD: lines). SkipKnown with Append leaves out any top level entry whose KeyProp property (ID unless named; the calendar importer uses ICAL_UID) the file already has, so importing the same thing twice adds only what is new. An asset already there is kept unless Overwrite. DryRun writes nothing and answers each file's text in Org.

    Response: Files (Filename, Entries, Skipped, Appended), Assets written and Warnings; a refusal is Ok: false with Msg.

    POST /languagetool/check — Check Text with LanguageTool

    The form LanguageTool's own /v2/check takes (text, language, motherTongue, level, disabledRules…), passed to the LanguageTool configured by languageTool: in orgs.yaml, and its answer passed back as it is. Behind orgs' login, so LanguageTool itself can listen on localhost.

    POST /local/{runtime}/{install,start,stop,pull,cancel,delete} — Managing Local Runtimes

    For an administrator (anyone with noAuth). runtime is llamacpp, lmstudio or mlx. install installs it on the server's machine (llama.cpp's GitHub release; LM Studio's own installer, llmster; MLX's mlx-lm into a python environment of its own); start and stop the server orgs runs (stop keeps it down until start); pull {Model} fetches a model in the background, installing the runtime first when it is missing (llama.cpp: owner/repo:QUANT or owner/repo/file.gguf from Hugging Face; MLX: owner/repo; LM Studio: a catalogue key such as qwen/qwen3-8b); cancel {Model} stops a pull, delete {Model} removes one. Response: {Ok, Msg}.

    POST /mapgen/render — Draw a Map

    Draws a map from its params and painted terrain, as a jpeg - what the map editor shows while the settings change. The last dozen maps drawn are kept, so asking again is quick.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {params, strokes: [{x, y, r, kind}]}, as GET /mapgen describes the params; strokes in fractions of the map's width and height.

    Response: the map, image/jpeg (a town: image/svg+xml), with X-Map-Width, X-Map-Height and X-Map-Hash.

    POST /mapgen/settle — Towns and Roads for a Map

    Places towns, cities, villages and ports on a generated region or world where people would live (flat, watered land by rivers and coasts), as many as a density asks for, and routes roads between them the easiest way across the map's own terrain - through forest, round mountains and lakes, avoiding swamp, crossing rivers only where it must. Writes nothing: the map editor takes the answer into the map.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {params, strokes, density, roads, seed, keep: [{kind, name, x, y}]}; density 0 (none) to 1 (quite a few); keep the places already on the map, which roads reach too.

    Response: {ok, places: [{kind, name, x, y}], roads: [{kind, pts}]}, in fractions of the map.

    POST /mapgen/surf — A Coast's Surf

    The coast of a generated region as lines - the shore, where the foam breaks, and lines of swell further out - for the map viewer to animate. A hex world, town or village has none.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {params, strokes}

    Response: {ok, lines: [[[x0, y0, x1, y1, ...], ...], ...]}, shore first, in fractions of the map.

    POST /media/resolve — Where an Org File's Pictures Can Be Fetched

    Body {File, Targets: [link, ...]}: an org file and the targets of the picture links in it, as written (file:x.png, ./img/y.jpg, a url).

    Response: {Ok, Urls: {target: {Url, Msg}}}. Url is a path under /images for a file inside the first org directory, or the link itself when it is already a url; otherwise Msg says why there is none (missing, or outside the folder the server shares).

    POST /mentions/link — Turn Mentions Into Links

    Rewrites unlinked mentions as links, each as an edit of its own line and nothing else. A heading target is linked by id - [[id:<ID>][text]], the text kept as written - and is given an :ID: (a uuid, as org-id makes) in its property drawer first if it has none. A file target is linked by the id in the drawer above its first heading if it has one, otherwise by a relative file: link.

    Each mention is checked against its line before it is written: if the text is no longer at that line and column, or now sits inside a link, it is refused with a message and the others still go ahead. Every mention is checked before anything is written, so a request whose mentions have all gone stale changes nothing - not even the id. Each file is written once.

    Linking a mention that is in a headline changes that headline's text, and with it the hash of that heading and every heading under it.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: A MentionLinkRequest: Hash (a heading) or Filename (a file) for the target, and Mentions, a list of {Filename, Line, Col, Text} exactly as /mentions answered them.

    Response: A MentionLinkResult: Ok when anything was linked, Linked, the Id used, NewId when the heading was given one, and a Results entry per mention with its own Ok, Msg and the Link written.

    POST /notifications/clear — Remove Notifications

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"ids": ["..."]} or {"all": true}.

    Response: The NoticeList after the change.

    POST /notifications/read — Mark Notifications Read

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"ids": ["..."]} or {"all": true}.

    Response: The NoticeList after the change.

    POST /notify/test — Send a Test Notification

    Sends one notification through the same path reminders take: published as a notify event, and popped on the server's machine when the notify plugin is configured to (not in its quiet hours, desktop on).

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): optional

    Field Type Description
    Title string Defaults to "orgs".
    Body string Defaults to a line saying it works.

    Response: A NotifyTestResult: Popped says whether it was shown on the server's machine, Backend how, Msg why not or what went wrong.

    POST /ollama/{install,start,stop,pull,cancel,delete} — Managing Ollama

    For an administrator (anyone with noAuth). install downloads the latest Ollama release for the server's machine into the user cache and starts it; start and stop the ollama serve orgs runs (stop keeps it down until start); pull {Model} fetches a model in the background (progress in GET /ollama/status), cancel {Model} stops a pull, delete {Model} removes one. Response: {Ok, Msg}.

    POST /orgfile — Save an Org File's Text

    Writes the whole text of an org file, exactly as given. Used by worg's editor. Only a file the server already reads can be written, and the write is refused when the file on disk is no longer Base (the text the editor started from), unless Force is set.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    Field Type Required Description
    Filename string yes The org file to write.
    Text string yes The new contents.
    Base string no What the file held when editing began.
    Force bool no Write even when the file has changed since Base.

    Response: A ResultMsg. A refusal because the file changed has Msg set to "changed", so a client can tell it from a failure.

    POST /record — Add A Record

    { "Type": "contact", "Name": "Jane Roe",
  "Fields": { "EMAIL": "jane@example.com", "PHONE_MOBILE": "+1-555-0100" },
  "Notes": "Met at the fair." }

    Files it under the collection's container heading. TargetHash files it under a heading of your choosing instead, and Filename appends it to the end of a file - which is how the first record of a collection with no container yet gets written.

    POST /record/update — Change A Record

    { "Hash": "...", "Set": { "PHONE_MOBILE": "+1-555-0101", "FAX": "" } }

    Every field named in Set is written and a field set to an empty string is taken off, the same rule the property endpoint follows. SetName with Name renames the heading and SetNotes with Notes replaces the body.

    Every change prepends a line to the record's LOGBOOK, so what was touched and when is on the record itself rather than in a log somewhere else.

    POST /records/collection — Start A Collection

    { "Type": "synth", "Name": "Synthesisers", "Icon": "🎹",
  "Fields": ["MAKER", "MODEL", "YEAR", "SERIAL", "IMAGE"],
  "Filename": "things.org" }

    Writes the container heading new records of that type are filed under. Refuses when that collection already has one, because a second container would quietly become the place things land.

    POST /records/collection/update — Change A Collection

    { "Hash": "...", "SetName": true, "Name": "Synthesisers",
  "SetIcon": true, "Icon": "🎹",
  "SetFields": true, "Fields": ["MAKER", "MODEL", "YEAR"] }

    Each part is only written when its flag is set, because clearing the icon and leaving it alone are different things and "" says both.

    SetType with a new Type renames the collection, which means rewriting the RECORD property of every record that carried the old name - otherwise the records would be left behind under a name nothing uses. The answer says how many moved. It refuses when another collection already answers to the new name.

    POST /refactor/list/apply — Turn A List Into Headings

    Writes what /refactor/list/preview showed, if the file still comes to the same change.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Hash, Line, Token, Expect}.

    Response: A RefactorPlan with Applied set.

    POST /refactor/list/preview — Preview Turning A List Into Headings

    Works out turning a list in a heading's text into child headings: each item a heading one level down (nested items deeper), [ ] the file's first open keyword and [X] its first done one, a description item's term the title, and the lines under an item its heading's text. The headings go at the end of the heading's own text, before its children.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Hash, Line}. Line is a zero-based row inside the list to convert (see /refactor/lists); 0 or less is the first list.

    Response: A RefactorPlan (see /refactor/tag/preview).

    POST /refactor/merge/apply — Merge One Heading Into Another

    Writes what /refactor/merge/preview showed, if the files still come to the same change.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Into, From, Token, Expect}.

    Response: A RefactorPlan with Applied set.

    POST /refactor/merge/preview — Preview Merging One Heading Into Another

    Works out merging From into Into: From's text after Into's text, its children after Into's children (re-levelled), tags unioned, properties added where Into has none of that name (Into wins every conflict, each reported in Warnings), logbook entries joined and From removed. When Into has no ID it takes From's; when both do, every [[id:From]] link is re-pointed at Into and From's id kept on Into as MERGED_IDS.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Into, From}, both heading hashes.

    Response: A RefactorPlan (see /refactor/tag/preview).

    POST /refactor/split/apply — Split A Heading Out To A File

    Writes what /refactor/split/preview showed. Send the preview's request with its Token and, when the preview made an id, NewId set to it. The new file is made first and exclusively, so one that appeared since the preview is refused before the old file is touched.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Hash, To, NewId, Token, Expect}.

    Response: A RefactorPlan with Applied set.

    POST /refactor/split/preview — Preview Splitting A Heading Out To A File

    Works out moving a heading and everything under it into a new org file: levels promoted so it starts at level one, its properties kept, given an ID if it had none (answered as NewId), and the old file's #+FILETAGS:, #+TODO:, #+TAGS: and #+CATEGORY: lines copied so it means the same there. Relative file links are rebased when the new file is in another folder. In the old file the heading becomes one headline at the same level whose title is [[id:…][Title]].

    The new file is only ever inside an org directory, and never one that exists.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Hash, To}. To is the new file's path (relative to the first org directory) or a folder; empty is a file named for the heading beside the one it is in.

    Response: A RefactorPlan (see /refactor/tag/preview) with NewFile, and NewId when an id was made.

    POST /refactor/tag/apply — Rename, Merge Or Delete A Tag

    Writes what /refactor/tag/preview showed, if the files still come to the same change. Send the preview's request again with its Token.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Old, New, Delete, Files, Query, Token, Expect}.

    Response: A RefactorPlan with Applied set, or Ok false and Stale when a file changed since the preview.

    POST /refactor/tag/preview — Preview Renaming, Merging Or Deleting A Tag

    Works out renaming one tag to another across every file - headline tags (right-aligned tags stay ending at the column they ended at), #+FILETAGS: and #+TAGS: lines - and answers with the change, writing nothing. A new name some heading already carries is a merge: the old tag is dropped there rather than written twice. Delete takes the tag off everywhere instead.

    Saved queries, filters and tag groups that name the old tag are listed in Mentions and never changed.

    All four refactors answer the same way; this is the one place it is said. Each has a preview that writes nothing and an apply that does it. The preview's answer is a RefactorPlan: Ok, Msg, Summary, Warnings, Files (per file: Filename, Created, Before and After text, Hash of Before, a unified Patch, Added=/=Removed counts), and a Token. The apply takes the same request with Token (and optionally Expect, a map of filename to Hash) from the preview, works the change out again from the files as they are now, and refuses with Stale set unless it comes to exactly what the preview showed.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {Old, New, Delete, Files, Query}. Files limits it to some files; Query to the headlines of the headings a query matches (FILETAGS and #+TAGS lines are then left alone).

    Response: A RefactorPlan.

    POST /reformat — Reformat Org Files

    Re-serializes and re-saves the specified org files, normalizing whitespace, indentation, and heading structure. This is a lossless rewrite that ensures the files conform to the parser's canonical output format.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): A JSON array of absolute file paths to reformat.

    ["/home/user/org/todo.org", "/home/user/org/notes.org"]

    Response: A Result JSON object with {"status": true} on success.

    POST /refresh/run — Run Something Now

    { "Key": "block:/org/dash.org#disk" }      one item, by the Key /refresh gave it
{ "Due": true }                            whatever is due
{ "All": true }                            everything on a timer
{ "File": "dash.org" }                     that file's dynamic blocks and tables
{ "File": "dash.org", "Blocks": true }     and its :schedule blocks

    Runs it now, whether or not it is due, and answers each item as /refresh would, after the run. A file need not be on a timer to be refreshed by name.

    POST /reloadconfig — Reload The Configuration

    Reads the server's yaml file again and takes from it everything that can change under a running server: capture templates, filters, tag groups, refile targets, goLinksFile/goLinksHeading, todo states, day page, archive, date tree and clock settings, the template path, babel, columns, log and the dnd paths.

    What a running server is built around is left as it is, and named in needsRestart when the file now says something different: ports, certificates, orgDirs, auth and keystore settings, voice, and the plugin, exporter and updater lists (a plugin is started once, with its settings).

    A file that does not parse changes nothing.

    Method: POST

    Parameters: None.

    Response:

    {"ok": true, "msg": "configuration reloaded", "file": "/home/me/orgs.yaml",
 "reloaded": ["captureTemplates", "filters", ...],
 "needsRestart": ["port"]}

    POST /review/act — Decide About One Heading, Undoably

    The one write behind inbox triage, the someday sweep and the weekly review. It calls what /move, /date/change, /heading/parts, /status/change and capture call, and around that keeps the text of every file it touched as it was before and after, so /review/undo can put it back.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): a ReviewAct:

    Field Description
    Hash The heading.
    Action refile, archive, schedule, deadline, unschedule, tags, status, done, promote, next, chase.
    To refile: a Target (as /move takes, e.g. {"Type":"hash","Id":...}).
    When schedule/deadline: typed (fri, +2w, tomorrow 10:00) or an org stamp; empty clears.
    Tags tags: the heading's whole tag list.
    Keyword status/promote: the keyword; next: the new child's keyword (NEXT).
    Text next: the new child's title; chase: a note to keep with the chase.

    promote sets the keyword and takes the someday tags off. chase writes org's own note line (- Note taken on [stamp] \\ / Chased) into the logbook, which restarts the waiting count.

    Response: ReviewActResult: Ok, Msg, Did (what happened, in words) and Undo, the token for /review/undo.

    POST /review/done — Finish the Weekly Review

    Records the review as done now, with whatever the client counted along the way (Summary, e.g. {"refiled": 4, "archived": 2}), and forgets the step it was on.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"Summary": {"refiled": 4}} (optional).

    Response: ReviewLast.

    POST /review/step — Remember Where a Review Is

    Records the step a weekly review in progress is on, so leaving and coming back (or switching between worg and orgs review week) resumes it, and optionally what it has done so far (Tally, kept until the review is finished). Step 0 forgets the review in progress.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"Step": 3, "Tally": {"refiled": 4}}

    Response: ReviewLast.

    POST /review/undo — Take a Review Action Back

    Puts back every file a /review/act changed, as it was before. Refused, with nothing written, when any of those files has been changed since by anything else: an undo never throws away somebody's later edit.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): {"Token": "..."} from the action's Undo; empty takes back the most recent action.

    Response: ReviewActResult with Did saying what was taken back.

    POST /table — Write A Table Back To Its File

    Replaces the rows and formulas of one table. Only the lines the table occupies are rewritten, the rest of the file is left alone. Every formula in Formulas is written to a single #+TBLFM: line, separated by ::.

    With Eval set the tables formulas are run after the save and the computed values are written to the file as well, exactly as /exectable would.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): A TableEdit object.

    Field Type Required Description
    Filename string yes The org file holding the table.
    Id int yes Ordinal of the table within the file, from zero.
    Data []TableRow yes Replacement rows, "data" or "sep".
    Formulas []string no Replacement formulas, e.g. ["$3=$1*$2;%.2f"].
    Name string no New #+NAME: for the table, empty removes it.
    SetName bool no Only touch the #+NAME: line when this is set.
    Eval bool no Run the tables formulas after saving.

    Response: A TableResult JSON object holding the table as it now reads back from disk.

    POST /table/calc — Work Out A Table Sent As Text

    { "Filename": "/org/budget.org", "Line": 12, "Text": "| a | b |\n| 1 |   |\n#+TBLFM: $2=$1*2\n" }

    Runs the #+TBLFM: formulas of the table in Text and answers with the table as it reads afterwards in Msg - the rows only, the formula lines are not repeated. Nothing is written to disk. Filename and Line say where the table lives, for the file's #+CONSTANTS: and the $PROP_ values of the heading above it; remote() reads other tables from the database as usual.

    This is what an editor uses: it holds the text, unsaved changes included, and putting the answer back itself keeps a recalculation one undo.

    Response: {"Ok": true, "Msg": "| a | b |\n...", "Colors": [{"Row": 2, "Col": 3, "Color": "red"}]}. Colors are the cells formulas coloured with highlight(), red(), gradient() and the rest, as @Row$Col, for the editor to show.

    POST /table/eval — Recalculate A Table

    Runs the #+TBLFM: formulas of one table and writes the computed values back to the org file. This is /exectable addressed by file and table ordinal rather than by heading and row.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    {"Filename": "/org/budget.org", "Id": 0}

    Response: A TableResult JSON object holding the recalculated table.

    POST /table/import — Write Delimited Text As A Table

    { "Filename": "/path/notes.org", "AfterLine": -1, "Text": "a,b\n1,2\n", "Header": true, "Name": "sales" }
{ "Hash": "hOpOB7vIg6oiYz5sMVS=", "Text": "...", "Separator": ";" }

    Reads csv, tsv or semicolon separated text (guessed from the first line when Separator is empty) and writes it as an aligned org table: under a heading by Hash, after line AfterLine (zero based), or at the end of the file. Header draws a rule under the first row; Name writes a #+NAME: above it. Only the lines added change.

    POST /users/add — Add A User

    Adds an account to this server's keystore. The caller must be logged in as an account marked admin: true; the new account may be marked one too.

    The account works immediately - the server writes the keystore it is already holding, so unlike orgs user add there is nothing to restart.

    Method: POST

    Body: A NewUser. The password is not in it: the client generates a salt for the new user and sends ClientHash(username, salt, password) under it, exactly as a login does, so the password never reaches the server.

    Field Type Required Description
    username string yes The new account's name. No whitespace, no :/?#[]@
    salt string yes A fresh salt the client generated for them.
    password string yes ClientHash(username, salt, password).
    admin bool no Whether the new account may add users itself. 
    {"username": "dana", "salt": "b3d1...", "password": "sha256c:9f2c...", "admin": false}

    Response: A ResultMsg. It is refused, with the reason in msg, when the caller is not an administrator (403), when authentication is switched off or this server has no keystore file to write (409), and when the name is not a usable one or is already taken (400).

    POST /voice/dictate — Transcribe a Moment of Dictation

    For worg's dictation in writing mode: one short clip (a phrase, cut at a pause), transcribed and answered at once. Unlike a voice note the audio is not kept - it goes to a temporary file for whisper and is removed - so dictating a chapter does not leave a thousand recordings behind.

    Method: POST, a multipart form.

    Field Required Description
    audio yes The clip, in whatever the browser records (webm, ogg, m4a).
    prompt no The text just before the cursor: whisper carries its spelling,
    names and punctuation on, and joins the clip to it more cleanly.
    language no Two letter code; else the configured one, else detected.
    model no A whisper model other than the configured one.

    Response: A VoiceTranscription. 502 when whisper cannot be reached or fails, with its reason in Msg.

    POST /voice/note — File a Voice Note as an Org Heading

    Writes the note into an org file: a heading, a property drawer carrying the link to the recording and what transcribed it, and the text underneath.

    The text written is the text sent, never a fresh transcription - what lands in the file has to be what was on screen when the button was pressed, corrections and all.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON): A VoiceNoteRequest.

    Field Type Required Description
    headline string yes The heading text.
    text string no The body, as edited. Line breaks are kept.
    id string no The recording this came from.
    target Target no Where to file it; the configured target when left out.
    tags []string no Tags for the heading, on top of the configured ones.
    props map no Extra properties for the drawer.
    segments []Segment no The timestamped segments, written as a list when withTimes.
    withTimes bool no Write the segments under the text.
    keepAudio bool no Keep the recording and link to it. Off deletes it.
    model string no What transcribed it, written as the WHISPER property.
    seconds number no The length, written as the DURATION property.

    The AUDIO property is a file link written relative to the org file that holds it, so moving the org directory as a whole does not break it.

    Response: A VoiceNoteResult with the filename and the line the heading landed on.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if there is no headline.
    • 404 if the target cannot be found or created.

    POST /voice/recording — Save a Recording

    Takes one recording and keeps it. Nothing is transcribed and nothing is written into an org file: this exists so that the words are safe on disk before anything that can fail is attempted on them.

    Method: POST (multipart/form-data)

    Form Fields:

    Field Type Required Description
    audio file yes The recording, in whatever container the client has.
    seconds number no How long the take ran, as the client timed it.
    filename string no The client's own name for it, used for its extension.

    The container is not converted - whisper decodes through ffmpeg, so webm from a browser, m4a from a phone and wav from a recorder are all acceptable.

    Response: A VoiceRecording JSON object, whose id addresses it in every other call here.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if there is no audio field.
    • 413 if the recording is larger than the configured maxMb.

    POST /voice/transcribe — Transcribe a Saved Recording

    Hands one saved recording to the go-whisper server and answers with what it heard. Nothing is written into an org file here - the transcript goes back to the client to be read and corrected first, because a transcript nobody has looked at is a guess, and an org file is not the place to find that out.

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    Field Type Required Description
    id string yes The recording to transcribe.
    model string no Override the configured model for this one call.
    language string no Two letter code; empty lets whisper detect it.
    prompt string no Names and jargon to expect, which biases whisper's guesses.

    Response: A VoiceTranscription with the whole text, the language whisper settled on, the duration it decoded, and the segments with their start and end in seconds.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 404 if there is no recording with that id.
    • 502 if whisper could not be reached, has no model, or failed on the audio. Msg is whisper's own words and is meant to be shown as it is.

    POST /voice/whisper/restart — Start the Transcription Service Again

    Stops the go-whisper server orgs is running and starts it again. This is the answer to a model that failed to load or a service that has stopped answering, and it is deliberately the only control over it: what to run is configuration, not something a client gets to choose.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: None.

    Response: A ResultMsg. The restart is not waited for - a large model takes a while to load - so watch GET /voice/config for state to come back to ready.

    Errors:

    • 401 if not authenticated.
    • 400 if orgs is not the one running whisper, which is the case when voice.models is unset or voice.url names somebody else's server.

    POST /watches — Watch a Query

    Starts watching a query, or changes a watch with the same name. The first check happens at once and is a baseline: what the query finds now is taken as known, and only headings found after that are announced. A heading is told apart by its ID or CUSTOM_ID when it has one, else by its file and outline path, so editing a file does not make its headings "new".

    Method: POST

    Request Body (JSON):

    Field Type Description
    name string What the watch is called. Defaults to storedQuery.
    storedQuery string A saved query by name, read afresh at every check.
    query string An expression of its own, when there is no saved query.
    label string What a notification calls it; the name when empty.
    left bool Also say when a heading stops matching.
    desktop bool Also pop up on the server's desktop through the notify plugin.
    paused bool Keep it, but do not check it.

    Every new match is a querymatch event on GET /events (to this user's streams only) and an entry in GET /notifications.

    For queries that move with the clock, DeadlineWithin(2) and ScheduledWithin(0) are true of a deadline (scheduled date) from today to that many days ahead; the watch notices those within five minutes of midnight with no file touched.

    Response: The WatchList after the change; ok false with msg when the saved query does not exist or the expression does not parse (400).

    POST /watches/check — Check the Watches Now

    Runs the user's watches at once rather than waiting for a file to change or the five minute timer. Notifications are made and sent exactly as a timed check would.

    Method: POST

    Response: A NoticeList of the notifications this check made.

    POST /writing/goals — Set Writing Goals

    Body {Daily, Weekly, Monthly, RestDays}: words a day, a week and a month (zero for none), and days off a week a streak survives. Kept per user in the extensions file beside the writing log.

    Response: {Ok, Msg}

    POST /writing/ideas — Make Ideas

    Makes count results of one generator. Each is a title, a summary, labelled facts, the same facts as an org description list (body), and prose: the idea as a short paragraph to put into a draft. entry is the compendium kind it would be filed as (character, place, group, thing), absent for a prompt. The same seed gives the same results.

    Method: POST

    Request Body: {type, options: {name: value}, count, seed}

    Response: {ok, type, seed, items: [{kind, title, summary, facts: [{key, value}], body, prose, entry, tags}]}

    POST /writing/log — Note Today's Word Count

    Body {File, Date, Words}: the file's word count now. The first count of a day is kept as its start and every later one as its end, so the day's words are End - Start. Kept per user in the extensions file.

    Response: {Ok, Msg}

    POST /writing/snapshots — Take or Delete a Snapshot

    Body {File, Snapshot: {Heading, Title, Text, Words}} keeps a new snapshot (the server gives it its Id and Time); {File, Delete: id} removes one.

    Response: {Ok, Msg, Snapshot}

    Commands

    Dnd

    The dnd command is the client side of the D&D character module. It talks to the server over the /dnd/* REST API, so the rules, the ruleset modules and the character sheet renderers all live on the server.

    orgs dnd new                          # guided character creation
orgs dnd new -level 3 -name Lyra      # with a head start
orgs dnd random -level 5 -out npc.org # roll a whole character
orgs dnd list classes                 # browse a ruleset
orgs dnd info -kind class -id wizard  # read one entry in full
orgs dnd characters                   # every sheet the server knows about
orgs dnd show -file lyra.org          # print a sheet in the terminal
orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -format pdf -out lyra.pdf
orgs dnd levelup -file lyra.org       # take the level you just earned
orgs dnd refresh -file lyra.org       # recompute after hand editing
orgs dnd rulesets                     # what content is loaded
orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678         # bring a character over from d&d beyond

    orgs dnd new walks you through creation the way a character builder does: every prompt lists the valid choices with a one line summary, marks the ones that suit your class with a star, and lets you ask for the full rules text, roll the choice randomly, or step back to change your mind.

    On a wide enough terminal the chooser is drawn in two panes: the list on the left, and the full rules text of whatever the cursor is on - the spell, item, feat or feature - on the right, so you can read before you commit. When a question takes several answers the header keeps a running count of what you have ticked ("selected 1 of 2") along with their names, and if you confirm the wrong number the list comes back with your picks still selected so you only have to correct them.

    Long lists are filtered by typing. The match is fuzzy on the name of an option, so eldbl finds Eldritch Blast, and a plain word also matches the summary beside it, so fire finds the spells that only mention it. The filter is editable: backspace takes a character off and the list widens again, ctrl+w takes a word, and escape clears it. The count beside the question says how much of the list you are looking at.

    Importing from D&D Beyond

    orgs dnd import converts a character you already have on D&D Beyond into an org character sheet, the same sheet orgs dnd new writes.

    orgs dnd import -ddb https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/12345678
orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678 -out characters/lyra.org -force
orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678 -preview      # convert and print, write nothing
orgs dnd import -json saved.json            # from a payload you saved yourself
orgs dnd import -forget                     # clear the saved session cookie

    D&D Beyond has no login api, so a character whose privacy is set to public imports with no credential at all, and a private one asks for the CobaltSession cookie your browser is already holding - the prompt says where to find it. The cookie is traded for a short lived token by D&D Beyond's own auth service and can be kept in your system keyring so you are only asked once; it is never sent to your orgs server, which only ever sees the character json. -cookie and the ORGS_DDB_COBALT environment variable pass it in without a prompt for scripting.

    Everything is matched onto your ruleset by name, and anything that does not match - a subclass from a book the srd does not carry, a homebrew item - is still written onto the sheet under its own name and listed afterwards as something to check, so nothing is quietly dropped. Importing over a sheet that is already there keeps that sheet's identity and its inventory history, which D&D Beyond has no equivalent of.

    The appearance questions - age, height, weight, eyes, skin and hair - come with suggestions drawn from your race and your class, so a hill dwarf druid is offered warm hazel eyes and leaf tangled hair, and a tiefling warlock is offered eyes that are a solid orb of colour. You can still type your own, but it has to make sense: heights and weights are read in either imperial or metric and have to land somewhere your race could plausibly be, and a colour has to be a word rather than a number.

    Drill

    orgs drill drills a deck of flashcards at the command line: the decks of worg's Flashcards tab, the same cards, the same scheduling. Ratings are written by the server into the cards' DRILL_* properties, org-drill's way, so a deck can be drilled here, in worg and with Emacs' org-drill by turns. The user guide is docs/drill.org.

    orgs drill                          # pick a deck, drill it
orgs drill Spanish                  # a deck by name (or the start of one)
orgs drill Spanish -cram            # everything not seen in 12 hours; nothing rescheduled
orgs drill -q 'HasTags("drill")'    # any query, without saving a deck
orgs drill Spanish -max 10 -minutes 5   # a shorter session than the deck's
orgs drill -resume                  # carry on where q left off
orgs drill ls                       # the decks and what each has due
orgs drill stats Spanish            # one deck at a glance
orgs drill cards Spanish            # every card: status, next review, ease, failures

    ls, stats and cards take -json and -format for scripts; drilling needs a person at a terminal.

    The screen

    Across the top is org-drill's prompt line: the time so far, the card's status letter (N new, Y young, o old, ! overdue, F failed, C cram) and how many are done, failed, mature and new. Under it, a rule shows how far through the session's limit you are.

    The card is drawn the way orgs pres draws a slide: tables, source blocks and pictures as they are written, in a slide theme's colours (-theme). Hidden clozes show as [...] or [hint...]; in the answer they are bold.

    Key Question Answer
    space, any show the answer
    0 - 5 rate it; each button says when the card comes back
    e edit the card in $EDITOR edit the card
    s skip it
    ? what the ratings mean
    ↑ ↓ PgUp PgDn scroll a tall card scroll
    q, esc stop stop

    A failed card comes back later in the session until you pass it. At the end you get org-drill's report, and its warning if too much was failed; k keeps going on what is left.

    q saves where you were, and orgs drill -resume carries on - reading the cards again, in case you edited them. Editing a card with e reads it again when the editor closes, so the card asked is the card as it now reads.

    A deck that asks for typed answers (in worg's deck settings) has a line to type into before the answer is shown, and your answer is shown beside it.

    Flashcards — drilling your notes, org-drill style

    What it is

    worg's Flashcards tab is spaced repetition over your org files. Any heading can be a card: its body is the question and its child headings are the answer. You rate how well you remembered it, from 0 to 5, and the card is scheduled again: soon if it was hard, much later if it was easy.

    The tab follows Emacs org-drill closely. It uses the same card types, the same [cloze] syntax, the SM5, SM2 and Simple8 algorithms with the same constants, the same DRILL_* properties written the same way, and the same session rules. A card can be drilled here on Monday and with M-x org-drill on Tuesday, and each picks up where the other left off.

    The difference is how cards are chosen. org-drill uses every heading tagged :drill:. Here, a deck is a query of your own, so you can keep as many decks as you like, spread across the same notes:

    Deck Query
    Spanish HasTags("spanish")
    Chemistry HasTags("chem") && IsInFile("school.org")
    Drill HasTags("drill") (org-drill's own cards)
    Hard ones a saved search, edited in the Saved Queries tab

    The same decks drill in a terminal with orgs drill:

    Making cards
    A simple card
    * What is the capital of France?                          :geography:
** Answer
Paris

    The question is the heading and its body. The child headings (here, Answer) are folded while you think and opened when you ask for the answer.

    Clozes

    Square brackets hide part of the text. Two bars add a hint.

    * Spain                                                   :geography:
The capital of Spain is [Madrid||starts with M], on the [Manzanares].

    In the question this reads "The capital of Spain is [starts with M…], on the […]". The answer shows both words, highlighted.

    A cloze must fit on one line. Checkboxes ([X]), progress cookies ([1/3], [50%]), dates ([2026-10-01 Thu]), footnote references ([fn:1]), links and code are never treated as clozes. org-drill does hide those; that is the one place this deliberately differs.

    Card types

    Set a type with the DRILL_CARD_TYPE property. It is inherited, so putting it on a parent heading sets the type for every card below it.

    Type What is asked
    simple (the default) the body, with every cloze hidden
    twosided one of the first two child headings is shown and the other is asked
    multisided one child heading, chosen at random, is shown and the rest are asked
    hide1cloze, multicloze one cloze is hidden at random and the others are shown
    hide2cloze two clozes are hidden
    show1cloze, show2cloze one or two clozes are shown and the rest are hidden
    hidefirst, hidelast only the first cloze, or only the last, is hidden
    hide1_firstmore usually the first cloze is hidden; every fourth review, another one
    show1_lastmore usually only the last cloze is shown
    show1_firstless usually one cloze other than the first is shown
    conjugate built from VERB_INFINITIVE, VERB_TRANSLATION, VERB_TENSE, VERB_MOOD
    decline_noun built from NOUN, NOUN_GENDER, NOUN_TRANSLATION, DECLINE_DEFINITE, DECLINE_PLURAL
    spanish_verb children named Infinitive and English, asked in a given tense

    A two-sided card:

    ** Dog                                                      :spanish:
:PROPERTIES:
:DRILL_CARD_TYPE: twosided
:END:
*** English
dog
*** Spanish
el perro
    Which headings are cards
    • A heading the query finds is a card.
    • A heading found underneath a card belongs to that card, as an answer or a side. Tags are inherited in queries, so this is what happens to a card's children.
    • A found heading with no text of its own, with found headings below it, only groups them. With * Vocabulary :spanish: over twenty words, the words are the cards and Vocabulary is not.
    • A card with nothing to ask (no body, and not a twosided or multisided card) and a card with an unknown type are left out. The deck lists them under "left out", as org-drill reports them.
    More
    • :DRILL_CARD_WEIGHT: 2 makes a card come round about twice as often.
    • A heading tagged :explain: above some cards adds its text to their answers.
    • A child heading that has been drilled as a card in its own right stays folded in its parent's answer.
    • A card failed more times than the deck's leech threshold (15) is tagged leech. By default a deck then skips it: a card you keep failing needs rewriting, not more drilling.
    Decks

    + in the deck list makes a deck. A deck has:

    • a name and an optional description;
    • the query that picks its cards, or the name of a saved search. With a saved search, editing that search changes the deck. Check the query counts the cards before you save;

    • the algorithm:

      • SM5 (the default) learns how quickly you forget, and keeps what it learns per person, not per deck;
      • SM2 is the classic one day, six days, then multiplying by the card's ease;
      • Simple8 works from your average rating alone;
    • org-drill's settings, each defaulting to org-drill's own value:
    Setting Default Meaning
    Cards per session 30 stop once this many have been passed (-1: no limit)
    Minutes per session 20 stop after this long (-1: no limit)
    Failure quality 2 a rating at or below this is a failure
    Learn fraction 0.5 how fast intervals grow; lower means more reviews
    Leech after failures 15 when a card becomes a leech
    Leeches skip skip them, ask with a warning, or ask as usual
    Days before old 10 a longer interval counts the card as old rather than young
    Overdue factor 1.2 how late, relative to the interval, counts as overdue
    Forgetting index 10 warn when more than this % of a session was failed
    Cram hours 12 cram asks what has not been seen in this many hours
    Spread reviews out off a little randomness on every interval
    Forget very overdue cards off a card over 90 days overdue is treated as forgotten
    Hide headings off for cards whose heading gives the answer away
    Type the answer off type before you look; your answer is shown beside the real one
    Clozes show their length off [......] with one dot per hidden letter

    Decks are kept per user, beside the server's configuration (in orgs_extensions.yaml), with your saved searches and kanban boards. A deck holds no cards: the cards and their history stay in your files.

    Each deck shows how many cards are due now, new, failed, overdue, young, old, not yet due, and due tomorrow. Browse lists every card with its status, next review, ease and failures, and a button to open the card in its file.

    Drilling

    Drill starts a session.

    The line above the card shows:

    • the time so far;
    • the card's status letter: N new, Y young, o old, ! overdue, F failed, C cram;
    • four counts: cards done, failed, mature (young, old and overdue) and new still waiting.
    Key Question Answer
    any key, ⏎ show the answer
    0-5 rate it
    e edit the card in its file edit the card
    s skip it (nothing is saved)
    ? what the ratings mean
    q, esc stop stop

    The ratings:

    Rating Meaning
    0 Completely forgot.
    1 Even after seeing the answer, it still took a bit to sink in.
    2 After seeing the answer, you remembered it.
    3 It took you awhile, but you finally remembered.
    4 After a little bit of thought you remembered.
    5 You remembered the item really easily.

    Each button shows when the card would come back after that rating.

    • 0-2 is a failure. The card comes back later in the same session, and keeps coming back until you pass it. Its schedule is taken off, so it starts the next session as failed.
    • 3-5 is a pass, scheduled further away the easier it was.
    The order cards come in

    Cards are asked in org-drill's order:

    1. those failed last time;
    2. overdue ones, most overdue first;
    3. young ones;
    4. new and old ones mixed together, in proportion to how many of each are waiting;
    5. last, the cards failed during this session. These keep coming even after a limit is reached, because a failed card must be passed before you stop.
    Stopping, resuming, and the report
    • q stops. Every rating you gave is already in your files. The session waits in the deck list as Resume session. Editing a card with e leaves it waiting the same way.

    • When the cards run out or a limit is reached, the report shows:

      • how many cards you reviewed, and for how long;
      • how your ratings divided up;
      • what share you recalled;
      • what is still waiting, and how many cards fall due tomorrow.
    • If you failed more than the forgetting index allows, a warning follows, as org-drill gives one.
    • Keep going starts again on the cards still waiting, with a fresh clock.
    Cram

    Cram asks every card not seen in the last 12 hours, with no limits, and writes nothing: no ratings, no schedules. It is for the night before an exam, not for remembering.

    At the command line

    orgs drill drills the same decks in a terminal, with the same rules and the same writes. It reads your deck list from the server.

    orgs drill                        # pick a deck
orgs drill Spanish                # or name it
orgs drill Spanish -cram
orgs drill -q 'HasTags("drill")'  # a query, without saving a deck
orgs drill -resume                # after q
orgs drill ls                     # what each deck has due
orgs drill cards Spanish          # the Browse table

    The keys are the tab's: any key shows the answer, 0-5 rates it, e edits the card in $EDITOR, s skips, ? explains the ratings, q stops. Cards are drawn like slides in orgs pres, so a table, code or a picture on a card shows as it is written; -theme picks the colours.

    A session stopped with q can be picked up with orgs drill -resume, the terminal's equivalent of org-drill-resume.

    What is written to a card

    After each rating the card's own lines change, and nothing else in the file:

    ** Capital                                                  :spanish:
   SCHEDULED: <2026-10-05 Mon>
   :PROPERTIES:
   :DRILL_LAST_INTERVAL:  4.0
   :DRILL_REPEATS_SINCE_FAIL: 2
   :DRILL_TOTAL_REPEATS:  1
   :DRILL_FAILURE_COUNT:  0
   :DRILL_AVERAGE_QUALITY: 4.0
   :DRILL_EASE:           2.5
   :DRILL_LAST_QUALITY:   4
   :DRILL_LAST_REVIEWED:  [2026-10-01 Thu 23:04]
   :END:

    These are org-drill's properties, written in its spellings: 4.0, not 4. An old LEARN_DATA property is read and replaced. A failure takes SCHEDULED off. A card that becomes a leech gets the leech tag.

    Differences from org-drill
    • Cards come from a query, not the :drill: tag. Use HasTags("drill") to drill org-drill's own cards.
    • Brackets that are not clozes are left alone: checkboxes, cookies, dates and footnotes (see Clozes).
    • The SM5 matrix is stored with each ease rounded to three places. org-drill stores it with a float that never matches the value read back from the property, so its SM5 rarely learns. The matrix is saved after every rating rather than only at the end of a session.
    • Spreading reviews out is repeatable within a day, so the interval a button promises is the one it writes.
    • org-drill also writes an ID on every card it scans. This does not.
    • t (edit tags) during a drill is not offered; use e to edit the card.
    • Typed answers are shown beside the real one for you to judge, as in org-drill; they are not marked.
    The API
    • GET /drill/cards?deck=NAME returns a deck's cards, drawn as html, with their status and the interval each rating would give.
    • POST /drill/review records one rating.
    • GET and POST /ext/drill/decks read and replace the deck list.

    The full API reference documents each one.

    Pres

    orgs pres gives an org file as a slideshow in the terminal: the deck worg's Presentations tab shows through reveal.js, drawn in box characters, colour and half-block pictures, for the talk given over ssh, in tmux beside the code, or from a laptop with no browser worth trusting on the projector.

    orgs pres talk.org                  # present it
orgs pres talk.org -presenter       # in a second terminal: notes, next slide, time
orgs pres talk.org -theme linen     # any slide theme; builtin and term too
orgs pres talk.org -at 12           # start on slide 12
orgs pres talk.org -print | less -R # every slide, every step, printed
orgs pres talk.org -json            # the outline, for a program
orgs pres -list-themes

    A name that is not a path is looked for in the configured org directories, and no server is needed: the file is read where you are.

    The deck

    The same rules as the html presentation exporters, because it is the same code deciding them:

    • #+SLIDE_LEVEL: 2 makes level-2 headlines the slides and level-1 headlines the sections; a section with nothing of its own is drawn as a divider in large type. Without it every headline is a slide.
    • #+TITLE:, #+SUBTITLE:, #+AUTHOR:, #+DATE: and anything written above the first headline make the title page.
    • Speaker notes - a :NOTES: drawer, a #+begin_notes block, or a child heading called Notes - never reach the slide.
    • :noexport: or :noslide: leaves a heading out.
    • :FRAGMENT: t on a slide reveals its top-level list one item at a time; #+ATTR_SLIDE: :frag above any element makes that element a step.
    • :BACKGROUND: #f4efe4 colours one slide, and its text turns light or dark to suit, as in the browser.
    • :ALIGN: center centres a slide; :TRANSITION: fade changes how it arrives.

    Settings are read with the presentation ladder: a slide's :TERM_FOO:, its :SLIDE_FOO:, its :FOO:, then the document's #+TERM_FOO: and #+SLIDE_FOO:. The TERM_ forms are for this renderer only.

    Setting Meaning Default
    #+SLIDE_THEME: palette, from templates/slides_theme_*.css built in
    #+TERM_TRANSITION: slide, fade or none slide
    #+TERM_WIDTH: widest a column of text gets 88
    #+TERM_FOOTER: nil no footer or progress rule shown

    A theme is the same file the html decks use: its --slide-bg, --slide-ink, --slide-accent and the rest become the terminal's colours, and its @hljs: style picks the nearest code colouring. term uses the terminal's own colours, for transparent terminals.

    What is drawn

    Paragraphs with bold, italic, underline, strike, code, links, sub- and superscripts (H2O as H₂O) and smart dashes; lists with checkboxes; tables in a rounded box with columns of numbers right-aligned; source blocks coloured by language, with line numbers for -n; quotes, verse, centred text, special blocks (#+begin_tip) as labelled cards; footnotes at the foot of their slide; and pictures (png, jpeg, gif) in half blocks, with their #+CAPTION:. An svg or a web image is drawn as a labelled frame.

    A slide too tall for the terminal gives up its blank lines first, then scrolls with the arrow keys; a marker says there is more.

    Keys

    Key Does
    → space l PgDn ⏎ next step, or next slide
    ← h PgUp ⌫ back
    N P next or previous slide, skipping steps
    ↓ ↑ j k scroll a slide too tall for the screen
    g G first or last slide
    12 then ⏎ slide 12
    o tab every slide, to pick from
    n speaker notes under the slide
    t r show the timer, restart it
    f footer and progress rule
    T next theme
    b . black screen
    e edit this slide in $EDITOR
    R reload now
    ? q keys, quit

    The file is reloaded whenever it is saved, keeping your place, so a deck can be written in one window and watched in another.

    Presenting with two windows

    orgs pres talk.org -presenter in a second terminal shows the speaker's view: this slide's notes, the step you are on, what comes next, the time since you started and the clock. The two windows follow each other, and either can drive.

    Snip

    orgs snip keeps the command lines worth keeping - and finds the ones you wrote down and forgot - in your org files. It does what pet does, with org source blocks for snippets: a heading says what the command does, its tags file it, the block is the command. Every shell block in your notes is a snippet, so a command written into a project's notes months ago turns up beside the ones saved on purpose.

    orgs snip                          # find one, fill in its parameters, run it
orgs snip docker logs              # start the search on those words
orgs snip print [words]            # print it instead (what the shell key uses)
orgs snip copy [words]             # put it on the clipboard
orgs snip run backup -set dest=/mnt -y   # no questions: for scripts and cron
orgs snip new 'rsync -av <src> <dest=/backup>'   # save one
orgs snip ls -t docker             # list, by tag (comma separated: any of them)
orgs snip show [words]             # what it is and what it asks for
orgs snip edit [words]             # open it where it is written
orgs snip shell zsh                # the ctrl-s key and snip-prev

    A snippet

    * Docker                                                     :docker:
** Tail a container's logs
#+begin_src bash
docker logs -f --tail <lines=100> <container=web>
#+end_src

    Any sh, bash, zsh or fish block is a snippet (-all takes every language). Its title is its heading, plus its #+NAME: when it has one; its tags are its heading's and the ones it inherits. A :dir header argument is where it runs. Its last #+RESULTS: is shown beside it.

    Parameters

    Written Means
    <name> a value to fill in
    <name=default> with a default (an = in it is fine)
    <flags?> optional: left empty, it is left out
    \<b> a literal <b>, not a parameter
    :var host"db.internal"= babel's way: a parameter where the body says $host
    :var env'("dev" "prod")= babel's way, with choices

    A choice is written as pet writes it, and the first is the default:

    kubectl -n <ns=|_dev_||_staging_||_prod_|> get pods

    The :var form keeps the block runnable with C-c C-c in Emacs. A name used twice is one parameter.

    Values are quoted for the shell as much as where they land needs: inside the command's own quotes they are escaped for those quotes; elsewhere a value is single-quoted only if it has a space or something the shell would act on.
