A glob or a $VAR in a value is left alone, because that is somebody asking for one.

    The form

    With parameters to fill in, a form shows the finished command - redrawn as you type, values in colour - above a field for each one, defaults already in. Tab and shift-tab move between fields, ↑ ↓ cycle a choice, ctrl-u clears, enter runs (or prints, or copies), esc cancels and runs nothing. -set name=value fills one in without asking.

    A snippet with no parameters is shown and asked about before it runs; -y skips the question. Commands run here, in your shell - never on the server.

    The picker

    Snippets you used recently come first. The pane shows the command coloured, its parameters and defaults, where it runs and what it last printed. enter does what the command was asked to do; ctrl-p prints, ctrl-y copies, ctrl-e edits, ctrl-/ hides the pane.

    Saving one

    orgs snip new 'du -ah <dir=.> | sort -rh | head -n <count=20>'   # asks what it does, and tags
orgs snip new -d 'Find big files' -t disk,find 'du -ah ...'      # asks nothing
pbpaste | orgs snip new -d 'From the clipboard'                   # the command on stdin
orgs snip new                                                     # type it, several lines if need be

    It is filed under "Snippets" in snippets.org in your first org directory, through the server's built-in Snippet capture template - which is also in worg's capture dialog and orgs cap. Define a capture template of your own called Snippet to file them somewhere else. A command already saved is refused (-force saves it again).

    In your shell

    eval "$(orgs snip shell zsh)"      # in ~/.zshrc
eval "$(orgs snip shell bash)"     # in ~/.bashrc
orgs snip shell fish | source      # in config.fish

    ctrl-s opens the picker on what you have typed so far and puts the chosen command, filled in, on your command line - to edit, run, and keep in your history like anything you typed. ORGS_SNIP_KEY picks another key. snip-prev saves the command you just ran (snip-prev -d 'what' -t tags).

    Configuration

    The command line and a server on this machine: no login

    A token is only the server's keys applied to a user name, so a command line that has read the server's own configuration - orgJWS, orgJWE and orgSalt - can make one itself rather than ask for a password. It does when it has no token of its own that is still good and url: is on this machine (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1).

    This is how the server VS Code sets up is used from a terminal: its binary reads the orgs.yaml beside it, which is that server's, so orgs agenda just works. Anybody who can read that file could make tokens anyway - it is the password file's equal, and written readable by its owner only.

    DnD

    The Dungeons & Dragons Module

    Introduction

    The dnd module turns orgs into a character builder and character sheet renderer. It gives you:

    • A guided character creation flow over REST, where the server offers the valid choices at every step with the summary and rules text for each one.
    • Characters stored as ordinary, hand editable org files.
    • A rules engine that derives everything else: modifiers, saving throws, skills, armour class, attacks, hit dice, spell slots, save DCs, carrying capacity and the collected feature text.
    • Two character sheet renderers, an html sheet for the screen and a latex sheet that compiles to a printable pdf.
    • An add on system: races, classes, subclasses, backgrounds, items, spells and whole rulesets are yaml files you can drop into a folder.

    The bundled rules are the SRD 5.1, published by Wizards of the Coast under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence.

    Setup

    Enable the exporters you want in your orgs.yaml, and point the module at any folders holding your own content:

    server:
  exporters:
    - name: "dndsheet"     # html character sheet
    - name: "dndlatex"     # .tex character sheet
    - name: "dndpdf"       # pdf, needs pdflatex on the server
      props:
        pdflatex: "/Library/TeX/texbin/pdflatex"
  dndPaths:
    - "/Users/me/dnd/homebrew"

    The REST API and the interactive builder work without any configuration at all: the SRD data is compiled into the binary, and templates/dnd plus ~/.orgs/dnd are searched for add on modules by default. Only the exporters need enabling, because that is how every orgs exporter works.

    The pdf exporter shells out to pdflatex. On a full TeX Live or MacTeX install nothing else is needed: the sheet uses tikz, and picks up ebgaramond and cinzel if they are installed, falling back to the standard fonts if they are not.

    Creating a character

    orgs dnd new                              # the guided flow
orgs dnd new -level 3 -name Lyra -open    # skip the first questions
orgs dnd random -level 5 -out npc.org     # roll a complete character

    Every prompt lists the valid options with a one line summary. A star marks the ones that suit what you have already picked (races that boost your class's primary ability, skills keyed to your best scores). Each prompt also offers to show the full rules text for every option, to choose for you, or to step back and change an earlier answer.

    Going back is safe. The server replays your remaining answers onto a fresh character, so switching class after picking skills cannot leave a stray proficiency behind.

    The character file

    A character is a normal org file. The property drawer of the top heading holds the state, and four sections are read back in: the equipment table, the spell tables, the inventory history and the coin history. Everything else is regenerated whenever the sheet is written.

    #+TITLE: Lyra Silverleaf
#+DND_ID: lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
#+DND_RULESET: srd
#+LATEX_CLASS: dndcharacter
#+LATEX_TEMPLATE: dnd_character.tpl

* Lyra Silverleaf                                          :dnd:character:
,:PROPERTIES:
,:DND_ID:         lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
,:DND_RACE:       elf
,:DND_SUBRACE:    high-elf
,:DND_CLASSES:    wizard:evocation:3
,:DND_BACKGROUND: sage
,:DND_STR:        8
,:END:

    DND_CLASSES is a comma separated list of class:subclass:level entries, which is also how multiclassing is stored.

    DND_ID is the character's identity. Every play session the character appears in gets a heading carrying the same id, so one query gathers the sheet and every night they played:

    MatchProperty("DND_ID", "lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a")

    A sheet written before ids existed does not need editing: the id is derived from the character's name until it is written down, so it is the same id either way, and the next orgs dnd refresh stores it.

    Because nothing derived is stored, levelling up is an edit and a refresh:

    # change DND_CLASSES to wizard:evocation:4, then
orgs dnd refresh -file lyra.org

    Hit points recompute, the proficiency bonus moves to +2, new spell slots appear, the new class features are added and every skill row updates. Set DND_HP_MAX to 0 first if you want the average hit point rule applied rather than keeping your rolled total.

    The character portrait

    A sheet can carry a picture of the character. It is three more properties in the drawer:

    ,:DND_IMAGE:       [[file:art/lyra.png]]
,:DND_IMAGE_FOCUS: 57% 29%
,:DND_IMAGE_ZOOM:  3.2

    DND_IMAGE takes anything that names an image, so whichever form your editor produced works:

    [[file:art/lyra.png][Lyra]] a full org link, description and all
    [[./art/lyra.webp]] a bracket link with no link type
    <file:~/pics/lyra.gif> an angle link
    file:art/lyra.png a plain link
    art/lyra.apng a bare relative path
    https://example.com/lyra.avif a url
    data:image/png;base64,iVBO... an inline data uri

    A relative path is resolved next to the org file, the way emacs would resolve it. Any format a browser can show works, animated gif, webp and apng included. A local file is inlined into the exported html, so the sheet stays one self contained document you can mail to somebody.

    The html sheet frames the picture in a round medallion and moves the character's name and experience onto the frame itself: the name curves around the top, the experience around the bottom, and the outer ring fills up as they climb toward the next level. The header beside it drops both, so nothing is said twice.

    Cropping to a face

    Portrait art is rarely framed for a circular medallion, so two properties choose the part of it to show:

    • DND_IMAGE_FOCUS is the point of the picture that lands in the middle of the medallion, written as x% y% from the top left corner. It defaults to 50% 50%.
    • DND_IMAGE_ZOOM is how far to magnify, so 3.2 shows a bit under a third of the picture. It defaults to 1, which fits the whole picture to the medallion.

    Together they crop a full body illustration down to a head: point the focus at the face and raise the zoom until the shoulders reach the rim.

    The printed sheet honours both, but pdflatex is stricter than a browser - it only reads png, jpeg and pdf files from the local disk. A url or an animated gif is left out of the pdf and noted in the sheet warnings.

    The sheet backdrop

    The portrait is the character's face; the backdrop is the room they are standing in. It is a picture - or a pile of pictures - washed out behind the whole html sheet, and it is three more properties in the drawer:

    ,:DND_BACKDROP:         [[file:art/tavern.jpg]], https://example.com/woods.png
,:DND_BACKDROP_CYCLE:   4m-12m
,:DND_BACKDROP_OPACITY: 18%

    DND_BACKDROP takes the same references DND_IMAGE does, one or more of them, separated by commas or by whitespace. A reference naming a folder stands for every image in it, in name order, so a folder of scenery is one property and dropping another picture into it is the whole of adding it:

    ,:DND_BACKDROP: ~/pics/druid

    A relative path resolves next to the org file, the way emacs would resolve it, and a local file is inlined into the exported html so the sheet stays one self contained document. That is worth remembering with a folder: nine photographs make a sheet a good deal larger than one, and a url is not inlined at all.

    Cycling

    With more than one backdrop the sheet changes picture on its own, picking the next one at random - never the one already up - and crossfading to it. How long a picture stays up is random too, so the sheet never falls into a visible rhythm. DND_BACKDROP_CYCLE sets that dwell time:

    8m eight minutes every time
    4m-12m a random time between four and twelve minutes
    45s forty five seconds
    10 a bare number is minutes
    off no cycling, the first backdrop simply stays

    Left out, a picture stays up for a random five to twenty five minutes. No wait is ever longer than twenty five minutes - a larger one is clamped down to it - and none is shorter than five seconds.

    How washed out

    DND_BACKDROP_OPACITY is how strongly the picture shows through, written as 18% or 0.18, and it defaults to 14%. The backdrop is desaturated a little on top of that, so a busy photograph still reads as a background. It shows strongest across the header and in the gaps between the panels, which sit on their own fill.

    The panels holding the sheet's content - ability scores, saving throws, skills, combat and the rest - go translucent over a backdrop and show a little of it too, a bit less than the bare page does. They paint the picture themselves, pinned to the window the same way the page's backdrop is, so the piece of it inside a panel is the piece that would be behind it and the panels read as glass over the same scene. The stat boxes sitting on them stay solid, so every number has plain paper behind it.

    The backdrop is a screen affair. Printing the sheet leaves it out, and so does the latex sheet - a page of toner spent on a picture nobody asked to print helps nobody.

    Rendering a sheet

    orgs dnd show  -file lyra.org                          # in the terminal
orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -format html -out l.html
orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -format pdf  -out l.pdf

    A backdrop can also be given to the export itself, which paints that one sheet and writes nothing into the character's org file. -backdrop takes a file, a folder or a url and may be given more than once:

    orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -backdrop ~/pics/druid -backdrop-cycle 4m-12m
orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -backdrop a.png -backdrop a.jpg -backdrop-opacity 20%

    The same flags work on orgs dnd import, where they are written into the sheet as it lands, so a character brought over from D&D Beyond arrives with its scenery already on it:

    orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678 -backdrop ~/pics/druid

    Both sheets are pongo2 templates in your template folder, dnd_character_html.tpl and dnd_character.tpl. They receive the whole computed sheet as sheet, so restyling them needs no go code:

    {% for s in sheet.skills %}{% if s.proficient %}*{% endif %} {{ s.name }} {{ s.mod }}
{% endfor %}

    Your armour class

    The sheet works out the armour class the character has while wearing what they are actually wearing. Armour rules the answer:

    • a suit of armour that is worn is the calculation - its own armour class plus dexterity as that armour allows it, all of it for light, at most +2 for medium, none for heavy,
    • and while no armour is worn, it is 10 plus dexterity, or any unarmored defence their classes grant if that is better: a barbarian's 10 + dex + con, a monk's 10 + dex + wis.

    An unarmored defence applies only while you wear no armour at all, which is what the rules say, and it is what makes the Worn column of the html sheet mean something: taking a jerkin off changes the number in the tile.

    Where more than one calculation applies - two unarmored defences from a multiclass, say - the best of them is shown. A shield is counted into each of those before they are compared, not added to whichever won, because not every calculation allows one: a barbarian may carry a shield with their unarmored defence and a monk may not.

    Armour can therefore lower a character's armour class: a barbarian in a leather jerkin is worse off than the same barbarian bare armed. Rather than quietly hand them the better number they are not entitled to, the sheet says what they would have without it - Leather (18 without armor) - so what the jerkin is costing is on the page rather than a surprise.

    Anything that raises AC without being worn as armour - a ring of protection, a cloak of protection - is added on top of whichever calculation won, and the sheet names what it used: Leather + Shield +1 magic, or Barbarian unarmored defense.

    A class in an add on module declares its own defence with unarmoredAc, and unarmoredShield: true if a shield may be carried with it:

    classes:
  - id: "stone-warden"
    name: "Stone Warden"
    unarmoredAc: "10+dex+str"
    unarmoredShield: true

    Your inventory

    The equipment box on the html sheet is live. It stacks identical things into one line with a count, splits them between the containers you are carrying, weighs the lot and tells you whether you are encumbered - and every change is written straight back into the org character sheet.

    • Add item opens a search across every item in your ruleset. The match is fuzzy, the way the character builder's lists are: pot heal finds a Potion of Healing and bkpk finds a Backpack, and a hit says how many you already own. Anything the rules have never heard of is added under the name you type, so loot and homebrew need no module.
    • Use takes one off the stack, which is what a potion or a ration is for.
    • Drop gets rid of some or all of a stack. Emptying out a container hands its contents back to you rather than losing them with the bag.
    • Move puts things into a container - as long as you actually carry it.

    Each container you own gets a tab of its own, beside On Person for what you carry loose. Which items count as containers comes from the ruleset: any item with container: true is one, and capacity is what it holds in pounds. The standard containers of the SRD - backpack, pouch, sack, chest, barrel, basket, bucket, quiver, and the bag of holding and handy haversack - are known without any annotation.

    A container marked extradimensional holds its contents somewhere else, so what is inside it is not part of what you are carrying: a bag of holding weighs fifteen pounds whether it is full or empty.

    The line at the top of the box is the weight you carry against your carrying capacity, and where that lands on the encumbrance scale: encumbered over five times your Strength, heavily encumbered over ten times, and past carrying it altogether over fifteen.

    How it is stored

    Storage is one column on the equipment table, holding the container a line is kept in. Blank means you are carrying it yourself.

    ** Equipment
| Item              | Qty | Equipped | Attuned | Weight | Container | Notes |
|-------------------+-----+----------+---------+--------+-----------+-------|
| Backpack          |   1 | no       | no      |      5 |           |       |
| Potion of Healing |   3 | no       | no      |    0.5 | backpack  |       |

    It is deliberately flat: a pouch inside a backpack is a line stored in the backpack, and the pouch's own contents stay listed under the pouch.

    Inventory history

    Everything that comes and goes is written into an Inventory History section of the character file, and shown on the Inventory tab of the session drawer - it is part of your character sheet rather than of any one night's session log, so it is there whether or not you are recording.

    ** Inventory History
| Date       | Time  | Action  | Item              | Qty | From     | To       | Notes |
|------------+-------+---------+-------------------+-----+----------+----------+-------|
| 2025-09-05 | 19:32 | added   | Potion of Healing |   3 |          | Backpack |       |
| 2025-09-05 | 20:11 | used    | Potion of Healing |   1 | Backpack |          |       |
| 2025-09-05 | 21:44 | moved   | Potion of Healing |   1 | Backpack | Pouch    |       |

    Nothing is derived from the log, it is only read and written, so a line you correct by hand stays corrected.

    Your money

    The purse has a tab of its own beside the inventory. It shows every denomination you hold, what the lot is worth, and what it weighs - fifty coins of any kind weigh a pound - and every change is written straight back into the org character sheet, the same way the inventory is.

    • Spend pays for something. Say the amount however you like: 15 gp, 3 gp 4 sp, or a bare number, which is gold. What goes in the box beside it is what the money was for, and it is kept in the history.
    • Gain is the other direction, for a reward, a sold sword or a purse picked up off the floor.
    • Change up rolls small coin into the largest denominations that hold the same value, which is what you do when the pouch gets heavy. Electrum is left alone: a purse that keeps turning gold into electrum is a nuisance.
    • Exchange trades one coin for another at the standard rate, refusing a swap that will not come out even - three silver is not two electrum and change.
    • Count purse says outright what is in it, for when the sheet has drifted from what is on the table.

    The exchange is D&D's: a gold piece is 100 copper, 10 silver, 2 electrum, or a tenth of a platinum piece.

    Coin In copper In gold
    Copper (cp) 1 0.01
    Silver (sp) 10 0.1
    Electrum (ep) 50 0.5
    Gold (gp) 100 1
    Platinum (pp) 1000 10

    Paying makes change, so what you can afford is what your purse is worth, not what denominations happen to be in it. A two copper candle bought out of a purse holding a single gold piece hands over the gold and takes back nine silver and eight copper; only a price your whole purse cannot cover is refused, and a refused payment leaves the purse exactly as it was.

    Coin history

    What has been spent and earned is written into a Coin History section of the character file, beside the inventory history and read back the same way.

    ** Coin History
| Date       | Time  | Action | Amount | Change    | Balance         | Notes             |
|------------+-------+--------+--------+-----------+-----------------+-------------------|
| 2025-09-05 | 19:32 | spent  | 50 gp  |           | 42 gp 5 cp      | potion of healing |
| 2025-09-05 | 20:11 | spent  | 2 cp   | 9 sp 8 cp | 41 gp 9 sp 8 cp | a candle          |
| 2025-09-05 | 21:44 | gained | 3 gp   |           | 44 gp 9 sp 8 cp | reward            |

    Change is what came back when a coin too large had to be broken, and Balance is what the purse held afterwards. Nothing is derived from the log, so a line you correct by hand stays corrected.

    The coins themselves live in the property drawer, as DND_CP through DND_PP, which is where the sheet reads them from.

    Casting a spell

    Every spell on the html sheet has a Cast button, which does the whole thing in one click:

    • a spell that needs an attack roll rolls it, reporting the normal, the advantage and the disadvantage outcome from the same pair of d20s,
    • a spell that does damage or healing rolls that too, with the critical total beside it when there was an attack to crit,
    • a cantrip's damage is whatever it has grown to at your level - fire bolt rolls 2d10 from 5th, 3d10 from 11th,
    • and a spell the target saves against says so in words ready to read out: "Dexterity saving throw against DC 15, half as much damage on a success".

    A spell that rolls nothing at all - mage armor, say - still lands in the history saying what it costs and how long it lasts, so the tray is a record of what was cast, not only of what was rolled.

    Casts are marked with a star in the roll tray so a spell is told apart from a die roll at a glance. The mark is the panel's; a cast written into a session log is plain text like every other row, with the spell's name, what it rolled, and the salient details - what it hit on, what it would have done on a critical, and what the target still has to roll - in the notes.

    What a spell does when it is cast comes from the ruleset where it says so (attack, save and damage are fields on a spell) and from the spell's own text where it does not, so homebrew spells that read like the SRD's cast correctly without being annotated.

    Spell slots

    Casting a spell of 1st level or higher costs a slot, and the sheet strikes one off as it rolls the spell: the row of boxes at the top of the spell tab fills in, the card in the roll tray says what the cast cost, and the count is written to the character file in the DND_SLOTS_USED property - one number per spell level, in order:

    :DND_SLOTS_USED:      2, 1

    A spell may always be cast from a higher slot than its own, so when the level it asks for is empty the cast reaches for the lowest slot above it that still has one and the card says where it landed. With nothing left at that level or above it the cast is refused, the dice are still yours to read, and nothing is written to the file.

    The boxes are a control in their own right. Clicking an empty one spends a slot of that level and clicking a filled one hands it back - which is how you record a spell cast from a scroll or a ring, which costs no slot at all, and how you take back a cast the table decides never happened. Cantrips cost nothing and are never counted.

    Resting

    The menu behind the stack of lines in the bottom corner of the html sheet has a Short rest and a Long rest button. Either one walks you through the rest a page at a time - what it asks of you, what it gives back - and when you take it, it writes the whole thing to the character file and, if a session is recording, to that night's notes.

    A short rest asks the one question a short rest has: how many hit dice you want to spend. Each die is thrown on the table like any other roll, lands in the roll tray, and adds what it rolled plus your constitution modifier to your hit points, and you decide after each one whether to spend another. Then it hands back every feature that recharges on a short rest, and one spell slot of every level you have spent one at - an hour with your book open is worth that much. A warlock, whose slots all come back on a short rest by the book, still gets all of them.

    That one-slot-a-level rule is this table's, not the SRD's: by the book a short rest returns no slots at all to anyone but a warlock. Rests are worked out in internal/common/dnd/rest.go if you want it back the way it was written.

    A long rest gives back every hit point, half your hit dice rounded down (at least one), every spell slot, and the uses of every limited feature. It also clears temporary hit points and any death saves you were carrying.

    The rest is written into the session log as one note:

    ** 22:14
   *Short Rest.* Hit points 23 of 27, 9 regained.
   - Spent 2 hit dice.
   - Recovered Second Wind (1 of 1).
    Uses per rest

    A feature that the rules ration - "you can use this feature twice, and you regain both uses when you finish a short rest" - wears a row of slots on the Features & Traits tab. Clicking an empty slot spends a use, clicking a filled one hands it back, and either way the count is written to the character file, in the DND_USES_SPENT property:

    ,   :DND_USES_SPENT: channel-divinity=2; second-wind=1

    The limits are read out of each feature's own rules text, so nothing needs annotating for the SRD to work: Second Wind is once per short rest, Wild Shape twice, Divine Sense is 1 + your charisma modifier, and features that grow - Channel Divinity at 6th and 18th level, Indomitable at 13th and 17th - grow with you. Where the srd names the same resource more than once as it improves ("Bardic Inspiration (d6)" and "(d10)") the entries share one pool.

    The three resources the rules print as a column of the class level table rather than in the feature's own text - a barbarian's rages, a monk's ki points, a sorcerer's sorcery points - say so in the ruleset instead, as that column, and get their slots the same way. A 5th level barbarian has three rages; a 20th level one has unlimited rages and so gets no slots at all.

    The reader itself stays deliberately careful, though: a limit nobody stated is never guessed at. If your own module has one worded too strangely to read, write it down and it is believed over the text:

    classes:
  - id: "barbarian"
    features:
      - name: "Rage"
        uses: "3"
        recharge: "long"
      - name: "Ki"
        usesByLevel: [0, 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]
        recharge: "short"

    uses is a bonus formula, so cha, 1 + cha and prof all work. usesByLevel is the level table's own column, indexed by level, and a zero in it means no limit at that level. recharge is short or long.

    Recording a session

    The html sheet can write what happens at the table into an org file. The Session button beside Roll starts a session and the Sessions button next to it lists the ones you have played; the drawer along the bottom of the page takes notes, reads them back formatted, and searches every session you have ever recorded.

    server:
  dndSessionPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dndsessions"   # relative paths hang off orgDir
  dndSessionTemplate: "dndsession.tpl"

    A session is an ordinary org file:

    #+TITLE: Goblin Ambush
#+DATE: [2025-09-05 Fri]
#+SUMMARY: Ambushed on the road to Phandalin, Sildar is missing.
#+CHARACTERS: Lyra Silverleaf
#+FILETAGS: :dnd:session:

* Characters
** Lyra Silverleaf
,   :PROPERTIES:
,   :DND_ID:        lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
,   :DND_CHARACTER: Lyra Silverleaf
,   :END:

* Notes
** 19:32
   The wagon tracks leave the road here.

* Rolls
#+NAME: rolls
| Time  | Character | Roll       | Formula | Result | Dice   | Notes          |
|-------+-----------+------------+---------+--------+--------+----------------|
| 19:33 | Lyra      | Perception | d20 +5  | 18     | d20 13 | adv 22, dis 18 |

    Notes are org markup and are stored as you typed them; headings inside a note are pushed down so they nest under the timestamped entry. Only the * Notes heading, the table named rolls and the #+SUMMARY: keyword are load bearing, so the rest of the file is yours to reorganise.

    Rolls and notes made while the server is unreachable are queued in the page and sent with the next one, and the sheet renews its login token while you play, so a laptop that sleeps mid dungeon loses nothing.

    Browsing the rules

    orgs dnd list classes
orgs dnd list spells -id wizard -filter fire
orgs dnd list subclasses -id fighter
orgs dnd info -kind class -id wizard
orgs dnd rulesets            # which modules are loaded
orgs dnd reload              # re-read them after editing
orgs dnd characters          # every sheet the server knows about

    Writing an add on module

    A module is one yaml file. Everything in it is merged into the ruleset named by its id, so adding content is as simple as dropping a file into a folder on your dndPaths:

    id: srd
races:
  - id: aasimar
    name: Aasimar
    speed: 30
    darkvision: 60
    abilityBonuses: {cha: 2}
    traits:
      - name: Celestial Resistance
        text: "You have resistance to necrotic and radiant damage."

    An entry whose id already exists extends that entry rather than replacing it, so a module can add one subclass to an existing class:

    id: srd
classes:
  - id: fighter
    subclasses:
      - id: ashen-guard
        name: Ashen Guard
        features:
          - {name: Bonded Flame, level: 3, text: "..."}

    Use extends to build a whole variant game that inherits the core data without copying it. Players then pick the ruleset as the first question of character creation:

    id: emberfall
name: "Emberfall"
extends: srd

    templates/dnd/homebrew-example.yaml is a working example of all three techniques, and templates/dnd/backgrounds.yaml adds the twelve backgrounds the SRD does not publish.

    Choices

    Anything of the form "choose N of these" is data, not code. A choices block on a race, class, subclass or background automatically becomes a prompt during character creation:

    choices:
  - id: elf-cantrip
    name: "Elven Cantrip"
    kind: spells        # skills|languages|tools|options|spells|expertise
    count: 1
    from: [wizard]
    spellLevels: [0]
    prompt: "Choose a wizard cantrip."

    countByLevel replaces count when the number grows with level, which is how warlock invocations and sorcerer metamagic work.

    The item catalog

    docs/dnd/ holds a browsable catalog of every item, one org file per source, generated separately from the ruleset yaml:

    File What it holds
    dnd-items-srd.org All 464 SRD 5.1 items, mundane and magic
    dnd-items-homebrew.org Yours. Seeded once, never overwritten
    dnd-items-index.org The master table, built from every source file

    Each item is a heading with a PROPERTIES drawer of normalised columns, a flavor quote, a Capabilities definition list and the full rules text. The index turns those drawers into one sortable table, plus a table per tier so a random treasure roll is a random row.

    python3 tools/dnditems/gen_items.py ../dndsrd docs/dnd

    To add your own items, put them in dnd-items-homebrew.org - or in a new dnd-items-<source>.org beside it for a third party or converted source - as second level headings with the same drawer keys, then run the generator again. It reads every source file back out of org, so anything you add shows up in the index. Only the SRD file and the index are regenerated; your files are read, never written.

    Because the items are ordinary org headings, the server can query them. Point an orgDirs entry at docs/dnd and the drawers become searchable:

    orgs grep -query 'MatchProperty("RARITY","^rare$")'
orgs grep -query 'MatchProperty("KIND","wand") && MatchProperty("ATTUNEMENT","yes")'

    The catalog is a reference for play, separate from internal/common/dnd/data/srd-items.yaml, which is the smaller set of items the rules engine needs for equipping a character.

    Regenerating the SRD data

    internal/common/dnd/data/*.yaml is generated from the markdown SRD at https://github.com/OldManUmby/DND.SRD.Wiki:

    python3 tools/dndsrd/gen_srd.py ../dndsrd internal/common/dnd/data

    Do not hand edit those files, put your changes in a module instead.

    The DM's journal on a map

    The DM screen (a saved map opened in worg's Files tab) keeps your notes on the map itself: a book mark at a spot, seen only on your screen - never the players'. Clicking one opens the note in a window over the map; the window moves by its strip, folds to one line, and grows with its corner.

    A note is an ordinary org heading, in any org file, with two properties:

    * The drowned shrine
:PROPERTIES:
:DND_MAP: ../dungeons/the-grotto.org
:DND_AT:  12.5 8
:END:
Water to the knees. A cracked statue of the king watches the door.

    DND_MAP names the map's org file, relative to the note's file, and is inherited: from a parent heading, or from a #+DND_MAP: line at the top of the file, so a file of notes for one map names it once. DND_AT is where, in squares (across, then down). The note is the heading and everything under it; a sub heading with a DND_AT of its own is a mark of its own as well. Notes cannot live in the map's own org file, which is written again from the map every time it is saved.

    The journal button on the tool rail opens the list of notes. From there:

    • New note on the map - type a title, click the map. It goes into <map>-journal.org beside the map and opens in the editor.
    • Put a heading on the map - pick any heading you already have, click the map. Only its properties change.
    • Drag a mark to move it. note under it adds a sub heading at a spot of its own; off the map takes the properties away and leaves the heading.

    The pencil edits the note's file in the org editor, at the note.

    Links that act on the table

    An org link to dnd: is a button in the window. Emacs and other readers see an ordinary link. While editing, the ⚡ button finds an action by typing and writes its link at the cursor (while reading, it copies it).

    Link Does
    [[dnd:picture:Monsters/dragon.png]] Shows a picture from the map's images folder (path or name)
    [[dnd:picture]] Puts the picture away
    [[dnd:fight:3 Goblin, Ogre]] Brings them into the initiative tracker
    [[dnd:fight]] The same, from the note's own \vert # \vert Monster \vert table
    [[dnd:sound:thunder]] Plays a sound: built in, or yours by name; sound:loop rain, sound:stop
    [[dnd:music:Tavern]] An album or track by name, a spotify: uri; music:stop, music:pause
    [[dnd:weather:storm 0.8]] Weather and its strength (0.1-1); weather:clear
    [[dnd:spell:fire]] Casts at the note; @party, @token:Ogre, @pin:Altar, @12,5
    [[dnd:aura:dome-blue 2]] A lasting effect, two squares out, placed the same way
    [[dnd:screen:quake]] hurt, shake, cracks, sting, eruption, quake, impact
    [[dnd:show:token:Ogre]] The players see it; hide:, toggle:; token, tile, pin, band or any
    [[dnd:reveal]] Lifts the fog over what can be seen from the note; reveal:3 three squares round
    [[dnd:cover:3]] Puts the fog back
    [[dnd:party]] Moves the party to the note
    [[dnd:ping]] A ping at the note, on both screens
    [[dnd:look]] Points the players' camera at the note
    [[dnd:note:The crypt door]] Opens another note on the map

    Several in one link run in turn: [[dnd:weather:storm;sound:thunder;show:token:Ogre][The ogre bursts in]]. A name like Goblin answers to Goblin 2 as well; * is everything of that kind.

    Picking things on the map

    A token, a tile or a pin picked on the DM screen gets a ring of buttons: the eye shows or hides it from the players (you always see it, faded when hidden), and a link button copies a dnd:show: link for it to paste into a note. Tokens can also be made large or small, tiles turned, pins changed in the pins panel, and any of them taken off the map. Tiles are picked while the tiles shelf (G) is open, as before.

    REST API

    Endpoint Method Purpose
    /dnd/rulesets GET Loaded rulesets and the modules behind them
    /dnd/reload POST Re-read the yaml modules
    /dnd/catalog GET Browse races, classes, spells, items…
    /dnd/session POST Start character creation, returns a prompt
    /dnd/session/{id} GET The prompt a session is waiting on
    /dnd/answer POST Answer a prompt, returns the next one
    /dnd/random POST Roll a complete character
    /dnd/save POST Write a character out as an org file
    /dnd/refresh POST Recompute a sheet after hand editing
    /dnd/sheet GET The fully computed sheet as JSON
    /dnd/characters GET Every character sheet the server knows

    The DM's journal on a map:

    Endpoint Method Purpose
    /dnd/journal GET Every note on a map (file the map's org file)
    /dnd/journal POST op place (also by hash), unplace or new: line edits

    The inventory:

    Endpoint Method Purpose
    /dnd/inventory GET What a character carries, and its history
    /dnd/inventory POST Add, use, drop or move something
    /dnd/money GET The purse, what it is worth, and its history
    /dnd/money POST Spend, gain, set, change up or exchange coin
    /dnd/items GET Fuzzy item search, as the add item box asks it

    Spells, slots and rests:

    Endpoint Method Purpose
    /dnd/spellbook GET What a character knows, prepared and in slots
    /dnd/spellbook POST Learn, give back, prepare or unprepare one
    /dnd/spells GET Every spell the character could take
    /dnd/slots POST Spend a slot on a cast, or hand one back
    /dnd/rest GET What a short and a long rest would give back
    /dnd/rest POST Take a rest
    /dnd/uses POST Spend or recover one use of a feature

    And the play session log:

    Endpoint Method Purpose
    /dnd/play/session POST Start or reopen a session
    /dnd/play/sessions GET Every session, newest first
    /dnd/play/session/{id} GET One session: its rolls and notes
    /dnd/play/session/{id}/roll POST Append rolls to the roll table
    /dnd/play/session/{id}/note POST Append notes
    /dnd/play/session/{id}/summary POST Set the one line summary
    /dnd/play/search GET Search every session log

    A prompt carries kind (select, multiselect, text, longtext, number, abilities, fields or done), the valid options, advice based on the character so far, and a progress counter, which is all a client needs to render the flow without knowing any rules.

    Licence

    This module includes material from the System Reference Document 5.1 by Wizards of the Coast LLC, available at https://dnd.wizards.com/resources/systems-reference-document and licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode.

    Appearance

    The appearance step is the one place where the rules have nothing to say, so the builder carries its own tables. Every race has a set of eye, skin and hair colours plus the height, weight and age ranges its people fall into, and each class adds a handful of suggestions on top - a druid is offered moss green eyes, a warlock unnaturally violet ones.

    A ruleset module can supply its own table by adding an appearance: block to a race, which replaces the built in one. Subraces extend their parent rather than replacing it.

    The values are also validated: age, height and weight have to be numbers (in any of the usual notations - 5'6", 168 cm, 12 stone is not accepted but 70 kg is) and have to land in a plausible band for the race, and the three colour fields have to be words rather than numbers. 44 is not an eye colour.

    Buying And Selling

    The inventory knows what a character carries and the purse knows what they can afford, and buying something is the one move that needs both at once. Done as two separate changes it is easy to get half right - the item added and the coin never paid - so a purchase is one call that either happens or does not.

    The price is the item's own cost from the ruleset, times how many are being bought, and it is paid out of the purse the way any other payment is: a two copper candle bought with a gold piece comes back with nine silver and eight copper in change (see money.go).

    Selling is the same move backwards, at half the price. That is the customary rate rather than a rule in the SRD, so it lives here as SellNumerator over SellDenominator where it can be read and argued with, and the line it writes into the Coin History says what was sold.

    Something the rules put no price on cannot be bought or sold for coin: the sheet says so rather than guessing at a value. Loot with no entry in the rulebook is still added and dropped the ordinary way, and the coin for it is gained and spent on the coin tab by hand.

    Casting A Spell

    A spell on the sheet knows what happens when it is cast: whether it needs a spell attack roll, what the target saves against, what it does for damage or healing, and how much of that a cantrip has grown by at this level. That is worked out once by the rules engine, into SpellEntry.Cast, so the html sheet can cast a spell with one click and the same answer would come out of any other client.

    Most of it comes straight from the ruleset - attack, save and damage are fields on a spell - and the rest is read out of the spell's own text:

    • a ranged or melee spell attack, from the phrase the spell uses,
    • the saving throw's consequence ("half as much damage on a successful one"),
    • a cantrip's damage at this character level, from the sentence that lists it: "increases by 1d10 when you reach 5th level (2d10), 11th level (3d10)…",
    • healing, from "regains a number of hit points equal to 1d8 + your spellcasting ability modifier".

    A spell with nothing to roll still says what it does to whoever is on the other end of it, which is the line the sheet shows in place of a result: "Dexterity saving throw against DC 15, half as much damage on a success".

    A cantrip that grows with the character's level carries those levels as well, in SpellCast.Tiers - one entry per level its own text names, up to the one this character has reached, each with the dice it rolls there. The last of them is what the cast button already rolls; the sheet offers the rest beside it the way a levelled spell offers its slots, so the progression can be seen and a lower tier rolled for someone further down the table. A tier is not a slot and spends nothing.

    Casting A Spell At A Higher Level

    Most spells say what happens when they are cast from a bigger slot than they need: "when you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, the healing increases by 1d4 for each slot level above 1st". That sentence is read the same way the rest of a cast is read - once, by the rules engine - into SpellCast.Upcast, one entry per slot level the character could cast it from.

    Each entry carries the whole cast at that level: the damage or healing already grown by the extra dice, the line of detail the roll history shows, and a note saying what the bigger slot bought. So the html sheet offers the levels beside the cast button, rolls the dice the chosen level asks for and spends a slot of exactly that level.

    What can be worked out is what the text actually states: dice or a flat amount added to damage or to healing, either for each slot level above the spell's own or for every two of them. A spell that spends its higher levels on something else - another target, a longer duration, one more dart - still offers the levels, because spending the bigger slot is a real choice, but it changes no dice and says so by quoting the spell instead.

    Character Portraits

    A character sheet can carry a portrait. It is a property in the drawer, so it round trips through the org file like everything else:

    ,   :DND_IMAGE:       [[file:art/lyra.png]]
,   :DND_IMAGE_FOCUS: 57% 29%
,   :DND_IMAGE_ZOOM:  3.2

    DND_IMAGE accepts anything that names an image:

    [[file:art/lyra.png][Lyra]] a full org link, description and all
    [[./art/lyra.webp]] a bracket link with no link type
    <file:~/pics/lyra.gif> an angle link
    file:art/lyra.png a plain link
    art/lyra.apng a bare relative path
    ~/pics/lyra.png a home relative path
    https://example.com/lyra.avif a url
    data:image/png;base64,iVBO... an inline data uri

    A relative path is resolved against the directory of the org file, the way emacs would resolve it. Any format a browser can show works, animated ones included - the bytes are handed to the browser untouched. Local files are inlined into the exported html so the sheet stays a single self contained document you can mail to somebody.

    Cropping to a face

    Portrait art is rarely framed for a circular medallion, so two more properties choose which part of it to show:

    • DND_IMAGE_FOCUS is the point of the image that lands in the middle of the medallion, written as x% y% from the top left corner. It defaults to 50% 50%, the middle of the image.
    • DND_IMAGE_ZOOM is how far to magnify, so 3.2 shows a bit under a third of the picture. It defaults to 1, which fits the image to the medallion the way object-fit: cover would.

    Together they crop to a head: point the focus at the face and zoom in until the shoulders sit on the rim.

    The printed sheet

    dndlatex and dndpdf include the portrait too, but pdflatex is stricter than a browser: it only reads png, jpeg and pdf files from the local disk. A url or an animated gif is left out of the printed sheet and noted in the sheet warnings. Focus and zoom are honoured, the crop is computed from the real pixel size of the file.

    Character Sheet Backdrops

    The portrait is the character's face; the backdrop is the room they are standing in. It is a picture - or a pile of pictures - washed out behind the whole html sheet, and like the portrait it is a property in the drawer, so it round trips through the org file:

    ,   :DND_BACKDROP:         [[file:art/tavern.jpg]], https://example.com/woods.png
,   :DND_BACKDROP_CYCLE:   4m-12m
,   :DND_BACKDROP_OPACITY: 18%

    DND_BACKDROP takes the same references DND_IMAGE does, one or more of them: a full org link, a bare relative or home relative path, a url or a data uri. They are separated by commas or by whitespace, and a bracket link may hold either inside it. A relative path resolves against the directory of the org file, the way emacs would resolve it, and a local file is inlined into the exported html so the sheet stays one self contained document.

    A reference naming a folder stands for every image in it, in name order, so a folder of scenery is one property and dropping another picture into it is the whole of adding it:

    ,   :DND_BACKDROP: ~/pics/druid

    The same thing can be handed to an export instead of written on the character, which paints one sheet and changes nothing on disk:

    orgs dnd sheet  -file lyra.org -backdrop ~/pics/druid -backdrop-cycle 4m-12m
orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678  -backdrop ~/pics/druid

    The import writes it into the sheet it creates; the export does not.

    Cycling

    With more than one backdrop the sheet changes picture on its own, picking the next one at random - never the one already up - and crossfading to it. How long a picture stays up is a random time too, so the sheet never falls into a visible rhythm.

    DND_BACKDROP_CYCLE sets that dwell time:

    8m eight minutes every time
    4m-12m a random time between four and twelve minutes
    45s forty five seconds
    10 a bare number is minutes
    off no cycling, the first backdrop simply stays

    Left out, a backdrop stays up for a random five to twenty five minutes. No dwell time is ever longer than twenty five minutes - a larger one is clamped down to it - and none is shorter than five seconds.

    How washed out

    DND_BACKDROP_OPACITY is how strongly the picture shows through, written as 18% or 0.18. It defaults to 14%, which is enough to colour the page without the text having to fight it. The backdrop is desaturated a little on top of that, so a busy photograph still reads as a background.

    The backdrop is a screen affair: printing the sheet leaves it out, as does the dndlatex / dndpdf sheet, because a page of toner spent on a picture nobody asked to print helps nobody.

    Concentration

    A spell that says Concentration on it lasts only as long as the caster keeps their attention on it, and a caster may hold only one such spell at a time. What breaks it is the part that gets forgotten at the table: taking damage calls for a Constitution saving throw at DC 10, or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.

    So the sheet remembers what is being concentrated on, in the character's own file:

    ,   :DND_CONCENTRATION: hex @2

    The name before the @ is a spell id or a spell name - whichever was written, so the property stays editable by hand - and the number after it is the slot level it was cast at, which is dropped when it is the spell's own.

    Casting a second concentration spell drops the first rather than refusing: that is what the rules do, and a sheet that argued about it would be wrong. Going to zero hit points drops it too, and so does a long rest.

    Drinking A Potion

    Using something up is already an inventory change - one fewer potion, a line in the Inventory History - but for the things that heal it should also be a roll and a change to the hit points, or the player has to drink the potion on one part of the sheet and then type the number into another.

    So an item's own text is read for what using it does:

    - id: "keoghtoms-ointment"
  text: "The creature that receives it regains 2d8+2 hit points..."

    gives 2d8+2 of healing, and the html sheet's Drink button throws those dice on the table and posts the total to the hit points along with the potion being used up.

    As with the use limits in uses.go this is prose parsing and so is best effort by design: an effect the text does not plainly state is never guessed at, and an item with no readable effect simply keeps the plain Use button it always had.

    A Potion of Healing is the awkward case, because the SRD prints one entry for all four strengths and puts the dice in a table:

    | Potion of ...    | Rarity    | HP Regained |
| Healing          | Common    | 2d4+2       |
| Greater healing  | Uncommon  | 4d4+4       |

    A table like that is read as variants, and the sheet asks which one is being drunk rather than picking for you.

    Fallback Portraits

    A character with no DND_IMAGE of their own still gets a face. The module ships one drawn portrait per race, and the html character sheet falls back to the one matching the character's race - or their subrace, if there is a portrait for it - so the medallion is never empty.

    They are flat, stylised busts in the sheet's own parchment and ink, drawn rather than photographed on purpose: a fallback should look like a stand in for a portrait, not like somebody's actual character art. They live in internal/common/dnd/data/portraits/*.svg and are generated - regenerate them with python3 tools/dndportraits/gen_portraits.py rather than editing the svg by hand.

    Each one is drawn to what its race's own entry says about it rather than being a recoloured human: a tabaxi has a cat's ears, muzzle, whiskers and slit pupils, a dragonborn a scaled snout and swept horns, a warforged plates and a lit eye slit, a triton fins and gills, a yuan-ti pureblood scales, slit pupils, no ears and its tongue out, an aarakocra a hooked beak where the nose and mouth would be and a plume of feathers for hair. Every one has brows, eyes and a mouth, because a bare oval reads as somebody the artist did not mean to draw.

    Portraits are carried for the races in the basic rules and for the ones the common supplement rulesets add - aarakocra, aasimar, firbolg, goliath, tabaxi, triton, warforged, yuan-ti and cairnborn - so a ruleset beyond the SRD still gets a face. A race none of them has heard of falls back to a hooded adventurer, so a portrait is always found.

    Nothing is written into the org file: the fallback is chosen every time the sheet is rendered. Setting DND_IMAGE at any point takes over from it, and clearing it hands the character back to their race's portrait.

    Inspiration

    Inspiration is the one thing on a character sheet that is neither earned by the rules nor spent by them: the DM hands it out for playing your character well, and you spend it on advantage when you like. It is a single bit, held in the DND_INSPIRATION property of the org character sheet.

    The html sheet's inspiration marker is a button. Pressing it posts to /dnd/inspiration, the server rewrites the character's own org file, and the answer is what the sheet redraws from - so the page and the file never disagree about whether you are holding inspiration, the same way hit points, coin and inventory work.

    Inventory, Containers and Encumbrance

    The equipment table on a character sheet is a flat list of lines, and the inventory is that same list read as a bag: identical things stacked into one line with a count, split up by the container each is stored in, weighed, and measured against what the character can carry.

    A line says where it lives in its Container column, which holds the slug of a container item the character actually owns:

    ** Equipment
| Item              | Qty | Equipped | Attuned | Weight | Container | Notes |
|-------------------+-----+----------+---------+--------+-----------+-------|
| Backpack          |   1 | no       | no      |      5 |           |       |
| Potion of Healing |   3 | no       | no      |    0.5 | backpack  |       |

    An empty container means carried on the person. Storage is deliberately flat: a pouch inside a backpack is just a line stored in the backpack, its own contents stay listed under the pouch.

    Containers come from the ruleset - any item with container: true is one, and capacity is what it holds in pounds. Rulesets that say nothing fall back to the standard list below, so the generated SRD needs no annotation. An extradimensional container (a bag of holding) carries its contents somewhere else, so what is inside it does not count against what the character is carrying.

    Encumbrance follows the variant rule: over five times Strength you are encumbered, over ten times heavily encumbered, and over fifteen times you are past your carrying capacity altogether.

    The Equipped column says what is being worn or wielded, and it is what the AC and the attack list are computed from: armour you are not wearing does nothing for you. On the html sheet the Worn column of the inventory is a toggle, so a ring goes on with a click. Only what can be worn or wielded offers one - armour, shields, weapons, rings, wands, staffs, rods and wondrous items, plus homebrew the ruleset has never heard of - and only on the person: something in a backpack has to come out first, the same rule that takes gear off when it is packed away.

    Levelling Up

    A character who has earned a level does not need building again. orgs dnd levelup takes the sheet you already have, works out what the new level actually asks you to decide, asks only that, and writes the answers back into the same org file.

    orgs dnd levelup -file lyra.org              # one level
orgs dnd levelup -file lyra.org -levels 3    # three at once
orgs dnd levelup -file lyra.org -class rogue # multiclass, or take a new class

    What it asks about, and nothing else:

    • hit points, every level - the average, a roll, or a number you type in because you rolled it at the table,
    • a subclass, when the level you are entering is the one your class picks at and you have not picked one,
    • an ability score improvement, at the levels your class grants one, with every feat offered as the alternative,
    • anything your class or subclass chooses that has come open at the new level - another invocation, a metamagic, a fighting style, expertise,
    • new spells and cantrips, when the level buys more of them.

    Several levels at once are taken one at a time, in order, so a choice that only exists because of an earlier level is asked at the right moment: a rogue going 2 to 4 is asked for their subclass at 3 and their improvement at 4, in that order.

    Nothing else on the sheet is touched. Your equipment, your coin, your notes and your backstory are exactly where you left them - only the property drawer and the sections the rules engine regenerates change.

    The flow is stateless: each answer is sent back with the ones before it, so there is no session to expire and stopping halfway costs you nothing. Any dice it rolls for you come off the seed in the request, so the same answers always produce the same character.

    Managing Spells

    The spell list on a character sheet is not a free text field: a class knows or prepares a fixed number of spells, drawn from its own list, and none of them above the level it has slots for. The html sheet's Manage Spells panel edits that list live - and this is the engine behind it, so the terminal client and anything else asking the server get the same answer about what may be taken and what is already taken.

    How a class holds its spells decides what the panel can do:

    • a known caster (bard, sorcerer, ranger, warlock) has one budget. Every spell it knows is always available, so taking a spell is the whole of it.
    • a list preparer (cleric, druid, paladin) prepares from the entire class list every morning. Its budget is the prepared count, and a spell on the sheet is a spell prepared today.
    • a spellbook caster (wizard) has two budgets: the spells written in the book, and the smaller number prepared out of it. Taking a spell writes it into the book, and preparing it is a second, separate step.

    Cantrips are their own budget in all three cases and are always prepared.

    Spells a subclass hands out - cleric domain spells, oath spells - carry the subclass as their Source. They are always prepared, never count against a budget, and cannot be given back, because the character did not choose them in the first place.

    Play Session Logs

    A play session is an ordinary org file that records what happened at the table: every die you rolled and every note you took. The html character sheet writes to it live, so the log is a normal org file you can read, edit, refile out of or archive like anything else.

    #+TITLE: Goblin Ambush
#+DATE: [2025-09-05 Fri]
#+SUMMARY: Ambushed on the road to Phandalin, Sildar is missing.
#+FILETAGS: :dnd:session:

* Characters
** Lyra
   :PROPERTIES:
   :DND_ID: lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
   :DND_CHARACTER: Lyra
   :END:
   [[file:/gtd/dnd/lyra.org][Lyra]]

* Notes
** 19:32
   The wagon tracks leave the road here.
* Rolls
#+NAME: rolls
| Time  | Character | Roll       | Formula | Result | Dice     | Notes          |
|-------+-----------+------------+---------+--------+----------+----------------|
| 19:33 | Lyra      | Perception | d20 +5  | 18     | d20 13   | adv 22, dis 18 |

    Only three things in the file are load bearing: the #+SUMMARY: keyword, the * Notes heading and the table named rolls. Everything else in the file is yours. New notes are appended to the end of the notes section and new rolls to the end of the table, so anything you add by hand between sessions is left exactly where you put it.

    Each character who played gets a heading carrying their DND_ID and an ordinary file link to their sheet, so the evening and the character are one click apart in either direction and the link graph knows about both. A session written before the sheet said where it lived has the link added the next time that character writes to it.

    A note already in the file can be said again: POST /dnd/play/session/{id}/note/{index} rewrites that one entry in place and leaves everything around it alone, which is what the Edit button on a note in the character sheet's session panel does.

    A roll can be corrected the same way: POST /dnd/play/session/{id}/roll/{index} rewrites one row of the table. The character sheet uses it to settle a d20. Every d20 is rolled twice, so the tray can show the flat roll, the better of the two and the worse all at once; clicking one of those says which the table was actually owed, and the row that was already written is rewritten to match rather than a second roll being logged. Only the roll still on the card can be settled - once you roll again it stands as it is.

    Ruleset Modules

    The dnd module is entirely data driven. Everything the engine knows about races, classes, backgrounds, items, spells and feats comes out of yaml "ruleset modules". A module is a single yaml file that looks like this:

    id: srd
name: "SRD 5.1 Core Rules"
version: "1.0"
races:
  - id: dwarf
    name: Dwarf
    ...

    Modules are merged together by id. Two files that both declare id: srd produce one combined srd ruleset, so dropping a new file into your dnd path is all that is required to add content:

    # ~/dnd/my-homebrew.yaml
id: srd
races:
  - id: aasimar
    name: Aasimar
    speed: 30
    abilityBonuses: {cha: 2}

    A module can also declare a brand new ruleset that inherits from another one, which is how you build a variant game without copying the core data:

    id: grimdark
name: "Grimdark 5e"
extends: srd
classes:
  - id: witcher
    name: Witcher
    hitDie: 10

    Within a merge, an entry whose id already exists extends the existing entry: scalar fields overwrite when they are set, lists are appended and subraces / subclasses / features merge by id. That means a module can add a single subclass to an existing class without restating the class.

    Modules are searched for in (in order):

    1. The built in SRD data compiled into the binary.
    2. Every directory listed in dndPaths in your server settings.
    3. <templatePath>/dnd and ./templates/dnd, or the dnd folder built into the binary when neither exists.

    Widening a class's spell list

    A book that hands an existing spell to a class that could not cast it before - Tasha's does this a dozen times over for the druid - is widening a spell list rather than adding a spell. Say so with spellLists, keyed by class id:

    id: srd
spellLists:
  druid: ["revivify", "Cone of Cold", "fire-shield"]

    That hands each of those spells to the druid without restating what any of them does, which matters because an entry under spells: whose id already exists replaces that spell outright rather than merging into it. Restating an SRD spell just to widen its class list would fork the generated data and go stale the next time it was regenerated.

    Spells may be named by id or by name, additions from different modules accumulate rather than overwriting each other, and a name nothing answers to is ignored - so a module written against a fuller ruleset still loads against a thinner one.

    Spells the books call something else

    The SRD renames seventeen Player's Handbook spells, because the wizards they are named after are product identity: Tasha's Hideous Laughter is published as Hideous Laughter, and Bigby's Hand as Arcane Hand. A character sheet written anywhere else - imported from D&D Beyond, or typed out by hand - uses the names the books use, so every one of those spells carries the book name as an alias and is found under either. Nothing needs configuring: the set is built in.

    Your own modules can do the same for anything they add:

    spells:
  - id: "hideous-laughter"
    aliases: ["Tasha's Hideous Laughter", "Laughter of Tasha"]

    An alias is only consulted once nothing has matched on id or on name, so it can never take a name that some other spell owns outright, and where two spells claim the same alias the first one loaded keeps it.

    Attaching numbers to a feature

    The SRD data carries the rules text of every feature but no mechanics - it is prose, and the generator does not try to read numbers out of it. A bonuses block attaches the numbers, so a value the sheet computes (and a roll made from it) agrees with the character:

    id: srd
classes:
  - id: bard
    features:
      - name: "Jack of All Trades"
        level: 2
        bonuses:
          checks: "prof/2"

    Features merge by name and level, field by field, so only the block above is needed - the srd rules text is left alone. The fields are:

    field effect
    checks ability checks, and skills not already adding proficiency
    abilities restricts checks to these abilities (default: all six)
    initiative initiative, on top of whatever checks gives it
    saves every saving throw, death saving throws included
    deathSave death saving throws only
    speed the walking speed, in feet
    minimum floors the evaluated bonus
    unless switches the block off while a condition holds

    Each value is a formula: terms joined with "+", where a term is a number, an ability id whose modifier is added, or the proficiency bonus as prof, prof/2 (rounded down) or prof/2up (rounded up). A feat takes the same block.

    unless is the one field that is not a formula. Every feature in the rules that moves a speed is qualified by what you are wearing, so those two qualifications are what it understands:

    value the block is off while…
    heavyArmor you are wearing heavy armour
    armor you are wearing any armour or carrying a shield

    A barbarian's Fast Movement is speed: "10" with unless: "heavyArmor". An unrecognised value never fires, so a module that invents one keeps its bonus rather than quietly losing it. Conditions the sheet cannot check - "while you are raging" - are deliberately left in the rules text instead.

    Sheet Templates

    Both the html and the latex character sheets are ordinary pongo2 templates that receive one variable, sheet, which is the computed sheet converted into plain maps and lists. That means a template can reach anything the engine knows:

    {{ sheet.name }} - {{ sheet.classLine }}
{% for a in sheet.abilities %}{{ a.short }} {{ a.score }} ({{ a.mod }}){% endfor %}
{% for s in sheet.skills %}{% if s.proficient %}* {% endif %}{{ s.name }} {{ s.mod }}
{% endfor %}

    The latex renderer passes every string through a tex escaper first, so ampersands, underscores and the rest of the special characters in a player's backstory cannot break the build.

    Spending A Spell Slot

    Casting a spell of 1st level or higher costs a slot of that level, and the html character sheet marks one off as it rolls the spell. The count lives in the character's own file, in the DND_SLOTS_USED property - one number per spell level, in order - so what the sheet shows and what the org file says are the same thing.

    A spell may always be cast from a higher slot than its own. When the level a spell asks for is empty, casting reaches for the lowest slot above it that still has one left and says so; when nothing at all is left, the cast is refused and nothing is written.

    Which levels a character has slots for is never decided here - that is the rules engine's answer for their classes and level - so the sheet cannot spend a slot the character does not have.

    Taking The Last Thing Back

    Every change the html character sheet makes is written straight into the org file, which is what makes the sheet trustworthy - and what makes a misplaced click expensive. Pressing Drink on the wrong line spends a Potion of Healing and heals you for it, and putting that right by hand means adding the potion back, taking the hit points off again and deleting two lines of history.

    So the last thing that happened can be taken back. Undo reverses one operation - the item that moved, and the hit points or the coin that moved with it - and takes its lines out of the history, so an accident leaves no trace rather than leaving a correction.

    It is deliberately only ever the last thing, and only when it really is the last thing. The character sheet is a file anyone may edit and a rest moves more than any one log records, so before offering to undo anything the plan checks that the character still stands exactly where the line it means to reverse left them. Anything else - a blow taken since, a night's sleep, a hand edit - and there is nothing safe to undo, which the sheet says rather than guessing.

    What can be taken back:

    Last operation What comes back
    Picked something up It goes away again
    Used or dropped It comes back to the container it left
    Packed away It goes back where it was
    Bought The item goes, the coin comes back
    Sold The item comes back, the coin goes
    Drank a potion The potion and the hit points both
    Hurt, healed, temporary The hit points as they stood

    A death saving throw is not on the list: the marks a save left are written to the sheet but the marks it found are not, so there is nothing to put back. The same goes for a rest, which moves hit points, hit dice, slots and every feature at once - undoing that is what the rest walkthrough's own cancel is for, before it is taken.

    The Interactive Builder

    Character creation is a server side state machine. The client never needs to know any rules: it asks for the next Prompt, shows the options (each of which carries a summary, a detail blurb and a "recommended" flag based on what has been chosen so far) and posts an Answer back.

    Because every answer is stored, going back simply drops the later answers and replays the remaining ones onto a fresh character, so changing your class half way through cannot leave stale proficiencies behind.

    The step list itself is generated from the ruleset, so a module that adds a class with a new "choose one of" block automatically gains a prompt for it.

    The Org Character Sheet

    A character is stored as a perfectly ordinary org file. Everything the engine needs lives in the property drawer of the top level heading, plus two hand editable tables (equipment and spells). Every other section is derived and regenerated whenever the sheet is written, so you can level up by editing one property.

    #+TITLE: Lyra Silverleaf
#+DND_ID: lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
#+DND_RULESET: srd
#+LATEX_CLASS: dndcharacter
#+LATEX_TEMPLATE: dnd_character.tpl

* Lyra Silverleaf                                          :dnd:character:
,   :PROPERTIES:
,   :DND_ID:         lyra-silverleaf-4c1f2a
,   :DND_RACE:       elf
,   :DND_SUBRACE:    high-elf
,   :DND_CLASSES:    wizard:evocation:3
,   :DND_BACKGROUND: sage
,   :DND_STR:        8
,   :END:

    The DND_CLASSES property is a comma separated list of class:subclass:level entries, which is how multiclassing is stored.

    The Rules Engine

    dnd.Compute(character, ruleset) turns the small amount of state stored in an org character sheet into a fully derived Sheet: ability modifiers, saving throws, every skill, armour class, initiative, hit dice, attacks, spell save DC, spell slots, carrying capacity and the collected feature text from race, subrace, class, subclass and background.

    Nothing derived is stored in the org file, which means levelling up or changing a single ability score in the property drawer immediately produces a correct sheet on the next export.

    Timeline Annotations

    The timeline works the shape of an evening out of the two logs and writes nothing back, which is what keeps it right after a session has been edited somewhere else. But a block it has found is worth naming: the flurry of rolls at 19:32 was the ambush at the ford, and the room it happened in is worth a line that the dice do not record.

    So an annotation is stored, and only the annotation. It is one entry under a * Timeline heading, stamped with the clock time of the block it belongs to and tagged with what kind of block that is:

    * Timeline
** 19:32 Ambush at the ford                                        :fight:
   They came out of the reeds on both sides. Kael went down in the first
   round and we never did find the fourth one.
** 21:10 The library                                                :note:
   Three floors of it, and every book about the same war.

    Nothing about the block itself is written down - not how many rolls it held, not how long it ran - because all of that is worked out from the logs and would go stale the moment a roll was corrected. The annotation carries the anchor and the prose, and the timeline hangs it on whichever block that time now falls in.

    An annotation whose time no longer lands in any block is not thrown away. It is drawn as a beat of its own at the time it carries, so a note about the room survives the rolls that happened to be in it being deleted - and so that a moment nobody rolled for can be written down in the first place.

    What A Condition Does To A Roll

    A character sheet that knows you are poisoned and then rolls your attack flat is not much of a character sheet. Every condition in the book is already written down on the character - it has a catalog, a picker, a history and a colour it paints the page - and until now none of that reached the dice.

    So the conditions are asked before every d20. Poisoned and prone take the attack roll down, exhaustion takes the checks down and then, at the third level, the attacks and saves with them, restrained takes Dexterity saves down in particular, invisible puts the attack roll up, and the four that leave you helpless - paralyzed, petrified, stunned, unconscious - fail your Strength and Dexterity saves outright.

    Three things are worth knowing about how it is done:

    1. The rules live here, not in the page. The sheet is handed a small map of what each kind of roll is owed and draws it; it never knows what "poisoned" means. A ruleset module that adds a condition adds its rules to conditionRules and the sheet needs no changes at all.
    2. Advantage and disadvantage cancel. That is the rule as written - one of each and you roll flat, however many of each you have - and it is surprisingly easy to get wrong by counting. The card says so when it happens, because a player who knows they are poisoned and sees a flat roll deserves to be told why.
    3. Nothing is forced. The sheet rolls two d20 for every check and shows the flat roll, the better and the worse; all a condition does is decide which of the three stands. The player can still click another, because the caveats are real - frightened only bites while the thing you are frightened of is in sight, and no character sheet can know that.

    What the rules text says but this cannot judge is carried as a note rather than applied: blinded fails checks that need sight, and only the table knows whether this one did.

    Editing

    Editing org files in worg

    The Files tab's Org view is read only until you press Edit. The editor takes vim keys (the default) or emacs keys; pick them under Editor keys in the settings menu. The org commands below work the same way in both. M- is Alt / Option, S- is Shift, C- is Control and SPC is the space bar in vim's normal mode. Open this page with F1, the Keys button under the editor, SPC ? or :help in vim.

    Snippets

    Type the snippet at the start of a line (nothing but indentation before the <) and press TAB. A snippet with blanks to fill in highlights them in turn: TAB goes to the next one, S-TAB back, and TAB off the last one finishes. ESC finishes too, except in a capture, where it takes the whole capture back out.

    Type You get
    <s #+BEGIN_SRC block: language, then the code
    <e #+BEGIN_EXAMPLE block
    <q #+BEGIN_QUOTE block
    <v #+BEGIN_VERSE block
    <C #+BEGIN_CENTER block
    <x #+BEGIN_EXPORT block: format, then the text
    <h #+BEGIN_EXPORT html block
    <l #+BEGIN_EXPORT latex block
    <a #+BEGIN_EXPORT ascii block
    <I #+INCLUDE: line
    <n #+NAME: line
    <tb a two-column table with a header rule
    <cb a checkbox item, - [ ]
    <p a property on the heading, in its drawer (made if it has none)
    <sch SCHEDULED: today on the heading's planning line
    <dl DEADLINE: today on the heading's planning line
    <t an active timestamp of today, <2026-10-02 Fri>
    <i an inactive timestamp of now, [2026-10-02 Fri 09:30]
    <c a capture template, picked from a menu and filled in right here

    <p, <sch and <dl go where org keeps those things rather than where you typed them, and the line you typed them on goes too if nothing else is on it. A property whose name you leave empty is taken out again when you finish, along with the drawer if that leaves it empty.

    Capture templates: <c

    <c TAB opens a menu of the server's capture templates. Type to filter, use the arrows or 1-9, and Enter to pick one. The template is written in place (it is not filed where the template would file it), as blanks to fill: an entry is a heading one level under the heading you are in, with a blank for its tags; dates and values the template answers itself are written in already. Lines that were only a blank you left empty are dropped when you finish, and the tags are written :like:this:. ESC takes the whole capture back out, <c included.

    Structure

    Keys vim normal also What it does
    M-Up / M-Down M-k / M-j move the heading (with its subtree) or list item past its sibling
    M-Left / M-Right M-h / M-l promote / demote the heading; dedent / indent the list item
    M-S-Left / M-S-Right M-H / M-L promote / demote the heading and its whole subtree
    M-Enter SPC n the next thing: a new list item after this one (keeping its bullet, its checkbox and its numbering), or a new heading at this level after the subtree
    M-S-Enter SPC N the same as a TODO heading, or a checkbox item
    C-Enter SPC h a new heading after the subtree, even inside a list
    TAB on a heading TAB, za fold / unfold it (zc zo zM zR in vim)
    TAB on an empty item indent it

    A heading moves with everything under it and never out from under its parent. A list item moves with the lines indented under it. A numbered list is renumbered when an item is added.

    Todo, priority, checkboxes and statistics

    Keys vim normal What it does
    S-Left / S-Right on a heading SPC T / SPC t cycle the todo keyword (back / forward, and off the end to none)
    C-c C-t SPC t next todo keyword, from anywhere in the entry
    S-Up / S-Down on a heading raise / lower the priority: [#A] [#B] [#C] none
    C-c , SPC , cycle the priority
    C-c C-c on a checkbox SPC x tick / untick it, and everything under it
    C-c C-c elsewhere SPC x recount the section's statistics; on a timestamp, put its day name right
    C-c C-x C-b SPC X give the item a checkbox, or take it away

    The keywords cycled are the file's own first #+TODO: line, or the server's defaults when the file has none.

    Ticking a box keeps its parents and their counts right, as org does: a parent item with a box is [X] when all its children are, [-] when some are, and [ ] when none are. A [n/m] or [%] cookie on an item counts its direct children; on a heading it counts the section's top-level checkboxes, or, when there are none, its child headings that carry a todo keyword (so cycling a keyword updates its parent's cookie). Put an empty [/] or [%] where you want one and C-c C-c fills it in.

    Dates, planning and properties

    Keys vim normal What it does
    C-c . SPC . an active timestamp of today; on a timestamp, select its date
    C-c ! SPC ! an inactive timestamp of now
    C-c C-s SPC s SCHEDULED: on the heading: added, or the existing one selected
