    C-c C-d SPC d DEADLINE: on the heading: added, or the existing one selected
    S-Up / S-Down on a timestamp change the part under the cursor: year, month, day (or the day name), hour, minute (in 5s)
    S-Left / S-Right on a timestamp a day earlier / later
    C-c C-x p SPC p set a property: a new line in the heading's drawer, or a new drawer
    C-c \vert{} SPC \vert{} the paragraph into a table (split on tabs, commas or spaces); a blank line starts one

    A date that goes in is left selected, so you can type over it or move it with the shifted arrows straight away, then TAB or ESC. The day name is always recomputed, and a time range keeps its length. Scheduling a heading with a deadline puts both on one planning line. A planning line or drawer that goes in takes the indentation the heading's body already has.

    Vim

    SPC in normal mode is the leader: the status line shows SPC- and the next key runs one of the org commands above (SPC ? opens this page).

    Keys What it does
    jk, jj leave insert mode, when typed quickly (within 200ms)
    :w save
    :wq, :x save and close
    :q close (asks if there are unsaved changes)
    :q! close, throwing the changes away
    :help this page

    The rest is vim: motions, operators, text objects, registers, visual modes, / search, :s substitution, macros. The mode is shown under the editor: NORMAL, INSERT, VISUAL, V-LINE, V-BLOCK, REPLACE. Leaving insert mode with jk or jj while filling in a snippet finishes it, keeping what is there.

    Emacs

    Keys What it does
    C-f C-b C-n C-p forward, back, down, up
    C-a C-e start, end of line
    M-f M-b forward, back a word
    C-v M-v page down, up
    M-< M-> start, end of the file
    C-SPC, C-g set the mark (select as you move), cancel
    C-k kill to the end of the line
    C-w M-w C-y kill, copy, yank the region
    C-d M-d M-DEL delete a character, a word forward, back
    C-t C-o transpose characters, open a line
    C-/ C-_ C-x u undo
    C-s search
    C-x C-s save
    C-x C-c close
    F1 this page

    Jump

    C-; in either key set (or SPC ; in vim's normal mode) jumps to anything you can see. Type a character or a word that is on screen: each place it is found is lit, with a letter tag over its first character, nearest the cursor first. Type the tag and the cursor is there. Keep typing the word instead to narrow it down: a tag is never a letter that would carry on the word, so a key always means one or the other. With more places than letters the tags are two letters long.

    Lowercase finds either case; type a capital and only that case is found. Enter goes to the nearest, Backspace takes a letter back, Esc (or a click) gives up. With text selected, the jump extends the selection.

    Saving

    ⌘S saves in either key set, and so does C-s in vim (in emacs C-s is search, so use C-x C-s). A save is refused when the file has changed on disk since you started editing - a capture, a kanban drag, Emacs - and you are offered to overwrite it or to throw your edit away and reload. Leaving the editor, the file or the Org view with unsaved changes asks first.

    Pictures

    A link to a picture - [[file:img/map.png]], [[./photo.jpg][a caption]], a https: url, or a bare file:x.png - has the picture drawn under its line, here and in the Org view. It is never part of the text: the cursor steps over it and nothing is written into the file. A link inside a source or example block is left alone.

    • Images on the status line shows or hides every picture in the file. The file's own #+STARTUP: inlineimages or noinlineimages decides until you choose; with neither, they are shown.
    • An eye at the end of a picture link's line, there while the pointer is on the line, shows or hides that one picture, whatever the file is set to. The eye on a picture's corner hides it too.
    • #+ATTR_ORG: :width 300 (else #+ATTR_HTML: :width) just above the link sets its width, in pixels, a percentage, or a fraction (0.5). Otherwise a picture is its own size, held to the column and to 60% of the window's height.
    • Click a picture to see it full size; Esc or a click puts it away.
    • A picture that cannot be shown says why: no such file, or outside the folder the server shares (the first org directory).

    What you choose is remembered for each file in this browser.

    Writing mode

    Write on the Files toolbar opens the editor in writing mode; the Writing button under the editor turns it on and off. It stays on for the next file until you turn it off. The bar over the text switches each part on its own:

    • Outline: the file's headings down the side, nothing else, with the words under each. The heading you are in is lit. Click a heading to go to it, the triangle to fold it. Drag a heading to move it with everything under it: drop on the top of another heading to go before it, on the bottom to go after it, in the middle to go in as its last child; the levels change to fit. With the outline focused: Up Down walk it, Left Right fold and unfold, M-Up M-Down move the heading, M-Left M-Right promote and demote it, Enter back to the text.
    • Typewriter: the line you are writing stays in the middle of the window, and the text fades out towards the top and bottom. Scrolling (wheel, trackpad) moves the cursor with the text, so it stays on the middle line. F8 turns it on and off. The menu beside it (▾) sets where the fade starts: how far in from the top and bottom edges, as a share of the window, the text goes from nothing to full strength (none at all, up to 45%). The plain editor has its own typewriter switch, on the status line by Writing (off unless you turn it on; F8 there too), sharing the same fade.
    • Focus: the paragraph, sentence or line you are in stays bright and the rest is faded back while you type.
    • Font: serif, sans or mono, in wrapped lines the width of the pane.
    • Column: the text in a narrow column in the middle of the pane, like a page. Off unless you turn it on.

    On a phone the outline and the assistant slide over the text from the left rather than sitting beside it; picking a heading in the outline puts it away.

    • Check: spelling (red), grammar (blue) and style (green) underlined as you write, over your prose only - not links, timestamps, drawers or source blocks. Rest the mouse on an underline to see what is wrong and click a fix; right-click the word to take the first fix (shift right-click for the browser's own menu). A misspelling can be added to your dictionary (kept in this browser) or ignored until the page is reloaded. The menu by Check turns each kind on and off and switches on LanguageTool (below). Without it, the built-in speller and rules are used and no text leaves the browser.

    Beside those, the icons on the bar:

    • Corkboard: the headings at one level as index cards - title, status as a coloured strip, synopsis (or the first words, greyed), words against the target, and how many cards are under it (click that to look inside; the path at the top goes back up). Click a card to edit its synopsis and status, double-click to write it, drag it onto the left or right half of another to move it there with everything under it.
    • Storyline: who is in which scene, as a chart. The scenes run left to right (the headings with nothing under them, or every heading at the level you pick, chapters say); each character is a line through them, and the lines of everyone in a scene are drawn together in it, so you can see who meets whom, who drops out of the story and for how long. Who is in a scene comes from its CHARACTERS property (commas between names) and POV (the point of view, drawn as a dot), and, with Names found in the text on, every name you write often enough (pick how often) that appears in the scene. A TENSION from 0 to 10 on the scenes draws the story's arc over the top; each scene's words and status are under it, and the chapters are bands behind it. Hover a line or a name to pick it out, click a name in the cast to hide it (a place found as a name, say), hover a scene for its synopsis and cast, click it to go there.
    • Second pane: another file, or this one as it was when you opened the pane, read only beside the text, with a list of its headings to jump to.
    • One section alone: only the heading you are in and what is under it, the rest hidden behind a bar with the way back (Show the whole file). Double-clicking a heading in the outline does the same for that heading.
    • Targets (the flag): words for this session (kept in the browser), for the file (#+WORD_TARGET: in the file) and for the heading you are in (WORD_TARGET on it). The status line shows the session and the file as rings; the outline and the cards show a heading's as a bar.
    • Goals (the chart): its Check In tab has your words today, this week and this month against the goals you set, with what is still to go and what that is a day; your streak (days in a row you met the daily goal, or wrote at all when there is none) and the longest; and a heatmap of every day you wrote, a square a day, Monday at the top. Hover a square for its words, click it for the files you wrote in that day. This file and Every file change what is counted. Clicking the word count under the text opens it too. Goals and look sets the words a day, a week (seven days' worth when left empty) and a month, and how many days off a week a streak survives; these are kept on the server, so every browser sees them. It also sets how the heatmap looks (kept in the browser): gradual (a smooth ramp up to the daily goal), solid (one colour for any words), stops (a step of colour at each word count you list, such as 100, 500, 1000) or liquid (each day fills from the bottom up to the goal); its hue, how many weeks, rounded or square cells, and the month and day names. A dot marks a day that met the goal. The flag's menu opens it too. The count is kept on the server per person, as the file's word count at the start and end of each day, so it is the words added less the words taken out.
    • Compile (the share icon): tick the headings that make the book (anything tagged notes or noexport, or with the status Notes, starts unticked) and pick a Word manuscript (with its style and paper), an ebook, a web page, the org text or plain text. Drawers and planning lines, and the synopses, statuses and targets, are left out unless you say otherwise. Nothing is written to your files: the server exports the text it is sent.
    • Full screen: the editor over the whole window, nothing else on it (⌘⇧Enter / C-S-Enter too); the browser's own full screen as well where it allows. Esc leaves the browser's full screen and the editor's with it.

    Each heading's synopsis, status and word target are edited from the pencil on its outline row or from its card, and kept as its SYNOPSIS, STATUS and WORD_TARGET properties, so Emacs sees them too. The statuses are To do, First draft, Revised draft, Final draft, Done and Notes; the outline can show the synopses under the titles (its first button). The same dialog keeps snapshots: a copy of the heading and everything under it, taken before a rewrite, compared with the text as it is now (removed lines red, added green), restored (undo takes a restore back) or deleted. Snapshots are kept beside the file, in .snapshots/<file>.json.

    The checker also marks a name spelt two ways - a capitalised word used once or twice that is one slip away from one used three times or more (Marra for Mara) - with the common one as its fix, and stops calling the common one a misspelling. Under style, a word used again within 25 words of the last time is marked (dotted), names and common words left alone.

    Revision

    Notes to yourself about the text, kept in the file as comment lines under the paragraph they are about:

    The letter was waiting when Mara came in from the boats.
# NOTE: too slow, start with the letter itself
# NOTE "the boats": which boats? set this up in chapter one
# NOTE[done]: check the tide tables

    A comment line is never exported - not by orgs, not by Emacs - and Compile leaves notes out of the org and plain text it makes too, so a note cannot end up in the book. Type them by hand, or:

    • Add a note: ⌘⌥M (Ctrl-Alt-M) in either key set, SPC r in vim, C-c r in emacs, or the Revision menu (the speech-bubble icon on the writing bar). The selected words, if they are on one line, become the note's quoted words and are lit in the paragraph.
    • In writing mode each note is a card in a margin beside its paragraph (the margin is there only while the file has notes; the Revision menu turns it off). A card's box marks it done, its × deletes it, a click on its words changes them - Enter keeps, Esc leaves. Note lines are folded out of the text, except the line the cursor is on, so a note typed by hand stays in view. On a phone, or with the margin off, notes fold to a pill at the end of their paragraph that opens them in place.
    • The status line counts the notes still to fix; click it (or Every note in the menu) for all of them, under their headings, to tick off or jump to.

    Show changes since (in the Revision menu) compares the text with an earlier one - when the file was opened, the last save, or a snapshot of a heading - and lights the words put in, strikes through the words taken out where they were, marks lines added and shows lines taken out struck through above where they were. It is worked out a second after you stop typing.

    Compendium

    The book on the writing bar opens the compendium: the people, places and things the story is about, kept in an org file beside it, and what the text says about them.

    • Where it is: the files named by #+COMPENDIUM: at the top of the manuscript (several, separated by spaces, relative to it), else <manuscript>.compendium.org beside it, else compendium.org in the same folder. With none, the pane offers to make <manuscript>.compendium.org.

    • Entries: a heading with a KIND property (character, place, thing, group, other), or any heading straight under a top-level * People, * Places, * Things or * Groups heading. ALIASES are its other names (commas between); every other property is a fact (EYES, BORN, ROLE…); the text under it is its notes.

      * People
** Mara Vell
:PROPERTIES:
:ALIASES: the harbourmaster's girl
:EYES: grey
:BORN: 1032
:END:
Grew up on the fishing boats.
    • Names are found as whole words in the prose (not headings, drawers or blocks): a name with a capital letter as written, an all-lowercase one ("the salt road") in any case. A character is also known by each capitalised word of its name (Mara Vell is Mara and Vell) unless that word names something else. The speller and Harper never flag a compendium name.
    • The pane: entries by kind, with a search. Click one for its facts (click a value to change it, empty removes it; the last row adds one), its notes, and the scenes it is in - click a scene to go to its first mention, or Next mention for the next after the cursor. The count beside each entry is how often the text names it; amber 0 is never. + adds an entry, named from the selected words if any. Every change is written to the compendium file as a small edit, refused if the file changed meanwhile.
    • Hover: rest on a name in the text for its card - kind, facts, notes, how often it is mentioned. The setting compendiumUnderline adds a faint dotted underline under every name it knows.
    • Things to check: one name given to two entries; a fact written two ways (the same entry in two compendium files, or a scene's FACT property, such as :FACT: Mara.eyes = green; Tobin.age = 40, against the compendium or an earlier scene); an age in a FACT that does not fit BORN and the scene's WHEN year; a character in a scene whose WHEN is before they were born. Click one in the manuscript to go to it.
    Ideas

    The light bulb on the writing bar opens the ideas pane: things made up on the spot to get a stuck scene moving or fill in a world. Nothing is sent anywhere and no AI is involved; the server rolls them from its own tables.

    • What it makes: under People, a Character (age, work, looks, manner, wants, fears, strength, flaw, habit, secret), Names that sound as if they come from one place, and a Relationship between two people. Under Places, a Settlement, a Scene setting (what you see, hear, smell and feel there, something off, something that could go wrong) and a Tavern (keeper, drink, regulars, tonight, the house rule and the talk). Under Societies, a Culture, a Religion and an Organisation. Under Story, a Premise, a Complication, a Conflict (by kind), an Opening, an Object with a past, Treasure (where it was found, in what, what's in it, and the catch) and Weather (sky, wind, how it feels, now and then something remarkable, the light and the mood, by season).
    • Genre: fantasy, science fiction, contemporary or any. It is chosen once for the pane, since a book is in one genre; each generator's other options (role, names, season) are remembered on their own. Invented names come from a small made-up language for each result, so a culture's people, towns and gods sound related.
    • Using one: a card shows the idea as a short paragraph; click its title for the details. The buttons under it put the paragraph into the text at the cursor (undo takes it out), leave it as a revision note on the cursor's paragraph, file it in the compendium (characters, places, cultures, faiths, organisations and objects; each detail becomes a property, the paragraph its notes), or copy the details.
    • The tables are orgs' own: over seventeen thousand entries in plain text files (internal/common/storygen/data/*.txt) compiled into the binary, so nothing ships beside it. Each table says at its top the sentence its entries are dropped into; to add to one, add lines and rebuild. An entry under = all= that suits only some genres ends with them in brackets: a crewmate left outside [sf], the vicar's bicycle [modern]. GET and POST /writing/ideas are the same generators for anything else that wants them.
    Harper

    Harper is a grammar checker that runs in the browser itself, so like the built-in checker nothing you write is sent anywhere. It is on unless you turn it off in the menu by Check (▾), and is used whenever LanguageTool is off.

    • Its spelling takes over from the built-in dictionary: it knows which English you write (American, British, Canadian, Australian or Indian, chosen in the menu - "harbour" is right in British) and suggests better fixes. Names you have written three times or more, and words added to your dictionary, are still never misspellings.
    • Its grammar and style rules sit beside the built-in ones: a problem either finds is marked, once. The built-in checks Harper does not make (a name spelt two ways, a word repeated close together) stay.
    • Its problems say "· Harper" and offer Ignore this rule; the rules switched off are listed in the menu, each with a × to turn it back on.
    • Runs: in this browser (the first check fetches Harper, about 20MB, and takes a few seconds; the built-in rules stand in until then), on the orgs server (each paragraph checked goes to orgs, which runs Harper; the page loads nothing - for phones, which cannot spare the memory), or automatically: the server on a phone or small tablet, this browser elsewhere. On a phone, Automatically never loads Harper into the page: if the server has no Harper, only the built-in rules check. The same rules, dialects and fixes either way.

    • For the server to run it, orgs.yaml needs:

      server:
  harper:
    enabled: true

      orgs then starts Harper's own language server (harper-ls) the first time a check asks for it. One installed (brew install harper, cargo install harper-ls) is used; otherwise orgs downloads the release for this machine from GitHub once (download: false stops it, path: names one).

    Prose

    The chart-with-a-magnifier on the writing bar shows the whole file in numbers, prose only (drawers, planning lines, code and link targets are left out). Every finding is a click from its place in the text.

    • The totals: words, sentences, words a sentence, sentences over forty words, reading ease (Flesch: 60-70 is plain English, higher is easier) and grade level, and how much is dialogue.
    • Sentence rhythm: a bar for each sentence in reading order, as tall as it is long and shaded short to very long; dashes mark the scenes. A run of bars all the same height is prose that drones; click a bar to go there.
    • Readability by chapter and dialogue and narration by scene (dialogue is what is inside quotation marks).
    • Words worth a second look: -ly adverbs, filter words (saw, heard, felt, noticed - the reader one step behind the character's eyes), weak words (very, really, just, suddenly), dialogue tags other than said and asked, your most used words (names and small words left out) and three-word phrases used three times or more. Open one to see every place it is used.

    None of it is a rule; it says how often and where. The refresh button counts again after you have written more.

    Scene synopses and the continuity check

    Two more uses of the assistant (below), each with its own button on the writing bar. Both use the backend and model picked in the assistant pane, and both see only what they say they send.

    • Scene synopses (the short lines): tick the scenes - those with no synopsis are ticked to begin with - and the assistant writes an index-card synopsis for each, two at a time, from that scene's text alone. Read them, change any, untick what you do not want; Save writes the rest as the scenes' SYNOPSIS, which the outline and corkboard show. Undo takes them back.
    • Continuity check (the ticked list): the assistant reads the scene the cursor is in, its chapter, or the selection, against everything before it in the file, your compendium, and the files you have let the assistant read, and lists what contradicts it: names, looks, ages, relationships, who knows what, where people and things are, times and the order of events. Each item quotes the words in the passage (click to go there), says what is wrong, and quotes the earlier text it contradicts. Nothing in the file is changed. It is an AI reading: it can miss things and can be wrong.
    Dictation

    The microphone on the writing bar (or F9) lets you talk instead of type: what you say is written in at the cursor, a phrase at a time, by the whisper the server already uses for voice notes (voice: in orgs.yaml).

    • Talk naturally. Each time you pause (most of a second) the phrase just said is sent off and appears at the cursor a moment later, while you go on. A long run without a pause is sent every twenty-five seconds anyway.
    • Phrases join the text sensibly: a space before them unless the cursor is after one or at the start of a line, a capital after a full stop or on a new line. The text before the cursor goes along as whisper's prompt, so it keeps your spelling of names and carries a sentence on across a pause.
    • Say “new paragraph” or “new line” (on their own) for a break, “scratch that” to take the last phrase out again, and “stop dictating”, F9 or Stop to finish. Stopping writes down what you were in the middle of saying first.
    • Everything goes in as ordinary typing: undo takes it out, and nothing is saved until you save.
    • The strip at the foot of the text shows that it is listening, how loud you are, how many phrases are waiting to be written down, and the last one. Whisper's noise for silence ([BLANK_AUDIO], a lone “Thank you.”) is dropped. A noisy room raises the level that counts as talking.
    • The audio is not kept: each phrase is transcribed and thrown away (voice notes keep theirs).

    The browser needs to be allowed the microphone, which it only allows over https or on localhost. On a phone it works the same way.

    The assistant

    The sparkle on the writing bar opens an AI assistant in a pane down the left of the text: Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini, whichever the server has keys for. The arrow at its top folds it to a strip; the sparkle again puts it away.

    • Backend and model: picked at the top, from those the server offers (assistant: in orgs.yaml, below). One with no key shows as "no key".
    • Keys (the key at the top, or Set up a key when none is set up): for each service, whether it has a key and where from, and how to get one - a link to the service's key page, then paste the key and press Test and save. The server tries it with the service first and keeps it only if it works, in its OS keyring (or, with no keyring, a file beside orgs.yaml only its owner can read); it is used at once, ahead of a key in orgs.yaml or the environment, and never sent back to the browser. Remove takes it away. Only an administrator of the server can set keys (anyone, with noAuth), since what the assistant does is billed to them.
    • Sees of this file: the section the cursor is in, the whole file, or nothing but what you type. Your selection is always sent along when there is one. The line under it says roughly how much that is.
    • Can read: this file, and nothing else unless you add a file there. Each added file is sent whole with every question; take it off with its ×. Added files are remembered for this file in this browser. The server reads only the files named, and only org files it serves; it refuses anything else.
    • Actions: Continue (from the cursor), Rephrase, Tighten and Show, don't tell (on the selection - select text first), Critique, Synopsis, Names and Questions. Anything typed in the box is added to the action's request.
    • Each answer has Insert (at the cursor; as a paragraph of its own at the start or end of a line), Replace (the selection) and copy. Both are ordinary edits, so undo takes them out again. Stop ends an answer part way; the bin starts a new conversation.
    Claude Code, on a subscription

    The Claude Code (subscription) backend runs the claude command on the server's machine, signed in with your Claude Pro or Max plan, so nothing is billed as API use. It is also the one backend that can look things up and make changes itself:

    • It reads the files under Can read when it needs them (they are not sent whole with every question), and can search them. It sees no other file.
    • The pencil on a file's chip lets it change that file; all are read only until you click one. Changes to the file you are editing go into the editor, unsaved, and one undo takes each back; changes to another file are saved to disk straight away. Pencils are remembered per file in this browser.
    • What it read and changed is listed above its answer. An edit that no longer fits the text (you changed that passage while it worked) is not made, and says so.
    • Each question starts the claude command afresh with its own tools, files, settings, hooks and CLAUDE.md all turned off, so it can do nothing else on the machine.

    To set it up, sign in once on the server's machine as the user orgs runs as (claude login), or make a long-lived token with claude setup-token and give it as apiKey, then turn it on:

    server:
  assistant:
    backend: claudecode          # make it the default
    claudecode:
      enabled: true              # it is off until this is set
      model: opus                # the claude command's names: opus, sonnet, haiku (the others are offered)
      effort: medium
      command: ""                # the claude command, if the server's PATH does not have it
      apiKey: "env:CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN"   # only for a token from claude setup-token

    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is taken out of its environment, since with it set the claude command would bill the API instead. It is meant for your own writing on your own server: a subscription is one person's, so do not turn it on for a server other people use.

    Local models, with Ollama

    Ollama (local) runs a model on the server's own machine through Ollama: nothing you write leaves it and nothing is billed. Local models are slower than Claude and the small ones write less well, but those that can use tools read and edit your files exactly as Claude Code does above (the pencils, the notes over each answer, undo).

    The chip button at the top of the assistant pane opens Local models:

    • Ollama: whether it is installed and running. With none installed, Install Ollama fetches the latest release from GitHub (about 200 MB) into the server's cache and starts it; one already running (Ollama.app, brew services) is used as it is. orgs starts ollama serve itself when it is needed and stops it with the server; Stop keeps it down until Start.
    • Context length: how much text the model holds at once - the instructions, what it sees of the file, what it reads. More takes more memory and is slower to load; a model's own limit is never passed. Kept in this browser; Server default is contextLength below. When what is sent will not fit, the answer says so rather than losing the start of it.
    • Installed: each model with its size and what it can do: tools (can read and edit files), no tools (sees only what is sent), thinks, loaded (in memory now). Use picks it for the pane (the model menu in the pane does too); the bin deletes it from the server, after a second click.
    • Add a model: any name from the Ollama library (qwen3:8b, gpt-oss:20b), or one of the suggestions. Downloads run on the server, so closing the page does not stop one; each shows its progress and can be stopped. A model needs roughly its size in free memory to run.

    Installing, starting, stopping and changing models are for an administrator of the server (anyone, with noAuth); everyone can pick among the models.

    server:
  assistant:
    ollama:
      enabled: true              # off until this is set
      model: qwen3:8b            # the default, if installed (else the first one)
      contextLength: 16384       # tokens; also OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH for an Ollama orgs starts
      url: http://127.0.0.1:11434   # another machine's Ollama works too (orgs only starts a local one)
      serve: true                # start ollama serve when nothing answers
      download: true             # allow Install Ollama from worg
      command: ""                # the ollama binary, if not on the PATH or in Ollama.app
      modelDir: ""               # where models are kept (default ~/.ollama/models)
      keepAlive: 30m             # how long a model stays loaded after a question
      think: false               # thinking on or off for models that can (unset: the model's default)

    Nothing is sent until you ask. The conversation is about this file and goes when you open another.

    On the server (keys never reach the browser):

    server:
  assistant:
    backend: claude              # the default; "off" turns the assistant off for everyone
    claude:
      apiKey: "keyring:anthropic"   # or "env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", or the key itself
      model: claude-opus-5-5
      models: [claude-sonnet-5-5]   # others to offer
      effort: medium                # low, medium, high, xhigh, max
    chatgpt:
      apiKey: "env:OPENAI_API_KEY"
      model: gpt-5
      url: ""                       # an OpenAI-compatible server (a local model) instead
    gemini:
      apiKey: "env:GEMINI_API_KEY"
      model: gemini-flash-latest

    With no apiKey each backend reads its usual environment variable, and Claude also an ant auth login profile. disabled: true hides one backend.

    LanguageTool

    LanguageTool is a real spelling, grammar and style checker. Switch it on in the menu by Check (▾) and it does all three; the built-in rules stand in for a paragraph until its answer comes. The menu has:

    • Server: the orgs server's own (one orgs runs for you, set up in orgs.yaml, below; your text goes to orgs and no further), public (api.languagetool.org, free, with limits), premium (api.languagetoolplus.com, with your user name and API key), or another server by its url (http://localhost:8081). The public and premium servers are sent each paragraph you check. Test sends one sentence and says what answered, in what language, and how fast.
    • Language: detect it (the default, steered by the preferred varieties, en-US unless you say en-GB), one from the list, or any code.
    • Mother tongue: finds false friends for a writer whose first language it is.
    • Picky: LanguageTool's stricter rules for style, tone and wordiness.
    • Check as I type: off, paragraphs are only sent when you press F7.
    • Rules and categories: rule and category ids to switch on or off. Ignore this rule on a problem's fixes adds its rule to the ones switched off.

    Add to dictionary works on LanguageTool's misspellings too: your words are never marked, whoever checks.

    To have orgs run LanguageTool, add to orgs.yaml either an unzipped LanguageTool (LanguageTool-stable.zip, which needs java 17 or later):

    server:
  languageTool:
    enabled: true
    path: "~/tools/LanguageTool-6.6"   # the folder holding languagetool-server.jar

    or, with no path, docker (the erikvl87/languagetool image unless docker: names another). It listens on port 8082 (port:); one already running there is used rather than started again, and orgs stops the one it started when it stops. ngrams: names LanguageTool's n-gram data for the their/there kind of mistake, javaArgs: ["-Xmx2g"] gives it more memory, and url: instead of enabled: passes the checks on to a LanguageTool somebody else runs.

    Keys What it does
    F7 the next problem, with its fixes
    S-F7 thesaurus: synonyms for the word at the cursor
    F8 typewriter on or off (in the plain editor too)
    ]s [s (vim) next, previous problem
    z= (vim), M-$ (emacs) fixes for the word at the cursor
    SPC y (vim), C-c y (emacs) thesaurus

    In a list of fixes or synonyms: the arrows or 1-9, Enter to take one, Esc to put it away. The thesaurus works anywhere in the editor, writing mode or not. It asks datamuse.com, sending only the word looked up. Spelling uses an English (US) dictionary inside the page.

    Babel: Python Sessions

    :session keeps one python running for a file, so that a block can use what an earlier block made - the way the cells of a notebook share a kernel:

    #+PROPERTY: header-args:python :session analysis :results output

#+BEGIN_SRC python
import statistics
xs = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
#+END_SRC

#+BEGIN_SRC python
statistics.mean(xs)
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS:
: 2.8

    Only python has sessions; a :session on any other language is ignored and each block runs on its own, as before. :session none, or no :session at all, is a fresh python for every block.

    • A session belongs to its name and its org file. Two files with :session main have one each.
    • Like a notebook, the value of a block's last line is shown after what it printed (:results output), or is the whole result (:results value). A line ending in ; is not shown.
    • A matplotlib figure the block drew is saved where :file says (further figures get -2, -3…), or under <file>_files/ when it says nowhere, and linked in the result.
    • A pandas table that is the block's value comes back as an org table.
    • An exception is written as the result, the traceback in place of the output, as a notebook shows it. The run still reports that it failed.
    • !ls, %pip install, %matplotlib inline, %%bash and their commonest relatives work, so a cell pasted from Jupyter runs.
    • A block that runs past babel.timeout is interrupted (a KeyboardInterrupt, which keeps the session); one that ignores that is killed, and the session starts again next time.
    • A session left alone for an hour stops, and every session stops with the server. POST /babel/sessions/stop stops one now, which is how a notebook is run again from the top.
    • :python /path/to/venv/bin/python picks the interpreter, as in org; babel.commands.python does it for every file.

    Babel: Results, Calls And Inline Code

    What org's C-c C-c does, from any client: run what is at a line and write what it produced into the file.

    Results

    A block's result is written under it as #+RESULTS:, replacing the one that was there. Its shape follows :results:

    Written Comes out as
    (text, short) : line for each line
    (text, ten lines on) an #+begin_example block
    table an org table
    list an org list
    file [[file:...]]
    raw the text as it is, to be read as org
    drawer inside a :RESULTS: drawer
    html, latex an export block
    code, org a source block
    silent, none nothing written
    append, prepend added to what is there instead of replacing it
    pp python's value pretty printed (:results value pp)
    link, graphics with :file: the code writes the file itself, and the result is the link

    :results words come in groups - collection (output, value), type (table, list, scalar, verbatim, file…), format (raw, drawer, pp, link…) and handling (replace, append, silent…) - and, as in org, a word nearer the block replaces an inherited one of its own group: :results replace on a block undoes a file's header-args :results append.

    A block named with #+NAME: writes #+RESULTS: name, so another block can take it as a variable. :eval no (or never) is never run.

    A block that fails (a non-zero exit) has what it printed and what it wrote to standard error written as its result, so the error is in the file where the answer would be. :stderr yes adds standard error after the output of a block that worked (for programs that warn, or answer there).

    Around the program and the result

    Header Does
    :prologue "text" put before the program (after its variables)
    :epilogue "text" put after it
    :wrap the result in #+begin_results … #+end_results
    :wrap example … in any block: :wrap src python, :wrap quote
    :post fmt(x=*this*) run block fmt with *this* standing for the result, and write what it returns instead
    :cache yes run only when the code or its inputs changed: the result is written as #+RESULTS[hash]: and a run with the same hash leaves it be
    :stdin name a table (or result) by name as standard input - for awk, which reads its program from a file

    Noweb

    With :noweb yes (or eval, no-export, strip-export, strip-tangle), a block's <<name>> is replaced by the code of block name (or of every block whose :noweb-ref is name) before it runs, and <<name(args)>> by the result of running name with those arguments, as a #+CALL: would. Text before a reference on its line is repeated on every line it brings in (:noweb-prefix no turns that off). Tangling reads references the same way.

    Calling a block

    #+NAME: double
#+BEGIN_SRC python :var n=1
return n * 2
#+END_SRC

#+CALL: double(n=21)

    runs double with n set to 21 and writes the result under the call. A call names its block by #+NAME:, looked for in its own file first and then in every file the server watches, so a file of useful blocks works as org's library of babel. Header arguments may go in square brackets after the name or after the arguments: #+CALL: double[:results raw](n=2) :results table.

    Inline code

    src_python{return 6*7} and call_double(n=4) in a paragraph run in place, and their result follows them as {{{results(=42)}}}=. An inline result has to fit on a line.

    Variables

    :var x=name takes a table by its name, the result of a named block (which is run first), a #+RESULTS: name already in a file, a named list (its items) or a named example block (its text). other.org:name names one in another file, relative to this one.

    An index picks part of a table or list, counting from 0 as org does, rules included: data[2,1] a cell, data[,0] a column, data[1:3] rows 1 to 3, data[-1] the last row, * everything at that level.

    A table's first row is its column names when a rule is under it: they are taken off before the block sees the table and put back on its result when that is a table the same width (:colnames no passes the header as data, :colnames yes always takes the first row, :colnames '(a b) names the result's columns). :rownames yes does the same with the first column. Rules are left out unless :hlines yes, which passes them as the language's null (None, nil…).

    Every language gets its variables in its own way: an assignment before the code for python, ruby, perl, lua, R, javascript, powershell and shell (a table as tab separated text); package-level var=s for go (a body with no =package main and func main is wrapped in them, as ob-go does, and :imports "os" "strings" adds imports); a let round the program for emacs-lisp; -v name=value for awk; and $name substituted in the SQL for sqlite (a table as the path of a csv file with its header, for .import; :db names the database, :colnames yes or :header prints a header, and the answer comes back as a table). A table handed to gnuplot is written to a file and bound as its name, so plot data using 1:2 works as it does in org.

    Pictures

    dot (graphviz), plantuml, ditaa, mermaid (mmdc) and gnuplot blocks draw a picture where :file says, and the result is a link to it. The picture's format follows the file's extension.

    Ledgers

    A beancount block is a journal, asked a question by bean-query: the question is :cmdline (BALANCES when it says none), and the answer comes back as an org table. A ledger block runs ledger -f over itself with :cmdline as the report (bal by default).

    #+BEGIN_SRC beancount :cmdline "SELECT account, sum(position) GROUP BY account"
2026-01-01 open Assets:Bank
...
#+END_SRC

    :cmdline works for every language: its words go after the code's file on the command line, split on spaces with quotes holding words together, and never through a shell.

    Bable Block Execution

    Capture

    The capture tool can take a quick snippet of text and turn it into a targetted org entry in a file of your choosing. With Refile capability Capture can be a major asset when helping you organize your thoughts.

    Configuration for the system is done through the captureTemplates entry in your orgs.yaml file:

      captureTemplates:
    - name: "BasicEntry"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicItem"
      type: "item"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicCheckItem"
      type: "checkitem"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicPlain"
      type: "plain"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "BasicTable"
      type: "table-line"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "Datetree"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+datetree"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures"
    - name: "OlpDatetree"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+olp+datetree"
        filename: "test.org"
        id: "Captures::Level1::Level2"

    The template string

    A template may also carry a template: of its own, which is the shape of what gets captured. The server does nothing with it - it hands the client's headline and content to the file exactly as they arrive - so the string is a form for the client to put up: worg reads it in worg/src/capture.ts and turns it into boxes to fill in, and anything else talking to /capture is free to do the same or to ignore it.

       - name: "QuickNote"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "notes.org"
       id: "Inbox"
     template: |-
       :PROPERTIES:
       :CREATED: {{now}}
       :SOURCE:  {{source|Where did this come from?}}
       :END:
       {{CONTENT}}

    Note the |-. A yaml scalar written over several lines without it folds its newlines into spaces, so the whole template arrives as one line - which is a property drawer that is not a property drawer. Use a block scalar for anything longer than one line.

    The syntax is four spellings of one thing:

    Written Means
    {{CONTENT}} The body - one big box, and where a
    dictation or a pasted picture lands
    {{name}} A value to fill in, labelled from the
    name
    {{name\vert prompt}} The same, asked for in your own words
    {{name\vert =value}} Pre-filled with a default, still editable
    {{name\vert prompt\vert =value}} Both

    The last two are written by the server, not by whoever writes the template.

    Some names answer themselves, and the server answers them. A placeholder whose name is in the table below is answered on the way out of /capture/templates, and the answer is written in as that placeholder's default:

      :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}}         ->  :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid|=f81d4fae-7dec-...}}
  :CREATED:   {{now}}          ->  :CREATED:   {{now|=[2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]}}
  :WHEN: {{now|When was it}}   ->  :WHEN: {{now|When was it|=[2026-09-29 ...]}}

    A default rather than a substitution, because both halves matter:

    • a client that knows nothing about any of this has a usable value in the box already, so :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}} works without a line of client code - and crypto.randomUUID is secure-context only in a browser, so for worg served over plain http from another machine the server is the only end that can answer it at all;
    • a client that would rather answer it itself still sees the name, and can ignore the default - which a substitution would have taken away. A value written in as literal text is a value nobody can change, and the timestamp on a capture is very often the one thing somebody does change: a thing captured today did not necessarily happen today.
    Name Becomes
    {{uuid}} / {{guid}} f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6
    {{shortuid}} js3xiyiy - 8 characters, a-z and 2-7
    {{daypage}} worklog/Mon_2026_09_28.org - the
    current day page, relative to the
    first org directory
    {{username}} / {{user}} ian - whoever asked
    {{hostname}} the machine holding the org files
    {{date}} 2026-09-29
    {{time}} 14:05
    {{datetime}} 2026-09-29 14:05
    {{today}} / {{active}} <2026-09-29 Tue>
    {{now}} / {{inactive}} [2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]
    {{timestamp}} [2026-09-29 Tue 14:05]
    {{tomorrow}} <2026-09-30 Wed>
    {{yesterday}} <2026-09-28 Mon>
    {{week}} 2026-W40
    {{month}} 2026-09
    {{year}} 2026
    {{day}} 29
    {{weekday}} Tuesday
    {{dayname}} Tue
    {{epoch}} / {{unix}} 1790690700
    {{iso}} / {{rfc3339}} 2026-09-29T14:05:00Z

    So a capture that wants an id of its own needs nothing but the property:

       - name: "Note"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "notes.org"
       id: "Inbox"
     template: |-
       :PROPERTIES:
       :CUSTOM_ID: {{uuid}}
       :CREATED:   {{now}}
       :AUTHOR:    {{username}}
       :SOURCE:    {{source|Where did this come from?}}
       :END:
       {{CONTENT}}

    Four things about the answering (internal/common/captemplate.go is the grammar, internal/app/orgs/capturefill.go the wiring):

    1. A name with no answer is left standing, braces and all, so a client's reading of a template is unchanged by this pass: it sees fewer holes, never different ones.
    2. One value per name per template, aliases counted as one name, so {{uuid}} written twice in one template is the same uuid both times and a :CUSTOM_ID: and an id: link to it in the body agree. Two templates in one answer get two uuids, because they are two different captures.
    3. It is idempotent. A placeholder that already carries a default is left alone, so a template cannot collect a second answer however many times it goes past.
    4. They are answered when the list is asked for, not when the capture is made. worg re-asks every time its capture dialog opens and orgs cap asks once per run, so a uuid is fresh per capture; a client that holds one list open all day and captures from it twice would offer the same uuid twice.

    /ext/capture/templates, which is where a user edits their own templates, is deliberately not answered: it hands back the template as written, or saving one back would bake this afternoon into it for ever.

    A line whose only content was a placeholder nobody filled in is dropped rather than written empty, so a template offering three optional properties writes the one that was answered.

    A template with no string at all asks for a headline and a body, which is what every example above is.

    Placeholders in the target filename

    The same names work in target: filename:, answered when the capture is made. There is nobody to ask at that point, so a name that does not answer itself (and has no |= default) refuses the capture rather than make a file called {{project}}.org.

       - name: "DayLink"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "{{daypage}}"
       id: "Inbox"
   - name: "Scratch"
     type: "entry"
     target:
       type: "file+headline"
       filename: "tmp/{{date}}_{{time}}_{{shortuid}}.org"
       id: "Notes"

    In a filename every value is made filename safe: brackets dropped, spaces to _, colons to -. So {{now}} is 2026-09-29_Tue_14-05 and {{time}} is 14-05. {{daypage}} keeps its /, being a path. A missing folder is created.

    A filename that comes out as the current day page, when that page does not exist yet, is created the way orgs daypage creates it - from the day page template, with last week's open tasks - rather than as an empty file.

    The filename is answered separately from the template body, so a {{uuid}} in both is two different uuids.

    Clock Table

    Time clocked under headings, summed. Two ways to get one:

    • orgs clocktable -block thisweek (and GET /clockreport) report every file at once, straight to the terminal;
    • a #+BEGIN: clocktable dynamic block writes the report into the file and rewrites it whenever it is refreshed. See Dynamic Blocks for its parameters.

    A range is one of:

    Written Means
    today, yesterday, today-N a day
    thisweek, lastweek, thisweek-N a week, Monday to Sunday
    thismonth, lastmonth, thismonth-N a month
    thisyear, lastyear, thisyear-N a year
    untilnow everything ever clocked
    2026-10-04, 2026-10, 2026 that day, month or year
    2026-W40, 2026-Q3 that ISO week, that quarter

    A clock running across the edge of the range counts only the part inside it, and one still running counts up to now.

    Clocking

    TODO: Fill in information on how to use the orgs clocking features

    Constants

    Constants are names a table formula can use. They are not template values; for those see Template values.

    • #+CONSTANTS: vat=0.2 shop=Corner anywhere in the file makes $vat and $shop available to every table in it.
    • The properties of the heading a table sits under are there as $PROP_NAME: :RATE: 40 is $PROP_RATE.
    • pi, t, f, True and False are always defined.

    Constants are text, not numbers: wrap one in value() to calculate with it, as in $2=$1*(1+value($vat)). The table formula guide (Tables) has the full story.

    Day Page

    The day page module is designed to quickly create a worklog file for you every day. It is driven off a template file:

    daypage.tpl

    This template file will expand into a new worklog file when asked. I tend to operate with a single day page per week as I find a daypage per day is to verbose and a daypage per month is to messy.

       dayPagePath: "C:/path/worklog/"

    My personal day page template looks about like so at the moment.

       #+TITLE:  {{day_page_title}}
   #+AUTHOR: Me Myself

   * Inbox

   * Mon
   * Tue
   * Wed
   * Thu
   * Fri

    Detangling and Auto-Tangling

    Detangle

    Tangling writes code out of an org file; detangling brings edits made to the tangled file back into the org blocks they came from (org's org-babel-detangle). It needs the markers a tangle writes with :comments link (or both):

    # [[file:setup.org::*Install][Install:1]]
brew install ripgrep
# Install:1 ends here

    orgs detangle install.sh reads the file, finds each marked section, and writes its code back into that block with a line edit - the block's own indentation kept, org's comma escape put back where a line would read as a heading. -dry-run says what would change. A block whose code has noweb <<references>> is left alone: the tangled file holds their expansion, and that cannot be put back as one block's code.

    Put :comments link on every block with #+PROPERTY: header-args :comments link.

    Auto-tangle

    A file that says so is tangled every time it is saved:

    #+auto_tangle: t

    Only files that ask: nothing is tangled on its own otherwise. A tangled file that says the same as before is not rewritten. One that has been edited by hand since orgs last wrote it is not overwritten: the tangle stops for that file and says so (an event, and the server log), so detangle it, or tangle it by hand with orgs tangle -w to throw the edit away.

    Dynamic Blocks

    A dynamic block is a part of a file that orgs writes for you and rewrites on request: a clock report, a column view, a list of headings a query finds. Everything between the #+BEGIN: and #+END: lines is replaced; nothing else in the file is touched.

    #+BEGIN: clocktable :scope file :maxlevel 2 :block thisweek
#+END:

    Refresh one with orgs dblock FILE LINE, every block in a file with orgs dblock FILE, and every block anywhere with orgs dblock -all (a cron line that keeps the week's clock tables current).

    clocktable

    The time clocked under headings, the way org writes it: one time column per outline level, a bold total, and a file column when more than one file is reported.

    Parameter Meaning
    :scope file (default), subtree, tree / treeN, agenda (every file), or a list
    of files: ("work.org" "home.org")
    :maxlevel deepest level listed (default 3)
    :block today, yesterday, thisweek, lastweek, thismonth, lastmonth,
    thisyear, lastyear, today-3, thisweek-2, untilnow, 2026-10-04,
    2026-10, 2026-W40, 2026-Q3, 2026
    :tstart start of the range, as a timestamp or a typed date (<2026-10-01>, -2w)
    :tend end of the range, exclusive
    :match an org tags match (+work-meeting); only matching headings count their time
    :query an orgs query (IsStatus("DONE")); only matching headings count their time
    :indent nil to write titles without the \_ indentation
    :fileskip0 with several files, leave out the ones with no time

    Weeks start on Monday, as they do in org. A clock that crosses the edge of the range counts only the part inside it, and a clock still running counts up to now.

    columnview

    org's column view written as a table.

    Parameter Meaning
    :id local (the heading the block is under, default), global (the whole
    file), file:notes.org, or a heading's ID / CUSTOM_ID
    :format a #+COLUMNS: line; otherwise the file's own, then the server default
    :maxlevel deepest level listed
    :hlines t for a rule between every row, N for one above each level <= N
    :indent t to indent the ITEM column by level
    :skip-empty-rows t to leave out rows with nothing but a title
    :exclude-tags (tag1 tag2) - headings carrying any of these are left out

    Summed columns (%EFFORT{:}) show the rollup. A #+TBLFM: line under the table is kept and run again after every refresh.

    query

    The headings an orgs query finds, as a table.

    #+BEGIN: query :q "IsStatus(\"NEXT\")" :columns "TODO ITEM FILE DEADLINE" :link t
#+END:

    :q is required. :columns defaults to TODO ITEM FILE and takes the names a #+COLUMNS: line takes, with or without their %. :scope file keeps to this file, :limit N stops after N rows, :link t makes each title a link to its heading.

    insertdatetime

    The moment the block was refreshed, as an inactive timestamp. :active t writes an active one, :format "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" writes it your way.

    Any other name is looked up among the dynamic blocks plugins register.

    Exporters

    TODO: Fill in information on working with exporters

    Finding Source Blocks

    GET /code answers with every #+BEGIN_SRC block the server holds, read rather than merely located: its language, the name another block would call it by, its switches, its babel header arguments, and its variables.

    The variables are the reason this endpoint exists rather than a grep. A variable may be a literal, or it may be the name of something else in the file - a table, a list, the results of another block - and there is no way to tell which by looking at the text. The database knows, so each variable comes back with what it resolves to and where that thing lives:

    #+NAME: monthly
| month | sales |
|-------+-------|
| Jan   |   120 |
| Feb   |   180 |

#+NAME: chart
#+BEGIN_SRC python :var data=monthly :var scale=2 :results file
  ...
#+END_SRC

    data comes back as a reference to a table of two columns and three rows; scale comes back as a literal. A name that resolves to nothing comes back with an empty kind, which is worth saying out loud: it is a block that cannot run.

    Parameter Meaning
    lang Only blocks in this language
    q Only blocks matching this text

    q is matched against the code, the name, the language, the heading, the file and the variable names - somebody looking for a block remembers any one of those.

    Importing A Jupyter Notebook

    orgs import analysis.ipynb (or worg's new file dialog, "Import a Jupyter notebook") turns a notebook into an org file that runs: every code cell a #+BEGIN_SRC block, its outputs the #+RESULTS: under it, and the whole file one python session, so running the blocks top to bottom is running the notebook.

    #+TITLE: Penguin measurements
#+PROPERTY: header-args:python :session penguins :results output
#+STARTUP: inlineimages

* Loading the data
#+BEGIN_SRC python
df = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv")
df.shape
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS:
: (344, 7)
    • The title is the notebook's own (metadata.title), else its first heading, else its file name.
    • Markdown becomes org: headings (so code lands under the heading it sat under), emphasis, inline code, links, pictures, lists, quotes, fenced code, tables and rules. $…$ and $$…$$ are left alone, since org reads them as they are. HTML that has no org spelling goes in an export block.
    • Outputs are written the way running the block writes them, so running it again replaces them rather than adding to them: printed text as =: = lines, a simple html table (a pandas dataframe) as an org table, a picture saved beside the file in <name>_files/ and linked, a traceback with its colours taken out. A cell with several outputs has them in a :results: drawer.
    • A cell that drew a picture says :file where, so running it again draws over the same picture.
    • Pictures pasted into markdown cells (attachment:) are saved too.
    • Raw cells become export blocks.

    nbformat 4 is read, and 3 as far as its cells go; anything older is refused with a message saying so.

    Keeping Blocks Current

    Some of a file is worth recomputing on its own: a source block that reports disk use or a CI status table, a clock table, a column view, a table's formulas. orgs reruns them on a timer, writes what changed with line edits (nothing else in the file moves), and hands an export a freshly computed copy so a published page is never stale.

    Scheduled source blocks

    A source block, or a #+CALL: line, with a :schedule header argument is run again on that schedule and its #+RESULTS: updated. It needs babel.enable, as running any block does.

    #+NAME: disk
#+BEGIN_SRC sh :schedule 1h :results table
df -h / /home | awk '{print $1, $5, $6}'
#+END_SRC

#+CALL: ci-status(repo="orgs") :schedule 15m

    The schedule is a length of time (30m, 1h, 2d, 1w, 1h30m), a word (hourly, daily, weekly), or a time of day (daily 07:30, 07:30: once a day, at or after that time). The shortest is a minute. Like any header argument it can be inherited: #+PROPERTY: header-args :schedule 1h puts every block in the file on the hour.

    A run that produces what the file already says writes nothing, so a block checked every five minutes does not rewrite its file every five minutes.

    Refreshing dynamic blocks and tables

    • :refresh 1h on a dynamic block's #+BEGIN: line refreshes that block.
    • #+REFRESH: 1h in a file refreshes all of its dynamic blocks and runs every #+TBLFM: in it.
    • refresh.every in the server settings does that for every file that has a dynamic block or a table formula.

    A table is written only when its values change, never just to realign it.

    On export

    An export (/file/html, orgs export, orgs site, typst and beamer pdfs) reads a copy of the file with its dynamic blocks refreshed and its table formulas run, in memory: the page is current and the file is not written because somebody exported it. refresh.onExport: false turns this off, and refresh=f on a request skips it once.

    Settings

    server:
  refresh:
    every: 1h          # every file's dynamic blocks and table formulas
    onExport: true     # default
    scheduled: true    # run :schedule blocks (default; babel.enable must be on too)
    tick: 30           # seconds between looks at what is due

    orgs refresh lists everything on a timer, when it last ran and how it went; orgs refresh run runs it now.

    Refile

    TODO: Fill in information on orgs server refiling

    Running A Source Block

    POST /code/run runs one #+BEGIN_SRC block and hands back what it produced, read the way org reads a babel result rather than as a lump of text: a table comes back as an org table, a list as an org list, a :results file as a link.

    It is off unless it is turned on, under babel: in the server settings. Reading somebody's org files and executing the programs inside them are different promises, and the second is made deliberately.

    What gets run

    The block's code, with its variables written in front of it in the language's own syntax. A :var scale=2 becomes an assignment; a :var data=monthly naming a table becomes that table as a list of lists, so the code can walk it. This is the whole point of babel and the reason the variables were resolved in the first place.

    Two languages take their code and not their variables: go and emacs-lisp are compiled or scoped in ways that do not survive a prepended assignment, and a variable silently missing is worse than one that was never offered.

    What comes back

    :results is read the way org reads it, and what is not said is guessed at from the output rather than assumed:

    Written Means
    :results output What it printed
    :results value What it returned - python is wrapped in a function
    :results table Read the output as a table
    :results list Each line an item
    :results file The output is a filename; comes back as a link
    :results raw As it stands
    nothing Output, and a table if it looks like one

    "Looks like one" is three shapes: lines already written as an org table, lines separated by tabs, and the list of lists a python or lisp block prints when it returns one. Anything else is text, because a paragraph split into columns on a guess is worse than a paragraph.

    Table Browsing And Editing

    The table endpoints let a client list every org table the server knows about and edit one as a spreadsheet. A table is addressed by the file it lives in plus its ordinal position within that file (Id), counted in document order starting at zero.

    Writing a table only rewrites the lines the table occupies, so the rest of the file is left byte for byte as it was. The #+TBLFM: lines of a table are rewritten as a single line holding every formula, separated by ::.
