    • upstream changed (closed, merged, reopened): the heading's keyword follows it, through the same state change as any other, so CLOSED and the logbook entry are written as the file's logging settings say;
    • upstream did not change but the heading did (you marked it DONE, or moved a DONE one back to TODO): the issue is closed, or reopened, upstream;
    • an item that no longer turns up in any of the queries (unassigned, review given) and is still open is gone: it gets the gone keyword and is no longer followed or written back.

    Pull and merge requests are only closed with close: all, never merged, and never when they are only review requests - DONE on a review means you reviewed it. Reopening is for issues only. A heading deleted from the file comes back on the next poll while the item is still open; archive it once it is DONE instead.

    Google Calendar Auto Sync

    This integrates with your google calendar Syncing the calendar locally as org mode files.

    This is currently a one way sync and cannot sync back to your calendar!

    To create your credentials, you need to go here: https://console.cloud.google.com/

       - name: "googlecal"
     credentials: "<your creds, usually a json filename>"
     token:       "<your token, usually a json filename>"
     output:      "path/filename you want to output to"
     numevents    30
     freq: 300

    Here we are polling every 300 seconds (5 minutes) and we are asking the google API for a copy of our calendar to store in path/filename.

    ICS Calendar Importer

    TODO More documentation on this module

       - name: "ics"
     timezone: "America/Los_Angeles"
     filename: "path to ics file to import"
     output: "where to output org data"

    Jira

    TODO More documentation on this module

       - name: "jira"
     endpoint: "your endpoint https://go-jira.atlassian.net"
     user: "The user operating on jira"
     queries: "List of JiraSearch objects"

    Notify

    The notify plugin tells you about what is coming up: a native notification before each timed appointment on today's agenda, and once a day a digest of the deadlines that are due or overdue. It shows them on the machine the server runs on - Notification Center on macOS, the desktop's notification service on Linux, a toast on Windows - and publishes every one as a notify event, so orgs notify listen can show them on another machine when the server lives somewhere else.

    A click on a notification opens the heading in worg (on macOS this needs terminal-notifier: brew install terminal-notifier). Saved-query watches with desktop and the end of each focus (pomodoro) phase go out the same way, with the same quiet hours.

     - name: "notify"
   freq: 60                # seconds between looks at the agenda
   remind: [10, 2]         # minutes before a timed appointment; one reminder each
   deadlines: "08:30"      # the day's deadline digest; "" for none
   quiet: "22:00-07:00"    # no popups in these hours (events still go out)
   sound: true             # the system's notification sound
   focus: true             # announce the end of each focus / break phase
   desktop: true           # pop on this machine; false: only publish events
   open: "http://localhost:8010"  # where a click goes; the server itself by default
   icon: "/path/to/icon.png"      # optional

    The older notifybeforemins and beep settings are still read: they mean a single remind and sound. Run orgs notify test to see a notification, and orgs notify status for what this server will do.

    Each reminder is sent once, and the server remembers which it has sent (notify_data.json beside the clock's state), so a restart does not repeat them. If a poll happens to cross two reminder times at once - a server started a minute before a meeting - only the later reminder is sent.

    Todoist

    TODO More documentation on this module

       - name: "todoist"
     token: "todoist api token"

    Trello

    Mirrors Trello boards into org files: a heading per list, a heading per card under it with its due date as a DEADLINE, its labels as tags, who is on it, its description, and its checklists as checkboxes. The files are written by the poller and rewritten when the board changes, so they are for reading, searching and putting on the agenda rather than for editing.

    server:
  plugins:
    - name: trello
      key: "your api key"            # https://trello.com/power-ups/admin
      token: "your token"            # or leave it out and keep it in the
                                     # keyring under orgs-trello
      doneLists: ["Done", "Shipped"] # cards in these lists are DONE
      boards:
        - id: "aBcD1234"             # the part of the board's url after /b/
          file: "~/org/trello-website.org"

    A card marked complete (its due date ticked) or in a done list is DONE; every other card is TODO. Archived cards and lists are left out.

    Querying

    Overview

    Many operations in orgs require you to select the nodes that the operation applies to.

    • Agendas
    • Filtered Tabular Lists
    • Various Exporters
    • Etc

    Lots of these things require a filtered list of nodes to operate. Orgs does this through a node filter. This is an expression that is applied to nodes in the DB and returns only those nodes that pass the query.

    The most common expression starts with:

    !IsArchive() && IsTodo()

    This will select all active nodes that have an active TODO status on them throughout all of your org mode files. Note the negation on IsArchive() these expressions support most common operators

    Agenda views will often add a date query:

    !IsArchive() && IsTodo() && OnDate('<specific date>')

    People who follow GTD will often want lists that follow the common patterns:

    !IsArchive() && IsProject()
!IsArchive() && IsTodo() && IsStatus('NEXT')
!IsArchive() && IsTodo() && ( IsStatus('WAITING') || IsStatus('BLOCKED') )

    This represents some of your common lists that you need to review regularly:

    • Projects List
    • Next Actions List
    • Waiting On List

    Orgs Expression Methods Reference

    • IsProject - returns true for nodes that are defined as a project (see project definition)
    • HasAStatus - returns true if a node has a valid status
    • IsPartOfProject - returns true if a task is a subnode of a project node
    • HasTags - returns true if a node has any tags
    • HasTagMatching - returns true if any tag on the node, its parents or the file matches a regular expression: HasTagMatching("^M[0-9]+$")
    • NoTags - returns true if a node does not have any tags on it
    • InTagGroup - cheat, returns true if any tags in a tag group are applied to a node
    • IsStatus - returns true if a node has a given status
    • IsTodo - returns true if a node has an active status (the same as IsActive currently)
    • IsActive - returns true if the status of a node is an active status (IE not DONE)
    • IsTask - Syntatical sugar for the following: "!IsArchived() && IsTodo() && !IsProject()"
    • IsNextTask - Check if a headline has a NEXT action status. This is GTD support and uses the defaultNextStatus value and #+NEXT comment
    • IsBlockedProject - Check if this is a project heading and it DOES NOT have a child marked NEXT.
    • IsArchived - Check if a headline is in the archived state or not (in an archived file or has an ARCHIVE tag)
    • IsPriority - Check if the priority matches a specific value.
    • HasProperty - Returns true if the headline has the specific property
    • HasTable - Checks if the node contains a table.
    • HasDrawer - Checks if the node contains a drawer.
    • HasBlock - Checks if the node contains a block object.
    • IsRecord - returns true for a record heading (anything with a RECORD property); IsRecord("contact") asks about one collection
    • IsCollection - returns true for the container heading a collection files its records under
    • InCollection - InCollection("contact") is true for anything filed in that collection - the records, the container, and anything written under it
    • HasBacklinks - returns true when something else links at this heading; HasBacklinks(2) asks for at least two
    • BacklinkCount - how many links point at this heading, as a number to compare: BacklinkCount() == 0 finds the orphans
    • HasLinks - returns true when this heading links out at all
    • LinksTo - LinksTo(REGEX) is true when a link under this heading points at something matching - the target as written, its description, or the file and headline it lands on
    • HasBrokenLinks - returns true when a link under this heading resolves to nothing
    • MatchProperty - MatchProperty(NAME, REGEX) returns true if the property value matches the implied regex
    • MatchHeadline - Run an RE against each headline and check for a match
    • OnDate - OnDate("2026 30 01") (year, day, month) is true when the heading lands on that day in the agenda: a timestamp, SCHEDULED or DEADLINE on it, a repeat of one, a range spanning it, and on today also an overdue SCHEDULED and a DEADLINE inside its warning period or past it (the rules of GET /agenda)
    • Today - returns true if a node is scheduled for today
    • Yesterday - returns true if a node is scheduled for yesterday
    • ThisWeek - returns true if a node lands in the agenda on any day of the last seven, today included
    • IsDone - returns true if the node's keyword is a finished one (DONE and kin), by the keywords of its own file
    • InFile - InFile(REGEX) is true when the path of the node's file matches, its absolute path included: InFile("work")
    • MatchContent - MatchContent(REGEX) runs an RE over the headline and the text under it
    • HasScheduled - returns true if the node has a SCHEDULED date
    • HasDeadline - returns true if the node has a DEADLINE
    • HasTimestamp - returns true if the node has a plain timestamp of its own
    • HasAnyDate - returns true if the node has a SCHEDULED date, a DEADLINE or a timestamp
    • ScheduledPast - returns true if the SCHEDULED date is before today (today itself is not past)
    • DeadlinePast - returns true if the DEADLINE is before today: overdue, where a deadline of today is only due
    • ScheduledWithin - ScheduledWithin(N) is true when the SCHEDULED date falls between today and N days ahead, in calendar days
    • DeadlineWithin - DeadlineWithin(N) is true when the DEADLINE falls between today and N days ahead, in calendar days
    • HasClock - returns true if time has ever been clocked against the node
    • DaysOld - how many days ago the node's newest date (SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, CLOSED or timestamp) was, as a number to compare; -1 with no date
    • OlderThan - OlderThan(N) is true when the node's newest date is at least N days ago; never true for a node with no date
    • HasChecklist - returns true if the node's own text has checkboxes
    • ChecklistDone - returns true if the node has checkboxes and every one is ticked
    • ChecklistCount - how many checkboxes the node's own text has, as a number to compare
    • ChecklistLeft - how many of the node's checkboxes are still open, as a number to compare
    • IsHabit - returns true for a habit (a :STYLE: habit heading)
    • HabitStreak - how many times in a row a habit has been kept, as a number to compare: IsHabit() && HabitStreak() > 7; 0 once the run is broken
    • MissedHabit - returns true when a habit has gone longer since it was last done than its repeater allows

    Records

    Records — the contact book, and everything else worth a list

    What a record is

    A record is one org heading that stands for one thing. The heading is the thing's name, the property drawer holds its fields, the body under it is whatever anybody wanted to write about it, and the LOGBOOK drawer is the history of what has been changed.

    * John Doe
  :PROPERTIES:
  :RECORD:       contact
  :ID:           b1d1a2f4-3c58-4f2a-9a3d-0f9a1c7e51aa
  :ADDED:        [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
  :EMAIL:        john.doe@example.com
  :EMAIL_WORK:   jdoe@acme.example.com
  :PHONE_MOBILE: +1-555-555-0199
  :PHONE_HOME:   +1-555-555-0100
  :ADDRESS:      123 Main St, Cityville
  :BIRTHDAY:     1990-05-15
  :IMAGE:        [[file:images/contacts/john-doe.jpg]]
  :LINKEDIN:     https://www.linkedin.com/in/johndoe
  :END:
  :LOGBOOK:
  - Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
  - Added [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
  :END:

  Met at the 2019 conference. Allergic to shellfish.

    It is an ordinary org heading. Nothing here needs a special file, a special mode or a particular place to live: write that by hand in any file the server watches and the contacts tab has it a second later.

    The one thing that makes it a record
    :RECORD: contact

    That property, and nothing else. Its value names the collection the record belongs to.

    contact is just the collection this was built for first. equipment, cards, wine and synths are records in exactly the same sense, read and written by exactly the same code. A heading with no RECORD property is not a record wherever it sits, and a heading with one is a record even if it sits on its own in the middle of a project file — which is what makes a record identifiable without any knowledge of where it lives.

    Programmatically:

    in a query
    IsRecord(), or IsRecord("contact") for one collection
    over rest
    GET /records?type=contact
    in a file
    grep -n ':RECORD:' *.org

    Fields

    A field is a property named NAME or NAME_LABEL.

    The label is free text and is how a thing has more than one of something:

    :PHONE_MOBILE: +1-555-555-0199
:PHONE_HOME:   +1-555-555-0100
:PHONE_WORK:   +1-555-555-0150
:EMAIL:        john.doe@example.com
:EMAIL_WORK:   jdoe@acme.example.com
:EMAIL_OLD:    jd@previous.example

    Nothing has to be declared first, and a label can be anything: PHONE_BOAT works.

    How a field knows what it is

    What a field is is worked out from its name, so a client draws a field by its kind and never needs a list of property names. This is the whole reason a guitar pedal and a person can share one view.

    Name Kind What you get
    EMAIL, MAIL email a mailto: link
    PHONE, MOBILE, CELL, TEL, FAX, TELEPHONE tel a tel: link
    ADDRESS, ADDR postal the text, and a map link
    URL, WEBSITE, WEB, HOMEPAGE, LINK, BLOG, SITE url a link
    LINKEDIN, FACEBOOK, GITHUB, MASTODON, … social a link, built from a bare handle
    BIRTHDAY, BIRTHDATE, DOB, ANNIVERSARY, DATE date a date, and a place on the agenda
    IMAGE, PHOTO, AVATAR, PORTRAIT, PICTURE, LOGO image the picture itself
    anything else text the text as written

    Two suffix rules cover the way things other than people get named, because PURCHASE_DATE is as natural as DATE_PURCHASED:

    Ends with Kind Example
    _DATE date :BOUGHT_DATE: 2024-03-02
    _URL, _LINK url :MANUAL_URL: https://…
    _IMAGE, _PHOTO image :BOX_IMAGE: [[file:box.jpg]]

    The suffix list is deliberately short. EMAIL and PHONE are not in it, because EMAIL_WORK is far commoner than WORK_EMAIL and MOBILE as a suffix is the label on PHONE_MOBILE — reading that as a kind would throw the label away.

    To add a social network or change any of these, see socialNetworks and fieldOf in internal/app/orgs/records.go. The worg side says the same rules again in worg/src/records.ts so that an add form can show the right input before anything has been saved — change one and change both.

    Social handles

    A social field takes either form:

    :LINKEDIN: johndoe
:LINKEDIN: https://www.linkedin.com/in/johndoe

    A bare handle is turned into the network's own address where the address is predictable. A network with no known address keeps the handle as text rather than being sent somewhere guessed at.

    Dates

    Three ways of writing a yearly date are read, and all three are exact:

    Written Means
    1990-05-15 the 15th of May 1990
    <1990-05-15> the same, as an org timestamp
    --05-15 the 15th of May, year not known (vCard's form)

    A birthday with no year gets no age — it is not guessed at.

    The 29th of February is kept on the 28th in a year that has no 29th, on the agenda and on the card alike.

    The bookkeeping fields

    Property Written by Means
    RECORD you or us which collection this belongs to — the identity
    ID us a uuid, so links and other records can point here
    ADDED us when the record was first written down

    They are kept out of the field list a client is handed to draw, because they are about the record rather than about the thing.

    The history

    Every change made through the record endpoints — from worg, from the CLI, or by anything else calling them — prepends a line to the heading's LOGBOOK drawer:

    :LOGBOOK:
- Noted [2026-09-26 Sat 14:10]
- Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
- Renamed [2026-09-26 Sat 13:55] John Doe
- Added [2026-09-01 Tue 09:12]
:END:

    Newest first, the way org writes a logbook. Renamed records the name it had before. The clock entries org puts in the same drawer are left alone and ignored, and a line somebody writes by hand that does not match is skipped rather than being a parse error.

    Changes made by editing the file in a text editor leave no line, which is right: the history is of what was done through the tools, not a claim to know everything that ever happened to the heading.

    Collections

    A collection is every record sharing one RECORD value. It does not have to be declared — the first heading with :RECORD: wine: on it makes the wine collection exist — but a container gives new records somewhere to go, and gives the collection a name and an icon:

    * Contacts
  :PROPERTIES:
  :COLLECTION: contact
  :ICON:       👤
  :FIELDS:     EMAIL, PHONE_MOBILE, ADDRESS, BIRTHDAY, IMAGE
  :END:

** John Doe
   :PROPERTIES:
   :RECORD: contact
   …
    Property Means
    COLLECTION this heading is where records of that type are filed
    ICON one emoji, for the tab strip
    FIELDS the fields an add form should offer, in this order

    FIELDS is a suggestion, not a restriction: a record may carry anything at all. Where a collection has no FIELDS, the server offers whatever its records already use, commonest first.

    A record does not have to be a child of the container. Being a child is only how new ones get filed; a record moved elsewhere is still the same record, because the RECORD property travels with the heading.

    Only the first container found for a type is used, so that a second one somewhere else cannot quietly become the place things land.

    Changing a collection

    The Collections tab's Define button changes a collection's own heading: what it is called, its icon, and the fields its add form offers.

    Renaming the type is the one with consequences. The type is what every record in the collection says it is, so renaming it rewrites the RECORD property on all of them - in every file they happen to live in, not only under the container. The dialog says how many will move before it does it, and the answer says how many did.

    POST /records/collection/update
{ "Hash": "...", "SetType": true, "Type": "synthesiser" }
→ { "Ok": true, "Type": "synthesiser", "Moved": 4 }

    Two things it deliberately does not do. It writes no history line on the records that move - the change happened to the collection, not to the thing each record stands for, and a hundred identical logbook lines is noise rather than history. And it refuses when another collection already answers to the new name, because two containers for one type means new records land in whichever was found first.

    Duplicating an entry

    Copy the heading, change the name and the values, and delete the ID and ADDED lines. The server fills those in the next time it writes to the record, and two records with the same ID is the one thing that will confuse a link.

    ** Jane Roe
   :PROPERTIES:
   :RECORD:     contact
   :EMAIL:      jane@example.org
   :PHONE_WORK: +1-555-555-0123
   :BIRTHDAY:   --09-28
   :END:

   Knows everything about postgres.

    That is a complete, valid contact. Nothing else about a record is derived, so one written by hand in a text editor is exactly the same as one added from worg or from the terminal.

    Where records are used

    The Contacts tab

    contact records, with a search, a card per person, and the birthdays coming up in the next six weeks across the top. Adding and editing write the heading for you.

    The Collections tab

    The same view over any other collection, with a strip to pick between them and a button to start a new one.

    The Search tab

    Records are left out of search results by default, with a Records toggle in the filter bar to put them back. A contact matches "jane" as readily as the task about ringing her and is rarely the one being looked for; the toggle is remembered per browser.

    In a query of your own: !IsRecord() && !IsCollection().

    The Agenda

    Birthdays and anniversaries appear as all-day entries with a cake on them, and colour the day markers on the little calendars. They are worked out from the records rather than stored anywhere, so a birthday corrected in the file is right on the agenda immediately.

    The terminal
    orgs contact                     everybody, one line each
orgs contact find jane           the ones matching
orgs contact show jane           one, in full
orgs contact add                 asked for, field by field
orgs contact edit jane           change a field on one
orgs contact birthdays           who is next, and how long
orgs contact collections         what else is being kept

    Every one of them takes -type to work on another collection:

    orgs contact list -type equipment
orgs contact show -type equipment thinkpad
orgs contact add -type wine "Ch. Example 2019" -set REGION=Bordeaux -set YEAR=2019

    The endpoints

    Method Path Does
    GET /records find records: ?type=&q=&body=1
    GET /record/{hash} one record, with its notes and history
    GET /records/collections what collections exist, and where they live
    GET /records/fields the fields a type uses: ?type=contact
    GET /records/birthdays occasions in a window: ?from=&to=
    POST /record add one
    POST /record/update change one
    POST /records/collection start a collection
    GET /contacts /records?type=contact
    POST /contact /record with the type filled in

    On /record/update, every field named in Set is written and a field set to an empty string is taken off — the same rule the property endpoint follows. SetName with Name renames the heading; SetNotes with Notes replaces the body.

    Deleting a record is /delete with its hash, like any other heading: a record is a heading and nothing about it needs a delete of its own.

    Importing contacts from Apple, Google or Outlook

    Export a vCard (.vcf) file - Apple Contacts: select the people, File → Export → Export vCard; Google Contacts: Export → vCard - and import it:

    orgs contact import contacts.vcf -dry-run     what would happen, nothing written
orgs contact import contacts.vcf              add the new, fill in the known
orgs contact import contacts.vcf -mode skip   leave people already here alone
orgs contact import old.vcf -mode overwrite   the card wins where they differ

    or use the Import button on worg's Contacts tab, which shows the same plan before anything is written.

    A person is recognised by the card's UID (kept as VCARD_UID), then by any email address, then by name. The default, merge, never changes a value you have: it adds what is missing, files a second email beside the first (EMAIL_WORK_2), and tells you about a birthday or company that differs rather than writing it. Notes are appended only when they are new, so importing the same file again changes nothing. Photos are saved in images/contacts/ beside the org file and linked from IMAGE, and each record's history says the change came from the import.

    The card's fields become EMAIL, EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE, PHONE_HOME, FAX_WORK, ADDRESS_HOME, BIRTHDAY (--05-15 when the year is not known), ANNIVERSARY, COMPANY, DEPARTMENT, TITLE, NICKNAME, WEBSITE, LINKEDIN / TWITTER / GITHUB and the other networks, IM_SKYPE, RELATED_SPOUSE, and a custom label becomes the field's label (EMAIL_OLD_WORK). Categories become tags.

    How the writing works, and why

    Every write here is a line edit on the file rather than a rewrite of the parsed document. A record usually shares its file with a hundred others and with whatever else is in there, and writing the document back through go-org would reformat all of it — every drawer re-indented, every table reflowed — to change one phone number.

    Three things follow from that and are worth knowing before changing it:

    1. The drawers are found by walking the lines under the headline, not by asking go-org. A drawer written in column zero ends the headline's body as far as the parser is concerned and hoists the rest of the heading to the top of the document, where looking for it is guesswork.
    2. After any edit that changes how many lines a record has, its range is found again rather than adjusted. Keeping half a dozen indices in step through an insert, a delete and a rename is how off-by-one bugs get written.
    3. The property drawer is re-aligned after an edit. It is cosmetic and nothing reads the padding back — but a record is a text file somebody opens in an editor, and a ragged column is what "written by a program" looks like.

    Records And Collections

    A record is one heading that stands for one thing - a person, a laptop, a playing card - and keeps what is known about it in its property drawer. The heading is the thing's name, the properties are its fields, the body under it is whatever anybody wanted to write about it, and the LOGBOOK drawer is the history of what has been changed.

    What makes a heading a record

    One property, and nothing else:

    :RECORD: contact

    The value names the collection the record belongs to. contact is just the collection this was built for first; equipment, cards, wine and synths are records in exactly the same sense and are read by exactly the same code. A heading with no RECORD property is not a record, wherever it sits, and a heading with one is a record even if it sits on its own in the middle of a project file - which is what makes a record identifiable without any knowledge of where it lives.

    A contact

    * John Doe
  :PROPERTIES:
  :RECORD:       contact
  :ID:           b1d1a2f4-3c58-4f2a-9a3d-0f9a1c7e51aa
  :ADDED:        [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
  :EMAIL:        john.doe@example.com
  :EMAIL_WORK:   jdoe@acme.example.com
  :PHONE_MOBILE: +1-555-555-0199
  :PHONE_HOME:   +1-555-555-0100
  :ADDRESS:      123 Main St, Cityville
  :BIRTHDAY:     1990-05-15
  :IMAGE:        [[file:images/contacts/john-doe.jpg]]
  :LINKEDIN:     https://www.linkedin.com/in/johndoe
  :END:
  :LOGBOOK:
  - Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
  :END:

  Met at the 2019 conference. Allergic to shellfish.

    Fields, and how a field knows what it is

    A field is a property named NAME or NAME_LABEL. The label is free text and is how a thing has more than one of something: PHONE_MOBILE, PHONE_HOME and PHONE_WORK are three phone numbers, EMAIL and EMAIL_WORK are two email addresses. Nothing has to be declared first.

    What a field is is worked out from the part before the label, so a client draws a field by its kind and never needs a list of property names:

    Name Kind Drawn as
    EMAIL, MAIL email a mailto: link
    PHONE, MOBILE, CELL, TEL, FAX tel a tel: link
    ADDRESS, ADDR postal text, with a map link
    URL, WEBSITE, HOMEPAGE, LINK, BLOG url a link
    LINKEDIN, FACEBOOK, TWITTER, GITHUB, … social the network's own badge
    BIRTHDAY, ANNIVERSARY, and anything *_DATE date a date, and on the agenda
    IMAGE, PHOTO, AVATAR, PORTRAIT, PICTURE, LOGO image the picture itself
    anything else text as written

    The social names are a list rather than a rule because that is what they are; see socialNetworks below to add one. Everything else is a rule, so a collection of guitar pedals gets MANUAL_URL drawn as a link and BOUGHT_DATE drawn as a date without anybody teaching it anything.

    The bookkeeping fields

    Property Written by Means
    RECORD you or us which collection this belongs to - the identity
    ID us a uuid, so links and other records can point here
    ADDED us when the record was first written down

    They are kept out of the field list a client is handed, because they are about the record rather than about the thing.

    The history

    Every change made through the record endpoints prepends a line to the heading's LOGBOOK drawer:

    :LOGBOOK:
- Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
- Renamed [2026-09-26 Sat 13:55] John Doe
- Added [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
:END:

    Newest first, the way org writes a logbook. The clock entries org puts in the same drawer are left alone and ignored, and a line somebody writes by hand that does not match is skipped rather than being a parse error.

    Collections

    A collection is every record sharing one RECORD value. It does not have to be declared - the first heading with :RECORD: wine: on it makes the wine collection exist - but a container gives new records somewhere to go and gives the collection a name and an icon:

    * Contacts
  :PROPERTIES:
  :COLLECTION: contact
  :ICON:       👤
  :FIELDS:     EMAIL, PHONE_MOBILE, ADDRESS, BIRTHDAY, IMAGE
  :END:

    FIELDS is the order an add form should offer, not a restriction: a record may carry anything. Where there is no container the server offers the fields the records of that type already use, commonest first.

    Duplicating an entry

    Copy the heading, change the name, change the values, and delete the ID and ADDED lines - the server fills those in the next time it writes to the record, and two records with the same ID is the one thing that will confuse a link. Nothing else about a record is derived, so a record written by hand in a text editor is the same as one added from worg.

    Settings

    Aliases

    This is a command line tool helper. These are stored prefixes for long command lines that are repetitive. Aliases provide a means of shortening command lines to common patterns Ex: If you alway refile from a particular inbox file you can add something as follows to your orgs.yaml and tri will expand to the source from your inbox file:

      aliases:
    triage: ["ref" "-from" "inbox.org"]

    Any additional parameters will end up after the alias

    Attachments

    Files that belong to a heading - a pdf, a photograph of a whiteboard, a spreadsheet somebody sent - kept the way org-attach keeps them.

    attach:
  dir: "data"
  tag: "ATTACH"
  maxMb: 64

    Nothing here is required; every value above is the default.

    dir is where a heading's folder is made, relative to your first orgDir. A heading's folder is that directory, then the first two characters of its :ID:, then the rest of it - data/8f/3c1a20-.../ - which is exactly what emacs' org-attach does, so a database written by either is readable by the other.

    A heading can also name its own folder with a :DIR: property (or the older :ATTACH_DIR:), which is read relative to the org file that holds the heading. A heading with one of those does not need an :ID: and will not be given one.

    tag is put on a heading the first time something is attached to it, so that IsTask() && HasTags("ATTACH") finds everything with a file on it. Set it to an empty string to tag nothing.

    maxMb is the biggest single upload that will be taken.

    Clock Into Drawer

    When using the clocking features org can choose to dump clock data at the top of a heading OR produce the clock data into a drawer of your choosing. This option lets you choose the name of the drawer.

     clockIntoDrawer: "LOGBOOK"

    This defaults to LOGBOOK

    Column View

    #+COLUMNS: is org's way of saying "show me these properties as a table", and the part that makes it more than a table is that a column may ask for a total: %EFFORT{:} makes a project heading show the effort of everything under it.

    columns:
  default: "%ITEM %TODO %PRIORITY %TAGS %EFFORT{:} %CLOCKSUM"

    This is used only for a file that does not declare a #+COLUMNS: line of its own; one that does gets exactly what it asked for. The built-in default is org's own columns (%ITEM %TODO %PRIORITY %TAGS, without org's terminal widths so worg shares the screen between them) with %EFFORT{:} %CLOCKSUM added, because adding effort up is the thing this view exists for and nearly no file declares a columns line.

    Date Tree Formatting

    These options control the format of your datatree

     * 2006
 ** January
 *** 01 Monday
     * 2006
 ** 2006-01 October
 *** 2006-01-02 Friday
 *** 2006-01-02 Saturday
    dateTreeYearFormat:  "2006"
dateTreeMonthFormat: "January"
dateTreeDayFormat:   "01 Monday"

    Day Page

    The day page system has a number of settings that can be used to control its behaviour.

    The first and most important is where your daypages should be generated This should be a folder inside your orgDirs.

     dayPagePath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/worklog"

    Default Author

    Default author parameter to use when generating new templates

     author: "John Smith"

    Dnd Music Path and Spotify

    Where the DM screen's music finds tracks: subfolders are albums (play one whole), and zip, 7z, rar and tar archives are read as folders. Every audio format plays (the ones a browser does not know are turned into Ogg Opus with ffmpeg). Left out, it is music in the shared folder (dndSharedPath).

    On a Mac with the Spotify app, the music can also be Spotify's: orgs plays, pauses and skips it in the app (AppleScript, nothing to set up). Searching Spotify and listing your playlists needs Spotify's Web API: make an app at https://developer.spotify.com/dashboard (any name), add the redirect URI orgs shows (http://127.0.0.1:<port>/dnd/music/spotify/callback), put its client id here, and connect once from the music panel. No secret is kept: the sign in is PKCE, and its token is kept in your user config folder (orgs/spotify.json, readable by you only).

     dndMusicPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dnd/common/music"
 spotifyClientId: "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"
 spotifyRedirect: ""   # only to use another than http://127.0.0.1:<port>/dnd/music/spotify/callback

    Dnd Paths

    Where the dnd module looks for ruleset yaml modules (extra races, classes, backgrounds, spells or whole homebrew rulesets). The built in SRD data is always loaded first, these directories are merged on top.

     dndPaths:
   - "/Users/me/dnd/homebrew"

    When this is empty the module still searches <templatePath>/dnd, ./templates/dnd (or, when neither exists, the dnd folder built into the binary) and ~/.orgs/dnd.

    Dnd Session Path

    Where play session logs are written. Starting a session from a character sheet creates a dated org file in this folder and every roll you make and note you take is appended to it.

     dndSessionPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dndsessions"
 dndSessionTemplate: "dndsession.tpl"

    A relative path is taken relative to your first orgDir, and when the setting is left out entirely the folder is <orgDir>/dndsessions. Keep it inside an orgDir so that the sessions land in your org database and can be searched, agenda'd and archived like everything else.

    Dnd Shared Path

    A folder of tokens and pictures every map can use, beside each map's own: its tokens folder (subfolders are categories, tokens.json marks large ones) and its images folder, as a map's own are laid out. The map viewer lists a map's own first, then these.

     dndSharedPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dnd/common"

    A relative path is taken relative to your first orgDir; ~ is your home. Left out, there is no shared folder.

    Dnd Sound Path

    Where the DM screen's sound board finds sounds (subfolders are categories; zip, 7z, rar and tar archives are read as folders), and where a sound played from the web is kept, under cache/.

     dndSoundPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dnd/common/sounds"

    A relative path is taken relative to your first orgDir; ~ is your home. Left out, it is sounds in the shared folder (dndSharedPath), and without that there is none.

    Enabled Exporters, Plugins, Updaters

    The list of enabled exporter modules

    exporters:
   - name: "gantt"
   - name: "mermaid"
   - name: "mindmap"
   - name: "html"
     props:
       fontfamily: "Underdog"
   - name: "revealjs"
   - name: "impressjs"
   - name: "latex"

    The same is true for updaters and plugins. You must explicitly enable the modules you wish to be active in your orgs installation for them to be available.

    Encryption

    A heading tagged :crypt: whose body is ciphertext on disk - org-crypt's format exactly, so a heading encrypted here opens in emacs and one encrypted in emacs opens here.

    crypt:
  key: ""             # a gpg key id. Empty means symmetric.
  tag: "crypt"
  bin: ""             # the gpg binary, found on PATH when empty
  unlockSeconds: 0

    Nothing here is required and there is nothing to turn on: if gpg is installed, /crypt/* works. GET /crypt/config says which mode it is in and how many tagged headings are still sitting in the clear.

    What this protects, and what it does not. It protects the file - a backup, a sync folder, a git remote, a stolen disk - and every part of this server that reads org files without going through the crypt endpoints: the search index, grep, the link graph, every exporter. None of them had to be taught to keep a secret, because there is no secret in what they read.

    It does not on its own protect against somebody who can reach the server. That is a question about who holds the key, which is why the server holds no passphrase: one arrives with the request that needs it, is handed to gpg down a pipe, and is forgotten.

    key is the arrangement worth having on a server other machines can reach. With a public key the server encrypts with no secret at all and cannot decrypt, whatever is done to it - decryption needs the private key, which lives where you keep it. A heading can name its own with a :CRYPTKEY: property, as org-crypt does.

    unlockSeconds holds a passphrase in memory for that long so it does not have to be retyped. It is off by default and is a number rather than a switch because it trades the property above away: for those seconds, reaching the server is enough.

    Filters

    Filters provide a built in set of expressions that can be used to filter your org mode headings. By default adding to filters in your config file will add new or override internal ones. If you find the internal list to be annoying you can simply turn on

       noInternalfilters: true

    Which will cause the internal filters to not be defined.

        "filters":
    	"alltasks": "!IsProject() && IsTodo() && !IsArchived() && !InTagGroup('PERSONAL')",

    Filters can be used as a macro in a query using handlebars style notation in the query passed to the server.

        	"query": "{{ alltasks }}",

    Go Links

    Where orgs gocap files a link, and the heading it goes under. Both are optional; these are the defaults.

    server:
  goLinksFile:    "links.org"
  goLinksHeading: "Links"

    The file is relative to the first of the orgDirs. It is the built in GoLink capture template's target, so a capture template of your own called GoLink replaces the whole thing.

    Harper

    Harper for writing mode's checker, run on the server rather than in the browser: for phones and small tablets, which cannot spare the memory Harper needs in a page. worg's Harper settings pick where it runs.

     harper:
   enabled: true
   path: ""          # harper-ls; empty: on PATH, else downloaded once
   download: true    # fetch harper-ls from GitHub when there is none
   version: 2.13.0   # the release to fetch, the same as worg's

    orgs runs Harper's own language server, harper-ls, the first time a check asks for it, and keeps it running. With no path and none on the PATH, the release for this machine is downloaded from GitHub once into the user cache directory (orgs/harper-ls-<version>/). brew install harper or cargo install harper-ls work as well.

    Https Only

    Serve https and nothing else: the plain http listener on port is not started, so nothing - a login, a token, a note - can cross the wire unencrypted, even on this machine.

     server:
   allowHttps: true
   httpsOnly: true
   tlsport: 8010
   servercrt: "server.crt"
   serverkey: "server.key"

    It needs allowHttps and a certificate. orgs cert makes a self-signed one for this machine (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) at servercrt / serverkey. Off by default. orgs -local is not affected: it serves itself over http on the loopback, for one command.

    Image Path

    Images and fonts are secondary html requests when loading an html document in vscode. In addition, orgs may want to provide quick links et al.

     templateImagesPath: "<path>"
 templateFontPath: "<path>"

    This defaults to: ./templates/html_styles/images

    The images and fonts built into the binary are served behind these folders, so either may be left out; a file of the same name in the folder replaces the built in one.

    Inbox Triage and the Weekly Review

    What orgs triage, orgs review week and worg's Inbox and Weekly Review tabs treat as the inbox, as someday, and as waiting:

    review:
  inbox: 'InFile("(^|/)inbox[.]org$") && !IsArchived() && !IsDone()'
  somedayKeywords: [SOMEDAY, MAYBE]
  somedayTags: [someday, maybe]
  waiting: 'IsStatus("WAITING") && !IsArchived()'
  waitingDays: 7

    Every key may be left out; the values above are the defaults. Only the outermost heading a query finds is an item - the headings under it go wherever it goes.

    LanguageTool

    A LanguageTool server for the spelling and grammar checker in worg's writing mode. Turn it on and orgs starts one when the server starts and stops it when the server stops; worg then picks "The orgs server's own" in the checker menu, and its text goes to orgs and no further.

    From an unzipped LanguageTool (LanguageTool-stable.zip, needs java 17 or later):

     languageTool:
   enabled: true
   path: "~/tools/LanguageTool-6.6"   # holds languagetool-server.jar

    Or with docker, when path is empty:

     languageTool:
   enabled: true
   docker: "erikvl87/languagetool"    # the default image

    Everything else:

     languageTool:
   enabled: true
   port: 8082                          # where it listens (whisper has 8081)
   java: "java"                        # the java to run path with
   javaArgs: ["-Xmx2g"]                # for java, before -cp
   ngrams: "~/tools/ngrams"            # n-gram data: their/there, to/too
   extraArgs: []                       # for the server, or docker run
   url: "http://otherbox:8010"         # one orgs does not start

    Something already answering on the port is used rather than started again, so a LanguageTool you run by hand works too. url instead of enabled proxies to a server somebody else runs.

    Link Protocols

    Teach orgs your own link protocols. A link written [[jira:ABC-123]] (or jira://ABC-123) is then followed wherever you say: either to a real url, or by running a tool of yours on it.

    server:
  linkProtocols:
    jira:
      urlPrefix: "https://mycompany.atlassian.net/browse/"
    wiki:
      url: "https://wiki.me.com/pages/{{path}}/view"
    rdar:
      cmd: "mytool --open {{link}}"
    ticket:
      cmd: "tkt show"
      withProtocol: true
    • urlPrefix replaces the protocol: jira:ABC-123 becomes https://mycompany.atlassian.net/browse/ABC-123.
    • url splices the link into a url, for when it does not go at the end.
    • cmd is a command line to run. {{link}} is the whole link, protocol included; {{path}} is what comes after the protocol. With neither, the path is added as the last argument, or the whole link when withProtocol is set.

    The server works out where a link goes and hands it back (GET /links/resolve, and Open / Command on /links/all); a command is run by the client following the link, never by the server. orgs go follows them, and orgs go jira:ABC-123 follows a link typed straight in.

    Localhost Only

    Serve this machine and nothing else. The http and https listeners bind to 127.0.0.1 (and ::1) instead of every interface, and any request that does not come from this machine, or that names some other host in its Host header, is refused with a 403.

     server:
   localhostOnly: true

    The Host check is what stops another web site from reaching the server through your browser by pointing its own name at 127.0.0.1 (DNS rebinding). Names under .localhost are accepted. Off by default. A reverse proxy on the same machine still gets through, because its requests come from localhost, so leave this off or check the proxy if you mean to publish orgs through one.

    Logging

    TODO: Fill in information on orgs server logging

    Login Lifetime

    How long a login lasts before it has to be renewed. A Go duration, plus d for days and w for weeks; one hour when not set.

     tokenExpiry: "8h"     # or "30m", "7d", "2w", "1d12h"

    The command line renews its token on its own while the old one is still good, so this is mostly how long a token copied somewhere else stays useful - and how long a stolen one would.

    Marking Something Done

    Org does three things when a heading reaches a DONE keyword, and orgs used to do none of them: it stamps CLOSED:, it writes a line saying which state the heading moved from and when, and - if the heading repeats - it moves the repeating date on instead of leaving the keyword sitting on DONE forever.

    These are the same three switches org has, under the same names, and they can be set here, per file with #+STARTUP:, or per heading with a :LOGGING: property. The narrowest one that says anything wins.

    log:
  done: "time"          # none | time | note
  repeat: "time"        # none | time | note
  intoDrawer: "LOGBOOK" # a drawer name, or "" to write into the body
  states: false         # log every state change, not only done ones
  repeatToState: ""     # a keyword, "previous", or "" for the first one

    done is org's org-log-done. time stamps CLOSED: and writes a State "DONE" from "NEXT" [...] line; note does the same and keeps a note with it; none does neither. repeat is org-log-repeat and says what to write when a repeating date moves on - a repeat is not a closure, so no CLOSED: is stamped and any existing one is taken off.

    intoDrawer is org-log-into-drawer. A name puts the lines in that drawer; empty writes them into the body as a plain list, which is what org does by default. It defaults to LOGBOOK here rather than to nothing, because the agenda's habit graph is built by reading those lines back out of LOGBOOK and can only work if that is where they go.

    states logs every change between keywords rather than only the ones into a DONE state. Per-keyword cookies in a #+TODO: line say the same thing for one keyword and always win: NEXT(n!) logs a timestamp on entering NEXT whatever states says, and WAITING(w@) keeps a note.

    repeatToState is org-todo-repeat-to-state: which keyword a repeating heading goes back to. Empty means the first keyword of the sequence, which is what org does; previous means whichever state it was in before it was marked done; anything else is used as the keyword.

    At the file level, the #+STARTUP: words org defines all work: logdone, nologdone, lognotedone, logrepeat, nologrepeat, lognoterepeat, logdrawer and nologdrawer. So does #+PROPERTY: LOG_INTO_DRAWER, and a heading's own :LOG_INTO_DRAWER: or :LOGGING: property.

    Org Dirs

    A list of directories containing your org files

     orgDirs:
   - "/Users/me/dev/gtd"

    Orgs Keys

    There are 2 keys that will be generated if not provided by the system.

     orgJWS: "this key is used to sign the JWT"
 orgJWE: "This key is used to encrypt the JWT"
 orgSalt: "Appended to the per user salt to help with rainbow tables"

    Orgs Keystore

    Orgs has various ways of storing credentials. You need something to protect your data. By default the yaml keystore is just a file with usernames and creds. Other keystores are possible.

     keystore: "path to yaml file"

    A relative path is taken relative to this configuration file. Until you set this, the only account that exists is admin/default and the server says so loudly on every startup. Add accounts with orgs user add; see "Users and the keystore" for the whole of it.

    Refresh

    What the server keeps current by itself: source blocks with :schedule, dynamic blocks with :refresh, files with #+REFRESH: (see Keeping Blocks Current).

    refresh:
  every: 1h          # every file's dynamic blocks and #+TBLFM tables
  onExport: true     # exports read them refreshed, in memory (default)
  scheduled: true    # run :schedule blocks; needs babel.enable (default)
  tick: 30           # seconds between looks at what is due

    Running Source Blocks

    Orgs can run the #+BEGIN_SRC blocks in your files and hand the result back - what org calls babel. It is off unless you turn it on, and that is deliberate: a source block is somebody else's program, the server may be reachable from anything on your network, and noAuth is a setting people use. Reading your files and running them are different promises.

    babel:
  enable: true
  languages: ["python", "sh", "emacs-lisp"]
  timeout: 30

    languages is an allow list. Empty means every language orgs knows how to run, which is the shorter way of saying yes to all of them. The names are the ones you write after #+BEGIN_SRC, and the aliases go with them - allowing python allows py too.

    timeout is in seconds and is a wall clock limit on one block, so a loop that never ends costs half a minute rather than the server.

    commands replaces how a language is run, for an interpreter that is not on the path or one orgs does not know:

    babel:
  enable: true
  commands:
    python: ["/usr/local/bin/python3.12"]
    julia: ["julia", "--startup-file=no"]

    The code is handed to the command on standard input.

    Tag Groups

    Tag Groups are a cheater way of helping to make your queries less verbose. They are defined on the orgs server and provide a grouping of tags that you can query against.

    Here is a quick example. The following entry in your orgs.yaml allows you to treat PERSONAL as any of FAMILY ME or PERSONAL tags and WORK as any of WORK BACKLOG or PROJECTX tags in an InTagGroup('GROUPNAME') query.

    tagGroups:
 PERSONAL:
   - FAMILY
   - ME
   - PERSONAL
 WORK:
   - WORK
   - BACKLOG
   - PROJECTX

    By default ORGS turns on tag groups that I find most useful If you would like to avoid those being defined turn on the following flag

       noInternalTagGroups: true

    Here is a query that might be using that in your vscode org.todoConfigs: I am defining a Todo view that will have filename, status, headline and a few property columns of various sizes and it is looking for active todo's that are either WAITING or BLOCKED that are not tagged with any tags in my PERSONAL tag group.

      "Waiting": {
    "query": "!IsProject() && IsTodo() && !IsArchived() && !InTagGroup('PERSONAL') && (IsStatus('WAITING') || IsStatus('BLOCKED')",
    "display": {
      "filename": 15,
      "status": 10,
      "headline": 25,
      "properties": {
        "EFFORT": 5,
        "ASSIGNED": 15
      }
    }
  }

    The Agenda

    GET /agenda works out what lands on each day (repeaters, ranges, overdue items carried to today, deadline warnings). A deadline starts showing on today this many days before it is due, unless its stamp names its own warning period (<2026-10-20 Tue -3d>):

    agenda:
  deadlineWarningDays: 14

    Unset is org's own 14. 0 shows a deadline only on its day (and as overdue after it).

    Timesheets and Invoices

    Who orgs invoice and orgs timesheet bill, and how. Time belongs to a client by a :CLIENT: property (inherited, or a file's #+PROPERTY: CLIENT acme), else by a tag naming one of the clients below; RATE and BILLABLE: no are read the same way.

    invoice:
  from:
    name: "Ian Davids Consulting"
    address: ["12 Harbour St", "Halifax NS B3H 1A1"]
    email: billing@example.com
    taxId: "GST 123456789"
  currency: CAD
  rate: 120            # an hour, when nothing else says
  round: 15            # bill each line in quarter hours
  roundMode: up        # up, nearest or down
  taxRate: 15
  taxName: HST
  termDays: 30
  number: "{CLIENT}-{yyyy}{mm}"
  payment: ["Transit 00123  Account 4567890", "e-Transfer: billing@example.com"]
  theme: classic       # classic, modern, minimal, ledger, studio, letterpress
  accent: "#7a2e3a"
  paper: letter        # or a4
  logo: ~/brand/logo.png
  clients:
    acme:
      name: "Acme Corporation"
      contact: "Accounts Payable"
      address: ["1 Road Runner Way", "Phoenix AZ"]
      rate: 150
      currency: USD
      taxRate: 0
      aliases: [acmeco]

    Every key may be left out.

    Update Check

    GET /version tells a client (the vscode plugin, orgs version) which version this server is and whether a newer release is out. To know that, the server asks github for the latest release of ihdavids/orgs, at most every six hours. Turn the question off with:

     noUpdateCheck: true

    Use Project Tag

    How should we define a project. If this is set a project is defined as a heading with a :PROJECT: tag on it.

     useProjectTag: true

    If this is false then a project is defined to be a headline that has a child headline that has a status on it.

     * Project
 ** TODO This task makes it a project

    Users and the keystore

    Orgs keeps its users in a keystore file, named by keystore: in the server block of your config. A relative path is taken relative to the configuration file itself, the same way orgs_extensions.yaml is.

    server:
  keystore: "orgs_keystore.yaml"

    Until you set this, the only account that exists is admin/default, which is built in so that a fresh server can be logged into at all. The server prints a large warning on startup for as long as that is true.

    Users are added with the orgs user command, which reads the same config file the server does and writes the keystore beside it:

    orgs user add ian          # prompts for a password, twice
orgs user ls               # who exists, and how their password is stored
orgs user passwd ian       # change one
orgs user rm ian           # remove one

    The command edits a file on disk, so it has to be run on the machine the server runs on. It never talks to the server, and the server picks the change up the next time it starts.

    Administrators, and adding a user over the wire

    An account marked admin: true may add another account without having access to the server's disk, which is what orgs adduser does:

    orgs adduser dana          # prompts for a password, twice
orgs adduser sam -admin    # and this one may add users too

    Unlike orgs user, this talks to the server (POST /users/add), so it works from anywhere you can log in - and the new account works at once rather than at the next restart, because the server writes the keystore it is already holding.

    The password still never travels: the client makes a salt for the new user and sends ClientHash of the password under it, the same as a login does.

    Somebody has to be an administrator before any of this can be used, and the only account that starts out as one is the built-in admin. On a keystore written by hand, or by a version of orgs older than this, mark one on the server's own machine:

    orgs user admin ian        # ian may now add users
orgs user noadmin ian      # and now may not
orgs user add dana -admin  # added as an administrator

    Deleting org files from worg's Files tab is for an administrator, or for an account given that one permission (delete: true in the keystore):

    orgs user candelete dana   # dana may now delete org files
orgs user nodelete dana    # and now may not

    The server will not add a user when it is running on its built-in admin/default account, because that keystore has no file behind it and there would be nowhere to write. It says so rather than appearing to work.

    The file it writes looks like this - the password is a hash, and the salt is per user:

    creds:
  ian:
    password: "sha256:9f2c..."
    salt: "b3d1..."
logins:
  ian: 2026-09-30T11:04:17Z

    A password: written out as cleartext still works, so a keystore typed by hand does what it looks like it does - but the server names those accounts in its startup warning, and orgs user passwd is how to convert one.

    Passwords are never sent to the server. A client asks for the user's salt, hashes the password with it, and sends the hash; the server hashes that again with orgSalt before comparing. Set requireHashedLogin: true to refuse a login that arrives as cleartext at all - worth doing once every client talking to this server is new enough to hash, and noted in the startup warning until then.

    Voice Notes

    Recording and transcription. Orgs does not transcribe anything itself - it runs a go-whisper server, hands it the recording, and files what comes back as an org heading.

    Two settings turn the whole thing on: where the models are, and the port to run whisper on.

     voice:
   models: "/Users/me/whisper/models"
   port: 8081

    With those, orgs starts gowhisper itself when the server starts and stops it when the server stops. The binary is looked for on your PATH and in the usual places; bin says where it is when it is somewhere else. Something already listening on that port is adopted rather than started again, so a whisper you run by hand still works.

    Everything else has a default worth leaving alone:

     voice:
   models: "/Users/me/whisper/models"
   port: 8081
   bin: "/usr/local/bin/gowhisper"   # when it is not on PATH
   gpu: true                          # let whisper use the GPU
   args: []                           # anything else for its command line
   url: "http://otherbox:8081"        # a whisper orgs does not start
   model: "ggml-medium-q5_0"          # empty asks the server for its first
   language: "en"                     # empty lets whisper detect it
   dir: "audio"                       # recordings, relative to your orgDir
   timeout: 600                       # seconds to wait for a transcription
   maxMb: 64                          # the largest single recording
   tags:
     - "voice"
   target:
     type: "file+headline"
     filename: "inbox.org"
     id: "Voice Notes"

    model is the model id to transcribe with - when it is empty orgs asks the server what it has and uses the first, which is right for a machine with one model installed and wrong as soon as there are two.

    dir is where recordings are kept, relative to your first orgDir, so that a note's audio sits in the org database beside the heading that links to it. timeout is how long to wait for a transcription - a long take on a large model is minutes, not seconds.

    target is where a voice note is filed when the client does not say, and takes the same shape as a capture template's target. tags are put on every voice note heading.

    Writing Assistant

    An AI assistant in worg's writing mode: a pane down the left side of the editor to talk over the text with, ask for a rewrite of a passage, a critique, a synopsis or names, and put what comes back into the file. Three backends: Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. The keys are kept here, on the server; the browser talks only to orgs.

     assistant:
   backend: claude                  # the default: claude, chatgpt, gemini, or off
   claude:
     apiKey: "keyring:anthropic"    # or "env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", or the key
     model: claude-opus-5-5
     models: [claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-4-5]
     effort: medium                 # low, medium, high, xhigh, max
   chatgpt:
     apiKey: "env:OPENAI_API_KEY"
     model: gpt-5
     url: ""                        # an OpenAI-compatible server instead
   gemini:
     apiKey: "env:GEMINI_API_KEY"
     model: gemini-flash-latest
   local:                           # models on this machine, no key
     enabled: true
     runtime: llamacpp              # llamacpp, lmstudio or mlx
     model: "llamacpp:Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M"
     contextLength: 16384
     llamacpp: { variant: cpu }     # or vulkan, cuda-12.8 (Linux, Windows)
     servers:                       # others orgs only talks to
       - { name: vllm, url: "http://gpubox:8000/v1" }

    local runs models through llama.cpp, LM Studio or MLX (Apple Silicon), each installed from worg's Local runtimes dialog: llama.cpp from its GitHub release, LM Studio by its own installer (llmster, the headless LM Studio), MLX into a python environment of its own. Models come from Hugging Face (llama.cpp's .gguf files, MLX's safetensors; nothing that runs code) or LM Studio's catalogue. Models are named runtime:name. With tools (on by default) a model can read and edit the files the writer allows, as claudecode and ollama can. chatgpt and gemini go through the same OpenAI-compatible tool loop (Gemini through Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoint), with tools on unless tools: false; their url is an OpenAI-compatible base.

    A backend with no key is offered as not set up. backend: off turns the assistant off for everyone; disabled: true on one hides just that one. With no apiKey each reads its usual environment variable, and Claude also an ant auth login profile. A keyring key is stored with security add-generic-password -s orgs -a anthropic -w on a Mac. maxContext caps how much of a file is sent (characters, default 400000).

    Stories

    A writer's book, start to finish

    The writer and the book

    Owen Hale is writing his second novel, The Tidewater Clock: a harbour town in 1912, a clock that runs two minutes ahead of the sea, and the engine under the tower that explains why. He wants 85,000 words by spring. He writes in the mornings, aims for 500 words a day and takes Sundays off. The rest of the day goes on what every book also needs: an agent who wants three chapters by Tuesday, an editor's notes he is waiting for, research to chase, a reading at the library.

    He keeps all of it in org files: the manuscript, a compendium of the people and places in it, and a file of tasks about the book. One orgs server reads them, so the writing tools, the agenda, the clock and the inbox all see the same notes.

    This guide follows him through the life of the book: planning it, drafting it a day at a time, revising, running the business side the GTD way, and compiling a manuscript to send. Writing mode in the editing guide is the reference for every tool shown here.

    Where he writes

    Owen drafts in worg's writing mode, because that is where the writing tools are. He is not tied to it:

    • In VS Code, with vscode-org-everywhere, the manuscript is an ordinary org file: headings fold, links follow, and with the server it clocks in on the heading under the cursor and runs a focus timer in the status bar. worg's views (Files, the agenda, the clock report, the mind map…) open as editor panels, so the corkboard is a tab away from the text.
    • In Sublime Text, with Org Everywhere, editing stays in Sublime and the agenda, clocking, capture and refile go through the same server. Org: orgs Open Web UI opens worg on any of its views.
    • At the command line, orgs write and orgs recap read the same writing log worg keeps, and orgs focus runs the same pomodoro timer.

    Whichever he uses, a word counted, a task ticked or a clock started in one shows up in the others.

    Planning the book

    Chapters as index cards

    The corkboard shows each heading as a card: its synopsis, its status and its words against its target. Owen plans a part by writing the synopses first, then drags the cards until the order feels right. Moving a card moves the heading, with everything under it, in the file.

    Who is in which scene

    The storyline draws a line for each character through the scenes, joined where they meet, under an arc of each scene's tension. It shows Owen at a glance that Ada disappears after the second chapter, and that Part One climbs steadily but never drops to give the reader a breath.

    A character bible

    The compendium is a second org file of people, places and things, named by the manuscript's #+COMPENDIUM: line. Every property on an entry is a fact. In the text, every name it knows is underlined, and resting on one shows its card. It also catches mistakes without anyone reading for them: a fact written two ways, a character in a scene set before they were born.

    The entries are records too (RECORD: character), so orgs rec ls -type character and worg's Collections tab list the same cast.

    Names and places when he is stuck

    The Ideas pane in writing mode, and orgs write ideas at a prompt, make up characters, names, places, taverns, cultures, premises, complications and weather from word tables in the binary. Nothing is sent anywhere. -seed makes the same idea again, and -org prints it as a heading ready to capture.

    The structure the tools read

    None of this needs a special file format. The tools read ordinary org: keywords at the top, parts and chapters as headings, and properties on them. Emacs, VS Code and Sublime see the same text.

    #+TITLE: The Tidewater Clock
#+WORD_TARGET: 85000
#+COMPENDIUM: novel.compendium.org
#+CHAPTER_NUMBERS: words
#+SCENE_BREAK: * * *

* Part One: The Wrong Tide                                    :part:
** The Apprentice
:PROPERTIES:
:SYNOPSIS: Wren winds the harbour clock and finds it two minutes ahead of the sea.
:STATUS: Final draft
:WORD_TARGET: 3000
:END:
*** The tower at dawn
:PROPERTIES:
:POV: Wren
:CHARACTERS: Wren, Silas
:TENSION: 2
:WHEN: 1912
:END:
The harbour clock of Saltmere had kept the town's time for ninety years…
# NOTE: Silas's silence lands better if we see him check his own watch first

    The statuses are To do, First draft, Revised draft, Final draft, Done and Notes, each with its own colour on the cards and in the outline.

    A writing day

    The session

    Owen opens the manuscript in writing mode, goes full screen, and writes. The outline down the side shows where every chapter stands; the status line counts the words in the file, the words written this session and the words in the heading he is in. The checkers underline as he types (spelling and Harper's grammar run in the browser, offline), and his revision notes wait in the margin.

    The speller knows American spelling. Owen chose Add to dictionary on harbour, grey and his characters' names the first time they were underlined, and it has not complained since (the list is kept in his browser).

    Pomodoros, when they help

    On days the words come slowly, Owen works in pomodoros: orgs focus -work 50 -break 10 picks a task ("Finish The Breakwater"), clocks in, and calls a break when the time is up. The same session shows in worg's Focus tab, in VS Code's status bar if he is there, and as 🍅 32:10 Finish "The Breakwater" from orgs focus status in his terminal's status line. The time lands in the task's logbook, so the week's recap knows where the hours went.

    How the week is going

    Every count the editor makes goes into the writing log on the server. The goals dialog (the chart button on the writing bar, or a click on the status line) reads it: today, this week and this month against his goals, his streak, and a heatmap of every day he has written.

    orgs write shows the same numbers at a prompt, and orgs write -short prints one line (✍ 437/500 · 19d) for a status bar. Goals are set with orgs write goals -daily 500 -weekly 3000 -monthly 12000 -rest 1, or under Goals and look in the dialog.

    Revising

    Notes, snapshots and what changed

    When he finishes a pass, Owen leaves notes for the next one as # NOTE: lines under the paragraph they are about. They are org comments, so they are in the file for him and never in the book. Before a big rewrite he takes a snapshot of the chapter from its section dialog in the outline (or with orgs write snapshot 'The Apprentice' -title 'Before the second pass'). Afterwards, Show changes since in the Revision menu lights what he put in and strikes through what he took out.

    The prose in numbers

    The Prose pane reads the whole manuscript: sentence lengths, readability by chapter, how much of each scene is dialogue, and the words worth a second look. Each one opens to the places it is used.

    What needs more than orgs

    Some tools in writing mode call out to something else. They are worth knowing about, and the editing guide says how to set each one up:

    • The assistant, scene synopses and the continuity check ask a language model: Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini with a key, or a model running on the server under Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio or MLX (orgs models). It sees only the file, and only when asked.
    • Dictation is transcribed by whisper on the server.
    • orgs lint runs the same grammar checker at the command line, and needs harper-ls on the server (or LanguageTool).
    • The thesaurus looks words up online.

    The business of the book

    Owen runs the rest of his writing life the GTD way, in book.org beside the manuscript: a heading for the draft, one for the agent and editor, one for research, one for admin, and two habits ("Write 500 words", "Walk before writing").

    • Capture: an idea for the last chapter at 11 at night goes into the inbox (orgs cap, worg's c, VS Code's capture), not into the manuscript.
    • Clarify: the inbox is emptied one item at a time with orgs triage or worg's Inbox: refile it, schedule it, or let it go.
    • Organise: the agent's deadline is a DEADLINE, the editor's notes a WAITING task, the reading an appointment on the agenda.
    • Reflect: on Friday, the weekly review walks what is stuck, waiting or stale. orgs recap is the week on one page, words included, ready to paste to his writing group.
    • Engage: in the morning, orgs dash says what is due before he opens the manuscript and forgets everything else.

    Compiling the manuscript

    When Part One is ready for the agent, Owen opens Compile from the writing bar, picks the headings to include, and chooses a format. The research notes start out unticked, because they are tagged :noexport:. His file is not changed.

    The same books come from the command line:

    orgs export -f manuscript novel.org -style shunn -out tidewater.docx
orgs export -f epub novel.org -theme literary -out tidewater.epub
orgs export -f manuscript -list-themes      # modern, novel, reader, shunn

    The Word manuscript is the one to submit: chapters numbered as #+CHAPTER_NUMBERS says, scenes broken with #+SCENE_BREAK, a title page from the keywords. The PDF is typeset by Typst (it needs typst on the server) with the article, report or notes template. It makes a good reading copy, but it is laid out like a document, not a book.

    Taking these pictures again

    The pictures come from their own notebook, docs/screenshots/writer: the manuscript, its compendium, book.org and an inbox. A month and a half of writing log, the goals and a snapshot are posted when the server starts.

    cd tools/screenshots
node capture.mjs -story writer                    # every picture here
node capture.mjs -story writer writer-goals       # just the ones named

    The shots are in tools/screenshots/stories/writer.mjs.

    An engineer's week at the command line

    Who this is about

    Marcus is a backend engineer on a payments team. He lives in a terminal and an editor, and he runs his week on two simple rules:

    • Getting Things Done. Anything that wants his attention goes into an inbox first and is decided about later. Every project always has one NEXT action. Once a week he reviews the lot, so he can trust it.
    • Pomodoros. He works on one next action for 25 minutes, then takes a five minute break. Every fourth break is fifteen minutes. Interruptions are written down, not acted on.

    This page follows him from Monday to Friday. Every step is an orgs command against one orgs serve, so his terminal, his editor, worg on his phone and the menu bar on his laptop all show the same clock, the same inbox and the same pomodoro.

    The pictures were taken against his notebook, kept in docs/screenshots/engineer-cli (node capture.mjs -story engineer-cli in tools/screenshots takes them again). The three borrowed from The command line, in pictures (the dashboard, the standup and the recap) show the smaller demo notebook those pages use.

    The shape of the week

    Monday is for deciding: the weekly review, then a plan for the week. Tuesday to Thursday are for making things. Friday is for looking back. The same short loop runs under every day: a glance in the morning, the standup, pomodoros, interruptions captured as they come, and the inbox emptied before he leaves.

    The loop he keeps

    GTD has five steps, and each one has a command:

    Step What it means orgs
    Capture get it out of your head, now orgs cap, or capture from the editor
    Clarify what is it, and is it mine to do? orgs triage
    Organise put it where it will be seen orgs ref, orgs sched, orgs todo, orgs kanban
    Reflect keep the system worth trusting orgs dash, orgs review week, orgs recap
    Engage do the next action, 25 minutes at a time orgs focus, orgs plan

    The inbox in the middle is what holds the loop together. A capture never asks where something belongs, so it takes seconds. Triage asks later, one item at a time.

    Setting it up once

    Marcus set this up once, the week he started.

    One template that files into the inbox

    An inbox is the top level of any file called inbox.org (the review.inbox setting can make it a query instead). His capture template files there, so the editor, worg and the command line all capture the same way:

    server:
  captureTemplates:
    - name: "Inbox"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file"
        filename: "inbox.org"
      template: |-
        :PROPERTIES:
        :CREATED: {{now}}
        :END:
        {{CONTENT}}

    The template is the body. At the command line the headline is its own box, and the keyword goes in it: orgs cap Inbox -head "TODO Call the bank".

    Saved queries, and a watch
    orgs q save next 'IsStatus("NEXT") && !IsArchived()'
orgs q save waiting 'IsStatus("WAITING") || IsStatus("BLOCKED")'
orgs q watch waiting -left      # tell me when something stops waiting

    Saved queries are shared with worg and the editors, so the same next list is in every one of them.

    The pomodoro where he can see it

    The timer runs on the server, so anything can show it. He has it in his tmux status line and in the macOS menu bar:

    # ~/.tmux.conf
set -g status-right '#(orgs focus status)'
set -g status-interval 5

# SwiftBar (brew install swiftbar); use xbar's plugins folder for xbar
orgs focus bar install "$HOME/Library/Application Support/SwiftBar/Plugins"

    orgs focus status prints one line, 🍅 12:31 Implement idempotency keys, and nothing when no session is running. The menu bar's menu can stop the session, add five minutes, skip to the break, and open worg's Focus tab.

    His editors

    Marcus writes code in VS Code and keeps Sublime Text for long notes. Both talk to the same server; see His editors, all week below.

    Monday morning: the weekly review

    The review comes first, before email, while the week is still his.

    What wants a decision

    orgs review lists everything that needs deciding, each check with a sentence saying what to do about it: projects with no next action, deadlines nobody scheduled, things waiting on other people, time clocked against something still open, notes nothing links to. A check that finds nothing prints a green line. "No NEXT actions untouched in a month" is worth hearing too.

    Walking it: the review, step by step

    orgs review week turns the list into seven steps, in GTD's order. Each step is the same screen, one item and one key per decision, and u takes the last decision back:

    1. Empty the inbox. The triage screen, below.
    2. Projects with no next action. The Developer portal has two open tasks and nothing marked NEXT. Marcus presses 1 and the guide becomes its next action.
    3. Waiting for. Read access to the production replica has waited nine days. c chases it, and the note goes into the item's logbook so the count starts again.
    4. Last week's time. Clocked against planned, by project and by tag. There is nothing to decide here, only something to look at.
    5. Stale scheduled items. Scheduled days ago, and nothing has happened since. Reschedule them, or admit they aren't happening.
    6. The someday pile. Keep, promote, schedule or drop.
    7. Done. The review is recorded, and the next one's first screen says how long ago this was.

    The step he is on is kept on the server, so he can stop halfway, get coffee, and finish it in worg's Weekly Review tab on his phone.

    Emptying the inbox: triage

    Step 1 is orgs triage, and he runs it on its own most evenings too:

    "Ask Priya why the staging deploy took 40 minutes" takes him less than two minutes, so he does it and presses d. "Update the on-call rota for November" gets s fri. The replay-traffic idea gets r, filed under Search reindex as something to bring up at the architecture review.

    Monday afternoon: planning the week

    The board and the chain

    orgs kanban shows his Sprint board, a saved query grouped by keyword. H and L move a card between columns, which changes its keyword. A board is only a query and a layout, so it never goes stale.

    Then he checks the order things have to happen in. Load testing waits on the idempotency work (AFTER: idempotency-keys), and the rollout waits on load testing:

    orgs deps

    One blocked chain, and he already knew about it: the idempotency keys are his priority this week. For projects measured in days rather than hours, orgs gantt <saved query> -crit draws the same chain as a chart with the critical path marked (see Schedules).

    Every morning

    The glance: the dashboard

    At nine he opens a terminal and runs orgs dash: today's appointments and the line where now is, what is late, the habits, the inbox, what his watches found, and the command for each card that wants something. orgs dash -w keeps it on a spare screen, redrawn as things change.

    The standup, ready to paste

    Five minutes before the standup:

    orgs standup -copy

    It lists what he finished since the last working day (Friday's, on a Monday), what he has clocked, what is on today and what is in the way, written in Slack's markup and put on the clipboard. He pastes it into the team channel and says the same thing out loud.

    Blocking the day

    After the standup he gives the morning to the one task that matters and puts the take-home review after his 1:1:

    orgs plan idempotency 10:00-12:00
orgs plan take-home 15:00-16:00
orgs plan                          # the day, and what is left

    A block is only a time range on the task's SCHEDULED. Emacs and every agenda see the plan, and worg's day planner shows the same blocks. Drag one there and orgs plan agrees.
